subsections.label: Kandla facility expansion
points: Company believes in building its own capabilities consistently; developing a new facility at Kandla on ~7 acres of land near Kandla Port on a 30-year lease basis.
Facility expected to be commissioned within approximately 9-10 months; strategic proximity to the port (~2.5 km) offers significant logistics advantage.

Kandla facility will substantially enhance capability to manufacture ultra-large tanks (diameter 8-9 meters, length up to 60 meters, weight up to 500 tons), opening opportunities for LNG mega storage tanks, large-scale aerospace tanks, and other high-value large-format products currently difficult to execute at the existing facility.

subsections.label: Keg manufacturing capacity
points: Installed keg capacity is ~300,000 kegs/year; presently utilized at about one-third of capacity.
Full utilization expected as customers (Heineken, AB InBev, Molson Coors and other breweries) complete initial trials and move to full-scale ordering in coming years.

Building and infrastructure allow scaling up to 1 million kegs/year without major machinery constraints, aligned with the company's aspiration in the ~4-5 million kegs/year global replacement demand market.

subsections.label: Geographic revenue mix strengthening
points: Revenue contribution from North and Central America increased from 14% (FY25) to approximately 26% (FY26), driven by LNG terminal-related orders, aerospace orders, disposable cylinder exports, and LNG-related shipments, despite tariff-related headwinds.
European market revenue contribution continued to improve because of opportunities in LNG and Cryo-Scientific areas.
Middle East, Southeast and Far East revenue improved from 8% (FY25) to 10% (FY26) despite global disturbances in the region.
Demand fundamentals remain robust across geographies; the primary constraint continues to be logistics and supply chain challenges rather than a slowdown in market demand.
Global economic environment marked by geopolitical issues, evolving trade dynamics, energy transition, and tariff pressure reshaping capital allocation and infrastructure investment calculus.

India's growth supported by robust domestic demand, relatively lower inflation, income tax and GST rate reductions, and accommodative monetary policy; manufacturing and services drove supply-side performance, though net exports weighed on GDP as imports increased.

Prolonged West Asian conflict poses significant risk to India as a major energy importer — exposure to sustained oil price increases, fiscal pressure from fuel subsidies, and rupee depreciation; with ~38% of remittance inflows from Gulf economies, labor market disruptions there could strain forex reserves.

India's macroeconomic buffers provide some insulation, but energy diversification, fiscal prudence, renewable energy exploration, and trade liberalization through FTAs remain critical to sustaining resilience.

subsections.label: Vendor and inventory management
points: Inventory remains totally in control according to management, despite rising contract assets from project orders.
Because of the growing order book, the company is paying vendors on a timely basis, and vendor payments are described as very strong, with no problems on the material/sourcing side.

subsections.label: Competitive positioning
points: Cryo-Scientific and cryogenic engineering space has very few global players (2-3 suppliers), positioning INOX among a select set of capable competitors.

LNG fuel tank segment: China-origin competition considered limited due to PESO regulatory barriers (no PESO-approved Chinese facility) and the need for customized tank design per truck dimensions plus ongoing maintenance/service support (company has placed personnel at Tata and Ashok Leyland conveyor lines) — services Chinese suppliers reportedly cannot match.
Keg segment: only 2-3 manufacturers in Europe and 1 in China; INOX positioned as the second player in Asia, competing for share of the ~4-5 million kegs/year global replacement demand.

Highview Power liquid air energy storage: INOX's cryogenic tank contribution is estimated at 20-25% of total capital cost of such a storage plant; company also offered non-cryogenic equipment for Highview's requirements to expand scope beyond pure cryogenic supply.
Disposable/industrial refrigerant cylinders: quota system among refrigerant gas manufacturers limits overall market growth; company targeting new/under-served US customers to gain share.

subsections.label: New business development
points: Company's vision described as 'remaining historically futuristic,' continually evolving into newer advanced business areas.
Data center cooling MoU with a European company represents an early-stage strategic move into a new advanced application area for cryogenic technology.
Kandla facility investment represents a strategic capability-building initiative to enable execution of ultra-large, high-value format products not currently possible at existing facilities.
Distribution partnerships established in Germany, Poland, and United Kingdom provide direct commercial access to the European keg market, supporting international market expansion strategy.

subsections.label: Macro and geopolitical risks
points: Ongoing West Asian conflict creating headwinds through elevated energy prices, shipping disruptions, and weakened investor confidence globally.

India remains exposed as a major energy importer to sustained oil price increases, fiscal pressure from fuel subsidies, and rupee depreciation from a prolonged West Asian conflict; ~38% of India's remittance inflows originate from Gulf economies, so labor market disruptions there could further strain forex reserves.
Tariff pressure (notably US tariffs) and global supply chain reconsideration add uncertainty requiring caution and precision in navigating the business.

Management noted the war has slightly impacted the Middle East region, but diversified product/geography exposure is expected to compensate for any regional plus/minus impact, limiting overall effect.

subsections.label: Operational / segment-specific risks
points: LNG truck segment adoption has faced near-term challenges despite long-term optimism.
Working capital/contract assets are rising structurally as the project order mix increases (now >60% of order book vs ~30% previously), pressuring operating cash flow relative to sales growth.

Potential import competition risk from Chinese LNG tank suppliers was raised by an analyst; management assessed this risk as limited due to PESO regulatory requirements and service/customization advantages, though acknowledged some initial Chinese tanks had previously entered India.
Beverage keg segment revenue was roughly flat despite 31% volume growth due to product mix shift toward smaller/lower-value kegs and de-bundling of the 'sphere' component.

subsections.label: FY27 outlook
points: Strong order backlog, expanding global customer base, growing share of high-value engineering products, and capacity augmentation at Kandla collectively place the company in a comfortable position to sustain and accelerate growth trajectory into FY27.
Company remains focused on operational excellence, innovation-led growth, and delivering long-term stakeholder value.
Revenue target for FY27 is around INR1,600 crores/INR1,632 crores base growing at 18-20%, with quarterly revenue and order booking (INR450-500 crores/quarter) expected to scale in similar fashion.
Despite regional war-related impact in Middle East, company does not expect much overall effect given diversified product and geographic exposure.

LNG segment expected to grow faster than standard products due to LNG's cost/clean-fuel advantages, though quarter-to-quarter order lumpiness is expected to persist; yearly targets expected to be met or improved.
Cryo-Scientific Division expected to grow substantially in coming years given limited global competition and strong execution track record.
Working capital/contract assets expected to remain elevated as project orders continue to grow as a share of the order book.

key_takeaways: Q4 and full year FY 2026 reflected a strong operational momentum for INOX India with healthy revenue of INR1,632 crores, growth across key business segments.

Our EBITDA margin is 23.8% for FY '26, remained in line with or better than the guidance provided earlier, demonstrating disciplined execution despite headwind arising from the U.S. tariffs, global logistic disruption, and geopolitical uncertainties.
During Q4, we received a significant aerospace order from a leading U.S. based private space company with a total order value of approximately INR200 crores.
Transport tanks also achieved a significant milestone in FY 2026 with annual sales exceeding 300 transport tanks and semi-trailers for the first time in the company's history.
One of the most significant highlights was the order received from the Cochin Shipyard... This is a landmark order for INOX India and marks our entry into the marine LNG ecosystem.

We have now secured approvals and active orders from 3 of the world's leading global breweries, namely Heineken, AB InBev and Molson Coors, collectively representing more than 40% of the global beer market volumes.
We are developing a new facility at Kandla... expected to be commissioned within approximately 9 to 10 months... will substantially enhance our capability to manufacture ultra large tanks.

As of 31st March, 2026, our order book stood at INR1,514 crores, providing strong revenue visibility for the coming quarters of this approximately 63% is from exports and 37% from the domestic market.

The key takeaway is that demand fundamentals remain robust across the geographies. The primary constraint continued to be logistics and supply chain related challenges rather than the slowdown in the market demand.

subsections.label: Revenue & EBITDA drivers
points: Strong performance driven by higher CUF, revenue contribution from BESS operations and renewable capacity additions.

Renewable energy portfolio delivered ~88-89% EBITDA margin while BESS business recorded ~82% margin; difference primarily because the cost of power purchased for charging batteries is accounted for within operating expenses, so blended margin should be viewed in that context.

Ex-BESS EBITDA margin of 91% for the quarter is broadly in line with the ~88-91% range seen across the last four quarters of the previous year (except Q2 FY26/Sept'25 at 88-89%), reflecting seasonality; margin could vary further depending on project profitability, with FDRE projects potentially improving margin due to healthier realizations versus plain solar bids.

Ex-BESS EBITDA growth (~20%) mainly driven by CUF improvement (28.5% to 30.9% YoY) and continuous repowering of existing plants; curtailment (only from state-based projects) contributed less than 1% impact on overall revenue.

subsections.label: Capital allocation
points: Successfully completed QIP, giving flexibility to prepone capex for under-construction projects and deliver better return economics.
Asset base expanded significantly following commissioning of new assets and batteries.

BESS module/component purchasing being done opportunistically; ~80% of non-module capex (transmission line, substations, plant infrastructure) done for certain projects, with module purchase timed to take advantage of lower Chinese module prices before a 6% China export tax kicks in from January.
Company minimizing interest during construction by balancing opportunistic buying against IDC costs.

subsections.label: BESS cost trends
points: Initial BESS orders were at lower prices; lithium carbonate is a volatile commodity and China supply-demand economics could push future BESS costs up, but not by a large percentage (5-10%), and remains within budgeted cost.
PCS component coming in lower than budgeted cost; building at substations where line/substation infrastructure already exists also helps save cost.
Cost figures do not factor in hedging gains; company has hedged >$300 million with locked-in rates of $89-93, creating a positive bias toward reducing costs from dollar movement.

subsections.label: PPA progress
points: Balance ~1,200 MW of projects for which PPAs are yet to be signed are progressing well and expected to be signed soon.
Hybrid PPA signed this quarter involved offering 1 hour of battery as a change to standard configuration; second signed project (at INR6.28/unit) had no change in configuration.
ACME Marigold LOA project (Northeast state, via REMCL) delayed due to Supreme Court proceedings on railway open-access status; bank guarantee already given, expected to be signed very shortly.

subsections.label: Bid pipeline & market structure
points: SECI has consolidated bids and introduced a rule not to release a bid until there is a firm commitment on power requirement, reducing bid-to-PPA cycle time but also reducing near-term bid quantum.

Expected large upcoming bid categories: midterm contracts, long-term peak power, RTC FDRE, CFD (contract for difference) related to peak power, and state bids (e.g., Bengal post-elections, Gujarat, Maharashtra).
Format of bids is shifting: pure solar bids are disappearing; wind bids continue; battery-related bids will be the focus except for pump-storage projects.
Rightsizing of battery bids is underway due to delays in VGF-based state projects, causing temporary volume realignment even as demand drivers remain strong.
Each megawatt of round-the-clock/FDRE power is roughly equivalent to 4 megawatts of solar in terms of impact, per Chairman.

subsections.label: Merchant route conversion (CERC)
points: CERC's free exit option for merchant-route conversion for parties lacking a signed PPA is viewed positively as it should free up connectivity where PPAs are not signed, benefiting ACME given most of its PPAs/LOAs are on track to be signed.
This freed-up connectivity also helps CTU plan future connectivity better and benefits batteries since nighttime capacity tied to Right of First Refusal connectivity may also become available.

Company demonstrated large-scale FDRE through battery operations by charging/discharging batteries in a 15-minute slot interval.

Secured short-term BESS contracts during the quarter (>INR1,400 crores of revenue for partial FY27 BESS commissioned capacity); will keep participating and tying up more contracts for full BESS capacity in FY27.
Operational performance for batteries better than design expectation across round-trip efficiency, depth of discharge, state of health and plant availability.

subsections.label: Open capacity & contracting plan
points: Target is to have zero open (non-PPA) capacity by end of the year; only a 300 MW plant (scaling to 300x4) currently remains uncontracted.

Chairman clarified that every year, at least 10 GWh of battery will remain exposed to the merchant market before moving into PPA the following year; company does not expose itself to the merchant market for the battery for the next 25 years, but the plan for the next 5 years is to keep 10-12 GWh available for the short-term power market.
Capex is allocated toward PPA in terms of final destination even though first year of operation may be merchant.
Currently contracted almost all (~90%) of the 20 GWh target battery capacity; wherever PPA is not signed, battery is not counted as needing to be ordered.

subsections.label: Locked-in revenue & realization
points: INR1,400 crores locked-in revenue represents ~70-80% of the 10 GWh targeted merchant capacity for the year; remaining 20% still to be contracted, which would push overall revenue higher than INR1,400 crores if tied up.
Realizations for contracted capacity range INR8-10/unit depending on month and contract volume, based on bids on the DEEP portal and HP-TAM markets (publicly available ranges).

Contract tenures are typically under 1 year (mostly 6-9 months); midterm bids of 5-year contracts are emerging from states but company currently has only one uncontracted project available for such an offer.

Management believes the INR1,400 crores+ run-rate can be assumed for financial modeling over the next 2-3 years, potentially even higher, given current PPA pipeline; beyond 2-3 years it is dependent on market dynamics, new PPA wins and profitability.

subsections.label: BESS demand & pricing outlook
points: Market is nascent: pure merchant BESS supply is not expected to be very high because most players (ACME, Adani, etc.) plan to put capacity into long-term PPAs rather than operate merchant plants for 25 years.

Demand-side trust in battery reliability is growing state-by-state as states (currently ~6-7 states buying) previously met peak needs via costlier thermal power; new bids will increasingly factor in BESS supply once trust builds.
All battery/FDRE/peak-power connectivity currently being allocated is co-located with solar; a 'sync' battery addition without solar has not yet been seen because of excess solar in the grid.

Duck curve phenomenon (driven by rooftop, KUSUM, B2B solar additions) is expected to push peak power/evening-morning demand higher; Chairman estimates current peak demand at ~300 GWh with potential progression to 400-500 GWh, and in a positive scenario, up to 1 TWh.

Management does not see slowdown in pricing over next 3 years despite El Nino-related state buying dynamics, monsoon effects, hydropower return, or air-conditioner penetration factors; anticipates continued strong demand due to duck curve dynamics, and hydro power (which runs 24/7) cannot itself meet peaking demand.

Sodium battery technology progress in China/globally (e.g., cold-climate deployment in Europe) could offer cost positives and extend battery life closer to pump-storage timelines, potentially improving future peak-power profitability dynamics.
Pump storage is most competitive for 8-hour solutions but will take at least 3-4 years to come online; gas peaker and pump storage are the other two short-term peak solutions besides battery.

subsections.label: Sector demand drivers
points: Strong start to FY27 supported by expanding economic activity, delayed monsoons, and elevated cooling demand, with India aggregate electricity demand growing 8.8% YoY to 485 billion units and peak power demand hitting a new all-time high of 271 GW in Q1 FY27 (~270 GW in July 2026).

subsections.label: Policy developments
points: MNRE extended commissioning deadline for Open Access and Net Metering renewable projects to 31 December 2026, ensuring smoother transition to cell-level List-II compliance and providing greater flexibility to evaluate/commission merchant BESS projects co-located with solar generation.

Ministry of Power extended graded ISTS waiver benefits for projects delayed due to transmission readiness, for PPAs signed up to 30 June 2026, reducing financial risk for developers and providing clarity for discoms, also benefiting offtakers where GNA availability is delayed.

CTU has begun granting BESS connectivity through Right of First Refusal route, expected to accelerate BESS deployment while strengthening grid reliability and enabling better participation during evening peak demand.

New circular allows use of surplus renewable generation (from solar) to charge batteries in state-based projects, which management plans to use to reduce/eliminate curtailment going forward; also pursuing regulatory changes to align state curtailment provisions with central grid provisions.

Data center demand seen as second-biggest driver of renewable/peak power demand after EV; SECI is also creating a platform to work with data centers as an aggregator/customer, which ACME would participate in if concretized.

subsections.label: ACME Suryodaya BESS fire incident
points: Media reports incorrectly suggested the fire originated within the battery system; detailed technical root cause analysis confirmed the incident was caused by an electrical short circuit in the AC cabling between the transformer and power conversion system, resulting in a localized fire and equipment shutdown.

No damage to any battery systems or other equipment at the site; incident was contained by already-deployed safety measures across detection, suppression and containment (AI-enabled video analytics for early fire detection, arc-flash sensors within PCS panels, additional aerosol-based fire suppression systems inside PCS enclosures, enhanced fire barriers between electrical equipment, improved cable protection).

Company has long-term warranty for BESS and other equipment from suppliers, and has built an in-house 50-member EPS BESS team responsible for overall integration including installation, commissioning and operation of BESS.

subsections.label: GNA / transmission connectivity delay
points: SJVN FDRE project (Heergarh, Bikaner II) has BESS already commissioned, but GNA (transmission) connectivity is scheduled only for next year (around June '27), which is the earliest solar can be commissioned; company will not commission solar on TGNA (temporary GNA) given curtailment risk in Rajasthan and other states which is IRR-dilutive.

Company plans to make plants fully ready (transmission line, substation, balance of plant) and operate the battery there, then feed solar once daytime GNA becomes operational, to avoid stranded modules or curtailed generation.
Fatehgarh II bay is already charged/capable of evacuating nighttime power, though not relevant for the current PPA (which does not need nighttime power).

subsections.label: Curtailment (state-based projects)
points: Curtailment on state-based projects contributed ~1% (less than 1%) impact on overall revenue this quarter; company plans to add a little battery to state-based projects in future to capitalize on/eliminate curtailment.

New ministry circular allowing surplus solar to charge batteries expected to help eliminate curtailment (seasonal effects notwithstanding); company also pursuing regulatory forums to extend central-grid curtailment provisions to states.

subsections.label: BESS/RE bid slowdown
points: General slowdown observed in bidding activity, especially in the last quarter and FY26, attributed to SECI's format changes (requiring firm demand commitment before releasing bids) which reduced near-term bid volume even as underlying demand drivers remain strong.
Rightsizing of battery bids by states is ongoing due to delays in VGF-based project execution amid competitive bid dynamics, contributing to currently low reported bid volumes.

subsections.label: Industry bid outlook

guidance_ledger.statement: Upgraded capex guidance to approximately INR15,000 crores to INR20,000 crores for the full year.
Upgrading BESS commissioning guidance from 10 gigawatt hour by calendar year 2027 to more than 10 gigawatt hour by fiscal year 2027, effectively bringing forward this milestone by nearly 3 quarters.
Expect to commission 1.5 gigawatt of contracted renewable energy generation capacity, subject to timely availability of substation and transmission lines.
By 2030, contemplate increasing target beyond 10 gigawatt as guided earlier, basis new growth opportunities seen in the market; will update in coming quarters.
INR1,400 crores+ revenue run-rate can be assumed for financial modeling for next 2-3 years, potentially even more, given current PPA pipeline and timelines; beyond that dependent on market dynamics.

At least 10 gigawatt hour of battery will remain exposed to the merchant market every year before moving to PPA the following year; company aims for zero long-term open capacity beyond a 5-year horizon.
Core EBITDA margin expected to vary between 88% to 92% (88% to 91%) depending on seasonality; may improve further with FDRE project mix given healthier realizations vs plain solar bids.
INR93 lakhs/MW capitalized cost could rise for future BESS orders by not more than 5% to 10%, but remains within budgeted cost.
Management does not see a slowdown in BESS demand or pricing over the next 3 years; beyond 3 years is susceptible to change.
Aim to have 0 open capacity outside PPA by end of this year, other than a 300 MW plant currently uncontracted.
Chairman expects peak power demand driven by duck curve to rise from current ~300 GWh estimate toward 400-500 GWh, and in a positive scenario up to 1 terawatt hour.
PPA with Northeast state (via REMCL) expected to be signed very shortly; bank guarantee already given.
Almost all (~90%) of the 20 GWh target battery capacity has been contracted; balance is where PPA is not yet signed.

Upcoming future operational capacity expected to have an operating battery portfolio of around 10 gigawatt hour, along with 1.5 gigawatts of contracted generation capacity, subject to timely availability of transmission connectivity and other external factors.

guidance_ledger.metric: Under-construction PPA-signed portfolio commissioning (3,280 MW + 12 GWh BESS)
guidance_ledger.statement: These will be commissioned by FY28.
Continue to focus on long-term 25-year contracts while also actively participating in short- and medium-term BESS opportunities to capitalize on evolving market demand and merchant market dynamics.
Full FDRE for SJVN will be ready by FY27 end (long-term open access per CTU targeted March '27).
NTPC solar ready; long-term open access slated to be commissioned by December '26; Pachora wind component ready but slated a couple of quarters later; by March '27, all this will be commissioned.

risk_register.risk: GNA/transmission connectivity delays pushing out solar commissioning

Contributed ~1% revenue impact this quarter; new circular allowing surplus solar to charge batteries and additional battery sizing on state projects expected to reduce/eliminate curtailment going forward; regulatory parity with central grid provisions being pursued.

Bid volumes reduced due to SECI's new rule requiring firm demand commitment before releasing bids, plus rightsizing of battery bids by states following VGF project execution delays; management expects large bids and revival within next 6-9 months given strong underlying demand drivers.

risk_register.risk: BESS input cost volatility (lithium carbonate, China supply-demand, export tax)
risk_register.note: Lithium carbonate volatility and a 6% China export tax from January could push future BESS costs up modestly (5-10%), but remains within budgeted cost; dollar hedging (>$300 million locked at INR89-93) provides a positive cost bias.

risk_register.risk: Profitability uncertainty in data center/C&I segment

risk_register.note: Caused delay in ACME Marigold LOA PPA signing with a Northeast state; now at advanced stage with bank guarantee given, expected to be signed shortly.
Average ~6 months delay historically, considered manageable; no penalty for such delays; company defers module procurement to mitigate capex exposure.
STU efficiency varies by state; company has consciously avoided STU-connected projects except one Gujarat wind project and a small 550 MWh AP battery project.

risk_register.risk: PPA signing / connectivity date attractiveness to DISCOMs
risk_register.note: Developers with later declared substation dates get lower DISCOM priority; ISTS waivers expiring 2028 add urgency.

risk_register.note: Achieving 10 GWh battery target depends on material supply, connectivity, financing and geopolitical factors, though considered less externally dependent than CTU-connected solar.

Management views tariff arbitrage sustainability as uncertain long-term ('anybody's guess'), though expects it to hold for at least 4-5 years given rising peak demand and gas constraints; could taper as more battery capacity is added nationally.
Real curtailment impact limited to INR5-6 crores for the full year; battery installation expected to further reduce curtailment issue as more batteries come online in Rajasthan.

key_takeaways: This quarter marks another milestone for the company as we delivered the highest ever revenue and EBITDA in our history.
Total revenue for the quarter stood at INR954 crores, which is up 63% year-on-year, while EBITDA increased 56% to INR831 crores.
We have secured short-term BESS contracts during the quarter, locking in more than INR1,400 crores of revenue for partial FY27 BESS commission capacity.

We are upgrading our BESS commissioning guidance from 10 gigawatt hour by calendar year 2027 to more than 10 gigawatt hour by fiscal year 2027, effectively bringing forward this milestone by nearly 3 quarters.
For FY27, we also expect to commission 1.5 gigawatt of contracted renewable energy generation capacity, subject to timely availability of substation and transmission lines.

By 2030, we contemplate to increase our target beyond 10 gigawatt as guided earlier, basis the new growth opportunities that we are seeing in the market, and we will keep you updated on the same in coming quarters.
We signed 600 megawatt of FDRE and hybrid PPAs with SECI during the quarter, which takes our total PPA signed capacity to 3,880 megawatts out of total under-construction capacity of 5,080 megawatts.
During the quarter, we also achieved the highest capacity utilization factor in the company's history at 30.9% compared with 28.5% in the corresponding quarter last year.
pressing_questions: Apoorva Bahadur asked about the depth of the merchant market and how much BESS capacity it can support given that arbitrage is very good and many players are jumping in, and for how long spreads will hold before compression.
Yogesh Patil asked whether the INR1,400 crores revenue run-rate could be sustained for the next 3-4 years given a normalizing El Nino effect, return of hydropower, and potential lower realizations.
Anuj Upadhyay sought clarity on whether the INR1,400 crores locked-in revenue is from the entire 10 GWh or only a 50% portion tied to upcoming FDRE projects, per the presentation.

quarters.summary: ACME Solar reported strong Q4/FY26 growth driven by capacity addition, higher CUF and early BESS deployment, with management guiding to ~1.5 GW of generation commissioning and ~10 GWh of battery commissioning in FY27, continued focus on long-term 25-year PPAs alongside opportunistic short/medium-term BESS merchant opportunities, and expectations that peak power tariff arbitrage (~INR6/unit) will sustain for at least 4-5 years amid rising RE capacity and CTU-linked connectivity.

subsections.label: Revenue & Margin Drivers
points: Revenue growth driven by capacity addition and higher CUF.
Other income primarily comprises recurring interest income from cash generated at SPV level until upstreamed to ASHL and recurring interest from DSRA balances maintained per debt covenants.
Since DSRA is largely funded from debt proceeds, corresponding finance cost is accounted for in finance cost.
EBITDA margin of over 90% attributed to favourable operating leverage and optimized operational efficiency.

subsections.label: Debt & Capital Structure
points: Refinancing of INR3,300 crores in operational project debt reduced interest rate by ~150 bps.
2.2 GW of operational projects carry an AA- stable credit rating.

subsections.label: Receivables & Working Capital
points: DSO improvement to 14-15 days from a historical high of 180 days is described as structural rather than one-time, driven by portfolio shift toward central offtakers who take cash discounts by paying within 6-10 days.
Historical high receivable days pertained to FY23 and prior, when central offtaker contribution was lower and there were payment delays from some DISCOMs, notably Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.

Government's Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) scheme has enforced payment discipline among state DISCOMs; non-payment leads to disconnection via PRAPTI portal reporting, and prior legal disputes (e.g., Andhra Pradesh court cases) are now settled.

subsections.label: Cash Flow & Capital Advances
points: Increase in non-current assets/other financial non-current assets on balance sheet mainly due to capex-related capital creditors.

Capital advances of INR323 crores relate to procurement of battery and turbine equipment, given as partial (10-20%) advances against bank guarantees to secure supplier commitments and enable raw material purchase, particularly for international/large equipment procurement.

subsections.label: Gross Block vs Run-rate EBITDA
points: Apparent high gross block-to-EBITDA ratio (~11x) explained by wind capacity commissioning late in the year (not yet contributing to run-rate EBITDA) and ~INR1,000-1,100 crores of the INR3,460 crores gross block increase relating to batteries commissioned at year-end that are not yet reflected in run-rate EBITDA.

subsections.label: Curtailment Impact
points: Only 2 projects in the portfolio are connected to the Rajasthan state grid; rest are on the central grid where curtailment is compensated via regulatory mechanism.
Pre-COD/pre-GNA curtailment (infrastructure not ready, e.g., Sikar plant before full commissioning) is not classified as true curtailment.
Adjusted for pre-COD curtailment, real curtailment impact for the full year was only INR5-6 crores, with INR3 crores from STU Rajasthan and INR2-3 crores from grid operator O&M maintenance.

subsections.label: LOA-to-PPA Conversion Regulatory Development (CERC)
points: CERC has proposed (discussion paper stage) a mechanism allowing surrender/exit of LOA-based connectivity where PPA signing is delayed beyond 1 year; developer would then be free to use capacity on merchant basis or apply it to another LOA.
Company does not foresee needing to surrender LOAs given its strong PPA conversion pipeline; if it happens, connectivity will be redeployed for future bids or battery-connected projects.

subsections.label: Demand & Bidding Outlook
points: Demand for peak power capacity (backed by battery) is strongest; partial peak power second; wind selling well but fewer opportunities; plain solar selling slowest as very few states have pure solar demand.

SECI now sole REIA, expected to aggregate demand for thermal-mimic, peak power, and CfD tenders which will find takers based on demand; at least 5 GW of tenders currently open with SECI (2 GW wind, ~1 GW PSP, plus thermal mimic and CfD).
Bid volume for FY27 expected to be lower than last year but PPA signing pace expected to be faster since developers hold sizable pipelines to execute before new bids are floated.
Some states (Southern states, Maharashtra, Gujarat) will continue state-level bidding successfully; others will rely on SECI's competitive rates due to limited renewable potential.

Overall capacity addition (state+central) expected at 20-30 GW next year, but overall capex requirement will be higher than last year because battery-backed 'thermal mimic'/long-duration storage bids carry large solar capacity behind the battery — implying 40-50 GW of solar deployment even if nominal awarded capacity is 25-30 GW.
CERC connectivity rules under regulation 5.2 mandate installing solar within 3 years of taking connectivity, driving battery-linked solar installations and reducing pure battery installations.

points: BESS capacities running on merchant and short-term contracts, capturing tariff arbitrage between sale and purchase of power during peak and non-peak hours.

CTU projects are structured, giving firm declared dates each quarter for substation readiness, whereas STU/state grid efficiency varies significantly by state (e.g., Gujarat cited as efficient; some states lack renewable potential and don't develop grids as much).

subsections.label: Battery Deployment Locations
points: Battery installations at operational substations: Fatehgarh-1 (1,000-1,200 MW), Fatehgarh-2 (1,000 MW with STOA allowing full battery transmission), and Bikaner-3 (bay ready for battery transmission) aggregate to ~2,500 MW of ready connectivity for night-time battery power sales.

Commissioning plan for FY27 includes Neemuch substation (first to commission, charging expected June, will commission NHPC and Tata FDRE plants), Fatehgarh substation (SJVN 570 MW, short-term open access available, long-term open access per CTU targeted March 2027), NTPC hybrid (solar ready, long-term open access targeted December 2026) and Pachora wind component (a couple of quarters later), Pavagada and Anantapur also targeted this year per CTU timeline.

subsections.label: Transmission & Connectivity Delays
points: CTU substations experience delay mainly in transmission line interconnection and right-of-way issues, dependent on bidding companies; historically ~6 months average delay, described as 'a wonderful job' given the grid's scale.
Some substations (~60%) are on time, others delayed; maximum typical delay is 6 months, though unfortunate events could extend this further.

Company mitigates delay risk by deferring capex on long-lead but flexible items (e.g., solar modules, which are just-in-time and abundant in India), while completing transmission line/substation work (fixed lead items, ~20-25% of project cost) ahead of schedule.
No penalty is levied for CTU-caused delays; developers get automatic timeline extensions, and states/developers are not penalized for delays beyond their control.

subsections.label: PPA/Connectivity Attractiveness Risk
points: DISCOMs prioritize signing PPAs with developers whose substations have nearer-term declared commissioning dates (e.g., 2027 vs 2029); developers with later connectivity dates face lower priority and risk not getting a 'seat at the table'.
Certain ISTS waivers are set to expire in 2028, adding urgency/attractiveness considerations tied to declared substation dates.

subsections.label: Regulatory/Tariff Uncertainty on Standalone BESS
points: Standalone 550 MWh Andhra Pradesh BESS project's zero date has not started, pending state regulator's decision on NHPC's trading margin structure (0.5% vs INR7 paisa) given the pure leasing/VGF arrangement.

subsections.label: Geopolitical/Supply Factors
points: Achieving the 10 GWh battery target depends on supply of material, connectivity, financing and supply tie availability; interplay of supply chain and geopolitical factors remain sources of uncertainty, though considered to have fewer external dependencies than CTU-connected solar plants.

subsections.label: Tariff Arbitrage Sustainability
points: Sustainability of BESS tariff arbitrage is 'anybody's guess' per management, though historical peak power realization of INR7-8 has persisted for several years even in low-demand years; current gas constraints have elevated prices further, and elevated peak demand is expected to keep arbitrage favorable for at least 4-5 years before it could taper as more battery capacity comes online (CEA estimates ~200 GWh battery needed nationally, rising as more daytime solar is added).

subsections.label: Forward Priorities
points: Key focus remains timely execution alongside healthy order book additions.
Continued focus on advancing commissioning and operation of large-scale BESS capacity utilizing transmission infrastructure of existing operational projects, running on merchant/short-term basis.

Upcoming future operational capacity expected to have operating battery portfolio of ~10 GWh along with 1.5 GW of contracted generation capacity, subject to timely transmission connectivity and other external factors.

Order book strategy: continue focusing on long-term 25-year contracts while also actively participating in short- and medium-term BESS opportunities to capitalize on evolving market demand and merchant dynamics.

subsections.label: Battery Installation Sequencing Rationale
points: Batteries are being commissioned ahead of solar/FDRE integration at operational (Brownfield) substations to prepone battery revenue realization since night-time power sales are now allowed per PPA construct and MNRE clarification, more than compensating for CTU timeline shifts.

Company purposely defers connecting installed solar to avoid FDRE classification, instead charging batteries from grid and selling merchant power at attractive summer prices; solar capex (~60% of project cost, modules) is deferred until LTOA is operational to save interest during construction and improve returns, since modules are just-in-time available.

guidance_ledger.statement: Targeting 1.5 gigawatts of projects commissioned in this financial year.

Upcoming future operational capacity expected to have an operating battery portfolio of around 10 gigawatt hour, along with 1.5 gigawatts of contracted generation capacity, subject to timely availability of transmission connectivity and other external factors.

risk_register.risk: LOA-to-PPA conversion / potential surrender under proposed CERC mechanism
risk_register.note: CERC discussion paper proposes surrender/exit option for LOA-based connectivity delayed >1 year without signed PPA; company does not foresee this affecting its portfolio given its strong conversion pipeline, but has a backup plan (future bids/battery projects) if needed.

themes.label: BESS ramp-up & merchant arbitrage
themes.note: ~2.3 GW BESS commissioned delivering ~INR2.2 crores/day net realization and 88-90% round-trip efficiency, with plans to reach ~10 GWh via merchant/short-term contracts capturing peak-off-peak tariff arbitrage.

themes.label: CTU vs STU connectivity mix
themes.note: Portfolio deliberately concentrated on CTU-connected substations for regulatory curtailment protection and central offtaker cash-discount payment terms, versus limited/no STU exposure.

themes.label: Receivables & working capital improvement
themes.note: DSO improved structurally to 14-15 days (from 180 days historically) as portfolio shifts toward central offtakers and LPS scheme enforces payment discipline.

themes.label: Regulatory tailwinds for BESS/FDRE
themes.note: MNRE clarification allowing merchant sale of grid-charged BESS power ahead of RE commissioning, CTU processing of BESS connectivity under RoFR, and CERC's draft SCOD extension order all support faster BESS deployment.

themes.label: Transmission/connectivity delay risk
themes.note: CTU substation delays (~6 months typical) require capex deferral strategies (delaying module procurement) but are non-penalized and considered manageable given grid scale.

themes.label: Order book growth & PPA conversion
themes.note: Under-construction portfolio expanded to 5.1 GW / total 8,071 MW after winning 301 MW FDRE with SECI; strong LOA-to-PPA conversion pipeline (6.2 GW signed) reduces surrender risk under proposed CERC mechanism.

themes.label: Peak power demand & tariff sustainability
themes.note: Management expects peak power/BESS tariff arbitrage to sustain for at least 4-5 years given rising peak demand, gas constraints, and historical INR7-8 realization, potentially rising to INR9-10 in peak hours.

key_takeaways: India has observed its all-time highest peak electricity demand of 256 gigawatt on 25th April '26, surpassing the previous high of 250 gigawatt (30th May '24) and 245 gigawatt (9th January '26).
India continues to maintain strong momentum in capacity additions with approximately 55 gigawatt of RE added in financial year '26, taking cumulative renewable energy capacity to 283 gigawatts.

In a significant milestone, India achieved 50% of its cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil fuel sources in June '25, 5 years ahead of the 2030 target set under its nationally determined contribution to the Paris Agreement.

In line with our continued focus on early BESS deployment, we successfully commissioned approximately 2.3 gigawatt BESS capacity to date, delivering net realization value of approximately INR2.2 crores per day and a round trip efficiency of approximately 88% to 90%.
Our total revenue for the quarter stands at INR 705 crores and INR 2,507 crores of FY '26, 31% and 59% increase year-on-year respectively, driven by capacity addition and higher CUF.

EBITDA margin of over 90%, both for the quarter and full year on account of favourable operating leverage and optimized operational efficiency. PAT stood at INR138 crores for the quarter and INR498 crores for the year with a margin of 19.6% and 19.9%, respectively.

During the year, we secured financing of around INR15,000 crores for various under construction projects, and refinanced debt amounting to INR3,300 crores for various operational projects, resulting in reduction of rate of interest of the refinance projects by approximately 150 basis points.

Upcoming future operational capacity is expected to have an operating battery portfolio of around 10 gigawatt hour, along with 1.5 gigawatts of contracted generation capacity, subject to timely availability of transmission connectivity and other external factors.

ACMESOLAR.about: Incorporated in 2015, ACME Solar Holdings is a renewable energy company in India with a portfolio of solar, wind, hybrid, and firm and dispatchable renewable energy (“FDRE”) projects.[1]

quarters.summary: Persistent announced two major events: (1) a net-new large deal with an existing US technology customer worth ~$125mn+ annually, ~$650mn+ over 6.5 years, expected to be revenue and margin accretive from Q2 onwards; and (2) a definitive agreement to acquire 100% of Nagarro (Munich-headquartered digital engineering firm) at an enterprise value of €1.27 billion, forming the "Persistent-Nagarro group" — a $2.9bn+, 46,000+ employee, AI-led digital engineering powerhouse spanning 40+ countries. The transaction is expected to be Cash EPS and Reported EPS accretive in Year 1 (ex transaction expenses), funded via committed bridge financing from Barclays, with closing expected around Q4 CY2026 or early Q1 CY2027 subject to regulatory approvals and open offer acceptance.

subsections.label: Valuation rationale
points: Enterprise value of €1.27 billion based on €81/share cash offer, representing 140% premium to undisturbed closing price (June 25-26) and 94% premium to 3-month VWAP.
Valuation implies 1.27x EV/Revenue and 9.12x EV/EBITDA (CY25 basis); on upper end of CY26 guidance basis, EV/EBITDA multiple drops to ~7.73x.
Management views this as a fair and attractive valuation, framing it as a 'control transaction' premium and comparing it to private market transactions rather than listed European peer multiples.
Management stated they were not 'buying cheap' but buying the right asset, right management team and capabilities for the future.
~70% of purchase price estimated as goodwill and ~30% as other intangibles, amortized over 8 years post-close.

subsections.label: Deal financing structure
points: Transaction to be completely funded through a committed bridge financing from Barclays.
Interest rate is Euribor plus a margin of 175-250 basis points, translating to roughly 4.1%-4.8% currently; exact rate will be set closer to actual requirement, hence given as a range.
Leverage (Net Debt/combined EBITDA) expected at 1.9x-2.5x depending on final open offer acceptance level (50%+1 share to 100%), expected to reduce to 1x by FY2030.

Total committed bridge financing facility of €1.4 billion includes refinancing of Nagarro's existing debt if required; Persistent Systems Limited (parent) will provide a corporate guarantee of €1.4 billion plus any outstanding accrued interest.
Entirely debt-driven transaction on current assumptions; management is confident of servicing the debt from combined cash generation.
Interest cost for FY28 basis and quantum of debt will depend on final open offer acceptance level; more clarity expected over coming months.

No QIP or equity dilution at Persistent level intended; management may consider private equity participation at the asset (Nagarro) level for deleveraging, but no decision taken — 'we may look at that over a period of time at the asset level, not at the Persistent level.'

subsections.label: EPS accretion mechanics
points: Transaction expected to be Cash EPS accretive in Year 1.
Reported EPS also expected to be accretive in Year 1 once one-time transaction expenses are excluded.
Cash EPS accretion driven by excluding amortization expenses (of the ~30% other-intangibles component amortized over 8 years).
Reported EPS accretion driven by excluding one-time transaction expenses incurred in Year 1.

subsections.label: Ownership and stake commitment at announcement
points: Existing committed stake secured via SPA of 21%, plus management board shares expected to tender of 13-14%, combining to ~35% committed/expected stake at announcement — well above the 50%+1 minimum acceptance threshold when combined with other expressed shareholder interest.

subsections.label: Cash flow / balance sheet approach
points: Both Persistent and Nagarro have good cash generation track records; intent is to use combined cash generation to repay loans over time.
Persistent has moved away from a CapEx-heavy model toward an OpEx model for funding working capital, which is expected to support cash flow post-combination.
Management intends to bring best cash-flow practices into the combined organization and ensure debt is serviced within generated cash flows.

subsections.label: Due diligence on Nagarro's books
points: Nagarro had received BaFin queries related to (a) the time it was carved out of Allgeier, and (b) accounting principles followed.
Persistent conducted legal/tax diligence and is confident these queries are administrative (addressing BaFin) rather than indicating issues with company performance or practices.

subsections.label: Large new deal with existing US technology customer
points: This is a net new deal valued at $125 million+ annually and $650 million+ total contract value over a 6.5-year tenor — testimony to the long-standing relationship and to what Persistent has delivered for this customer over the years.
Reflects Persistent's engineering prowess, deep domain expertise, and the belief that AI will enable even better delivery going forward.
Expected to cement growth momentum and continue Persistent's 24-quarter streak of consecutive growth.
Customer name undisclosed due to NDA obligations.
Persistent will be responsible for end-to-end product engineering and product support for a significant portfolio of the customer's products globally.
Minimal ramp-up required as the deal may involve employee transitions.

Expected to be revenue and margin accretive from Q2 onwards; margins on this deal are described as 'fairly healthy,' though large deals of this nature typically do not come at company-average margins — 'a company is always a sum of parts.'

subsections.label: Vertical mix complementarity
points: Persistent has dominant share from TMT, BFSI and HLS (Healthcare & Life Sciences) verticals.
Nagarro adds significant strength in Industrial and Consumer verticals plus a fledgling Public Sector business.
Nagarro brings a very strong ERP and CX (customer experience) consulting practice, complementary to Persistent's offerings.

Nagarro counts some of the largest auto manufacturers as clients but automotive is not their biggest segment — broader industrial segment is larger; automotive slowdown fears are seen as not materially impacting Nagarro given small revenue share and digital-side nature of work.

Nagarro has partnerships with Siemens (product engineering and go-to-market implementation), significant work for Lufthansa, and significant work for SAP itself (including next-gen work showcased in SAP customer briefing centers).

Segments cited as having declined for Nagarro include horizontal tech, energy & utilities, telecom and travel; management attributes recent Nagarro growth softness partly to management distraction during a prior 'take-private' transaction attempt, not structural issues.

subsections.label: Customer base / account mining opportunity
points: Nagarro's average client size is significantly smaller than Persistent's, with a longer tail of accounts (highest single customer revenue for Nagarro is under $50 million, vs. Persistent's top 4-5 customers averaging over $100 million each and 2 accounts already above $100 million with a 3rd approaching).
Only single-digit overlap (fewer than 10 customers) between the two companies, and even there they work in different parts of the organization.

Management views the smaller/long-tail Nagarro account base (180 logos of $1mn+) as an opportunity to mine deeper (cross-sell/up-sell) rather than a risk, citing Persistent's own history of growing account sizes.
Possibility exists of rationalizing some tail accounts over time to release SG&A for reinvestment where needed.
Combined entity's 350+ accounts of $1mn+ quality are seen as having significant untapped mining potential that could be value accretive without needing to hunt for new logos.

subsections.label: Service line and delivery model
points: Nagarro's revenue is 65%-68% Time & Material (T&M); management differentiates Persistent/Nagarro's 'build' side of digital engineering work (including AI-led) from bigger peers' support/managed-services-heavy T&M work.
Management expects the T&M model to gradually decline over the next few years but not disappear, as some deals evolve toward business-outcome-based constructs.

AI-driven cannibalization is expected to reduce T&M revenue for current scope of work, but management frames this as an opportunity to win more business by disrupting themselves — citing Persistent's own SASVA platform as an example of using AI/IP to do 'more for less' and win incremental business despite cannibalization.
Nagarro's constant-currency growth in recent years has been above 5%.

subsections.label: European expansion rationale
points: Persistent has long stated an ambition (in earnings calls and elsewhere) to expand its footprint in Europe via a scaled acquisition; Nagarro combination fulfills that stated M&A strategy.
Combined entity's Europe revenue share rises to 22% (from Persistent's standalone 8%-8.5%), fulfilling management's stated dream of European business at 15%+.
Deal also gives nearshore delivery presence in Europe and adds presence in Middle East, Japan, Israel and other geographies where Persistent's footprint was previously minimal or absent.
Nagarro has a fairly decent practice across various industry verticals within the Middle East, an area where Persistent's footprint is minimalistic.

Nagarro, despite being Europe-revenue-focused, has a culturally heterogeneous employee base (13,500 in India vs 1,500+ elsewhere, ~500 in North America), which management believes eases integration versus a 'pure play onshore European' company.

subsections.label: Global positioning post-combination
points: Combined group would be the 2nd largest digital engineering player globally and 7th largest technology services company from an India-listed landscape perspective.

Geographic diversification (North America 62%, Europe 22%, RoW 16%, across 40+ countries and 46,000+ combined employees) seen as providing scale that is important for larger competitive bids, giving 'a seat at the table' for large customer RFPs.

Geopolitical balance from combined geography mix cited as a benefit, alongside ability to bring AI adoption learnings from ahead-of-curve North American/West Coast customers into typically slower-adopting European markets.

subsections.label: Deal rationale and strategic fit
points: Combination described as an 'expansion play,' not a consolidation play — bringing together complementary people, capabilities and markets.

Fulfills each of Persistent's stated strategic priorities: being a forward-looking technology services firm (not general-purpose IT services), going deeper/broader into service lines, adding verticals, expanding in Europe, and having European nearshore delivery presence.
Nagarro brings ERP capability (strong SAP implementation partnership, including product engineering for SAP) and CX/consulting capability that complements Persistent's digital engineering strength.

Nagarro is an accredited OpenAI reseller with a forward-deployed engineering practice around OpenAI; Persistent has partnerships with Anthropic and other hyperscalers — together creating a strong AI-led forward-deployed engineering capability.
Combination helps reach Persistent's stated $5 billion revenue aspiration by FY31 at a 'nice scale,' partly by adding verticals (industrial, consumer, public sector) that Persistent lacked at scale.
Adds a small embedded software practice that would have been costlier and harder to integrate if acquired as a standalone separate asset ('sum of parts' argument).

subsections.label: Deal structuring / share purchase and open offer
points: Persistent has already secured a 21% stake in Nagarro via a share purchase agreement (SPA) from the major shareholder.

Nagarro's Management Board has expressed interest to tender their shares (roughly 13-14%) into the open offer, taking the committed/expected stake closer to ~35%; other shareholders have also expressed interest, giving management confidence of reaching 35-40% and comfortably exceeding the 50%+1 threshold.
Both Nagarro boards (management and supervisory) fully support the transaction and have signed a business combination agreement.
Persistent extends a voluntary public takeover offer to all outstanding shares at €81/share cash, with a minimum acceptance threshold of 50%+1 share.

Management's goal is to get as close as possible to 100% acceptance to ease integration and squeeze-out; with 50%+ control, Persistent would gain significant control over the supervisory board and be able to drive integration with management support, similar to Indian open-offer 'majority of minority' style rules with some local (German) nuances.

Cross-shareholding/PE interest: significant inbound interest from private equity and other market participants received even within 24 hours of announcement; Persistent may consider PE participation at the Nagarro asset level (not Persistent level) for deleveraging purposes, but no decision taken; explicitly, no QIP or equity dilution planned at the Persistent level.

Expected transaction timeline: filing with BaFin within 4 weeks post-announcement, BaFin document clearance in 10 working days to 2 weeks post-filing, open offer acceptance period of 4 weeks post-launch with an optional 2-week extension, Persistent AGM in the last week of July 2026, and expected close in Q4 CY2026 or early Q1 CY2027.

subsections.label: Cultural and integration fit
points: Management cites strong cultural alignment between Persistent and Nagarro — both engineering-first companies with similar customer, employee and culture philosophies; also aligned in ESG/community commitments.
Nagarro's own heterogeneous employee base (large India presence within a Europe-headquartered company) is seen as easing integration compared to a 'pure play onshore European' target.

Integration is expected to be gradual/planned ('slow roll'), not rushed; Nagarro's team, especially in its areas of strength (geography, verticals), is expected to take on a bigger role rather than Persistent imposing leadership from outside.

Nagarro founders Manas and Vikram remain with the organization since inception; complemented by Annette (6+ years) and recently joined CFO Prateek Aggarwal, a seasoned CFO from an Indian-listed company background.

Management team of Nagarro is committed to staying on; European law and minimum pricing regulations govern incentive structures since part of management is also an investor; appropriate incentive plans will be put in place as integration proceeds, similar to Persistent's senior management practices.

Deal is not a private-equity-style share swap because it is a public-to-private transaction under German rules, which management says have different dynamics than easy equity-swap structures used by some PE-backed peers.

Persistent does not intend to enter a domination and/or profit-and-loss-transfer agreement (DPLTA) for two years post-close; will work with existing Nagarro management via agreements to drive synergies before considering a squeeze-out at the right time, calling this the standard approach in mature European public-to-private transactions.

subsections.label: Growth and margin synergy ambitions
points: Management does not believe the combined entity will operate at materially lower margins than Persistent's current levels, citing Persistent's own track record of significantly improving margins over the years and expected cost synergies at combined scale.
Ambition is to reinvest a significant part of cost synergies into growth and expansion initiatives rather than purely drop to the bottom line.

Management is confident of bringing Nagarro back to 'industry leading growth,' partly attributing recent growth softness to distraction from Nagarro's earlier attempted take-private transaction, and citing Persistent's demonstrated ability to grow disproportionately (23.9% 5-year CAGR) versus the broader industry.

A detailed value creation plan will be shared only after regulatory approvals (including RBI and other country-level approvals) are obtained; a value-creation hypothesis has already been presented to Persistent's board to secure approval for the transaction.

CY21/CY22 growth for Nagarro included contribution from a couple of acquisitions at that time; management's own analysis is based on the combined entity as it existed in CY25 and Q1 CY26, and all growth factored into the current deal thesis is organic from that base.
Revenue and cost synergies to be detailed post regulatory approvals.

subsections.label: Integration and execution risk
points: Large-scale acquisition (nearly two-thirds the size of Persistent) carries integration execution risk; management acknowledges 'these things have to slow roll' and take time to create value.

Two-year standstill on domination/profit-loss-transfer agreement means Nagarro will initially run with its existing management under Persistent's controlling shareholding rather than full integration, which analysts flagged as a potential complexity.

Analyst flagged risk that Nagarro's much smaller average client size and long-tail account base versus Persistent's scaled clients could be a risk to combined growth; management frames this as an opportunity rather than a risk but acknowledges possibility of rationalizing tail accounts.

subsections.label: Regulatory approval risk
points: Transaction subject to multiple regulatory approvals, including BaFin (Germany), RBI (India), and other country-level approvals, before integration plans can be finalized and shared.

Open offer outcome (acceptance level between 50%+1 and 100%) is not yet certain, though management expresses confidence of clearing the 50% threshold given committed/expected ~35-40% stake and premium pricing.

subsections.label: Financial/leverage risk
points: Entirely debt-funded transaction via bridge financing; leverage of 1.9x-2.5x Net Debt/EBITDA at close depending on acceptance level, to be reduced to 1x by FY2030 — dependent on cash generation and debt service execution.
Interest rate exposure to Euribor plus margin (175-250 bps) introduces some rate variability, described as a range 'because the requirement will be a few months later.'

subsections.label: Historical Nagarro growth softness / distraction
points: Nagarro's revenue growth has been flat for two years with some margin pressure; certain segments (horizontal tech, energy & utilities, telecom, travel) saw sharp declines.
Management attributes at least part of the softness to management distraction during a prior attempted take-private transaction of Nagarro, rather than structural issues in the portfolio.

subsections.label: AI-led cannibalization of T&M revenue
points: AI-driven cannibalization is expected to reduce Nagarro's (and Persistent's) T&M revenue for existing scope of work over time, applicable across the industry, not unique to Nagarro.
Management's mitigation is to win disproportionately more new business by using AI/IP (e.g., Persistent's SASVA platform) to offset the cannibalization of legacy T&M revenue.

subsections.label: Valuation/market perception risk
points: Nagarro's stock price is down 85% from its 212-level peak, raising analyst questions on whether the acquisition premium is justified given the growth and margin profile; management responds that stock price reflects both fundamentals and market multiple, and that the premium paid reflects a 'control transaction' comparable to private deal premiums, not listed peer multiples.

subsections.label: Combined entity growth confidence
points: Management is confident of maintaining Persistent's standalone growth momentum and of sustaining similar revenue growth momentum for the combined Persistent-Nagarro group going forward.
New large customer deal ($125mn+ annually, $650mn+ over 6.5 years) is expected to cement Persistent's growth and continue its 24-quarter growth streak.

subsections.label: $5 billion revenue aspiration
points: Combination is expected to help Persistent reach its stated $5 billion revenue aspiration by FY31 at a nice scale, by adding verticals and geographic scale that would otherwise require multiple smaller acquisitions.

subsections.label: Margin outlook for combined entity
points: Management does not believe combined entity margins will be materially lower than Persistent's current levels and believes there is room to improve margins further via cost synergies, while reinvesting a portion into growth initiatives.

FY'27, Q4 exit run rate expected in the range of $500 million or so.
Aspiration continues to be in the 16-17% range (not guidance, an aspiration).
Healthcare life sciences, BFSI followed by tech expected to lead growth directionally (no guidance).
Should be able to have a decent growth in the coming year.
So far able to deliver more value and get more in return; no forward-looking guidance beyond that.
With the Nagarro combination, Persistent gets to its $5 billion aspiration by FY31 at a nice scale.
Combination gets Persistent to 22% Europe revenue mix, fulfilling the dream of having European business at 15%+.
Confident about maintaining growth in existing Persistent business and sustaining same revenue growth momentum for the combined organization for times to come.
Confident of bringing Nagarro back to industry-leading growth once transaction distraction is behind them and with single-minded management focus on growth.
Do not believe combined entity will be at any significantly lower margins than what Persistent has today; ambition to maintain and better margins via cost synergies while reinvesting in growth.
Leverage of 1.9x-2.5x at close expected to reduce down to 1x by FY2030.
Transaction expected to be Cash EPS accretive and Reported EPS accretive in Year 1, the latter after removing one-time transaction expenses.
New $650mn+ large deal expected to be accretive to revenue and margin from Q2 onwards.

risk_register.risk: Regulatory approval uncertainty (BaFin, RBI, other country approvals)

risk_register.risk: Integration execution risk / two-year standstill on full integration
risk_register.note: No domination/profit-loss-transfer agreement for two years; management to work with existing Nagarro leadership via agreements before considering squeeze-out.
Leverage of 1.9x-2.5x Net Debt/EBITDA at close, targeted to reduce to 1x by FY2030 via combined cash generation.

risk_register.risk: Interest rate variability on bridge financing
risk_register.note: Rate set at Euribor + 175-250bps, currently ~4.1%-4.8%; exact rate to be fixed closer to actual funding requirement.

risk_register.risk: Nagarro historical growth softness and margin pressure
risk_register.note: Nagarro revenue flat for two years with margin pressure; attributed partly to management distraction during a prior attempted take-private transaction rather than structural portfolio issues.

risk_register.risk: Declines in specific Nagarro verticals (horizontal tech, energy & utilities, telecom, travel)
risk_register.note: Management does not see structural issues; frames constant-currency growth of >5% even amid these declines as reasonable given prior distractions.
Applicable across industry, including Nagarro's 65-68% T&M revenue base; mitigated by strategy of winning more new business via AI/IP tools like SASVA.

risk_register.risk: Long-tail / smaller average client size at Nagarro
risk_register.note: Flagged by an analyst as a potential growth risk versus Persistent's scaled clients; management frames it instead as a mining/cross-sell opportunity, with possible rationalization of some tail accounts.

risk_register.risk: Valuation premium scrutiny / stock price decline
risk_register.note: Nagarro stock down 85% from peak of €212; analysts questioned rationale for premium multiple versus European peers; management defends as fair 'control transaction' pricing.

risk_register.risk: Cash flow sustainability given free cash flow exceeding PAT
risk_register.note: Analyst queried sustainability of Nagarro's free cash flow (almost double PAT) in context of ~$41mn debt-related interest cost; management to provide further detail via best cash-flow practices integration.

risk_register.risk: Middle East war / geopolitical tension and oil price impact on inflation
risk_register.note: No direct company exposure to Middle East, but prolonged war could raise oil prices, impacting inflation and affecting the entire sector; management hopes overhang settles in coming weeks.

risk_register.risk: AI-led SDLC compression / self-cannibalization in tech vertical
risk_register.note: Possible compression in tech business from AI productivity gains; company may cannibalize its own SDLC business, though ample outsourcing opportunity remains given company's relatively small size.

risk_register.risk: Delayed tax refunds and insurance premium payment timing
risk_register.note: Contributed to decline in OCF to PAT to 77% in Q4 FY26 vs 91% in Q3 FY26; unbilled revenue proportion also higher, expected to normalize next quarter.

risk_register.risk: US macro weakness / tariff uncertainty / GenAI deflation (FY26 headwinds)
risk_register.note: Cited as challenges faced through FY26, now compounded by additional war-related overhang entering FY27.

risk_register.risk: Healthcare payor account weakness at peer level
risk_register.note: Some larger peers seeing weakness in top payor accounts; Persistent states it has been able to grow in shared accounts despite sector headwinds.

themes.label: M&A / Nagarro acquisition
themes.note: Persistent to acquire 100% of Nagarro for €1.27bn EV, forming a $2.9bn+ AI-led digital engineering powerhouse with 46,000+ employees across 40+ countries.

themes.label: Geography mix shifts
themes.note: Combined group's Europe revenue mix rises to 22% (from Persistent's 8-8.5%), fulfilling stated ambition of 15%+ Europe exposure; North America mix moderates to 62%.

themes.label: $2 billion FY27 run-rate target
themes.note: Not discussed directly this call, but new $650mn+ large deal and Nagarro combination are framed as cementing/expanding Persistent's growth trajectory toward its long-term $5bn FY31 aspiration.

themes.label: Margin trajectory
themes.note: Persistent margins at 15.6% EBITDA/12.6% PAT; Nagarro EBIT margin improved from 10.9% (CY25) to 12.1% (Q1 CY26); management confident combined margins will not be lower and can be bettered via cost synergies.

themes.label: AI-led SDLC compression / cannibalization
themes.note: AI-driven cannibalization expected to reduce T&M revenue (65-68% of Nagarro's mix) over time, offset by strategy of winning disproportionately more business via AI/IP tools like SASVA.

themes.label: Large deal wins
themes.note: Net-new $125mn+ annual / $650mn+ 6.5-year deal with an existing US technology customer, accretive to revenue and margin from Q2, extending Persistent's 24-quarter growth streak.

themes.label: Integration & leverage risk
themes.note: Entirely debt-funded (Barclays bridge financing) acquisition creates 1.9x-2.5x leverage at close, with two-year standstill before full integration/squeeze-out; regulatory approvals and open offer acceptance remain pending.

key_takeaways: Persistent has agreed to acquire 100% of Nagarro shares at an enterprise value of €1.27 billion based on €81 per share in cash; a premium of 140% to the undisturbed closing price on June 25-26 and 94% to the 3-month volume weighted average price.
Transaction values Nagarro at 1.27 times the enterprise value to the revenue and 9.12 times enterprise value to the EBITDA.

It has already secured 21% stake in Nagarro via share purchase agreement from the major shareholder. Management Board has already expressed their interest to tender their shares into the open offer. Both Nagarro boards fully support the transaction and have signed a business combination agreement.
This will be completely funded through a committed bridge financing from Barclays. The interest rate is going to be Euribor plus a margin of 175-250 basis point, translating to around 4.1%-4.8%.
The leverage, that is the Net Debt over the combined EBITDA, is going to be 1.9 times-2.5 times based on how much will be the open offer acceptance; expected to reduce down to 1X by FY2030.
The transaction is expected to be Cash EPS accretive as well as Reported EPS accretive in Year 1 if you remove the transaction expenses that will be incurred in the first year.

Persistent also announced a net new deal with an existing global technology leader worth roughly $125 million plus annually and about $650 million plus over 6.5 years, expected to cement Persistent's 24 quarter streak of growth.

The combined Persistent-Nagarro group will be 46,000+ team members globally spread across 40+ countries, a $2.9 billion+ powerhouse, positioned as the 2nd largest digital engineering player globally and 7th largest technology services company from an India listed landscape.
Persistent does not intend to enter into a domination and/or profit loss transfer agreement for two years post-close.
pressing_questions: Have we done any incremental due diligence on the books of Nagarro? Are we confident that all issues related to their books are behind, and what has been the rationale behind the acquisition multiple given the growth profile?
Beyond industry and geographical expansion, are there sizable cross-selling opportunities given similar service line capabilities between the two companies?
Is the Nagarro management team staying on, and are there run-out or retention commitments attached for a certain period of time?
Nagarro revenue has been flat for two years with margin pressure, and the stock is down 85% from peak levels — what gives confidence that this is a turnaround asset?
Can you clarify the EBIT margin discrepancy — is it high single digits (as the analyst understood) or 13.9%+ as stated?
How much of Nagarro's CY21/CY22 growth was organic versus acquisition-driven?

What changes would be made in the combined entity so that vertical performance is as consistent as Persistent's, given automotive/manufacturing/industrial growth is consistent but other Nagarro verticals are volatile?
How much interest cost should be baked in once the transaction is over, assuming an FY28 basis?
Given the size of the acquisition (almost two-thirds of Persistent's size), would a cash-plus-share swap have been a better risk mitigation strategy than an all-cash deal?
Regarding the large new deal — any details on ramp-up timeline, margin implications, and whether it is a consolidation or scope-expansion project?
Can you walk through the EPS accretion math on a GAAP basis in Year 1 without assuming margin expansion? Is the interest expense on the new debt tax-deductible?

Given the complexity of a two-year integration plan before squeezing out minorities, how will the combined entity ensure the growth engine (given Nagarro's 3-4% growth) is bumped up to Persistent's growth level?

In different open-offer acceptance scenarios (below 50%, exactly 50%+1, or higher), what happens to the transaction, and is the eventual goal to take Nagarro private via DPLTA — what would the timeline be?

quarters.summary: Persistent delivered its 24th consecutive quarter of revenue growth in Q4 FY26 with broad-based vertical and geography growth, margin expansion, and continued AI platform investment; management reiterated it is steadily marching toward a $2 billion revenue run-rate by FY27 exit (Q4 FY27 run-rate of ~$500 million) and an aspirational 16-17% EBIT margin band, while flagging macro/geopolitical uncertainty (Middle East war, oil prices/inflation) as a watch item for FY27.
