subsections.label: BFSI vertical performance
points: BFSI growth attributable to expanding relationships with existing customers and new client wins across North America, Europe and Australia.

BFSI vertical depth underpinned by strong customer base including Top 4 of 5 banks in US and India, Top 3 of 5 large global fintechs, Top 3 of 5 brokerage/wealth managers/retirement service providers.

Growth attributed to three pillars of execution: (1) specialized sub-vertical focus on retail/commercial banks, capital markets, insurers, payment providers, fintechs; (2) doubling down on product engineering, data modernization and cloud transformation; (3) sharper focus on top 30 existing clients and winning new strategic clients.

Strong engineering DNA, deep domain knowledge, and AI platforms (SASVA, iAURA, GenAI Hub) create differentiated positioning; increasingly being brought in as credible challenger to Tier-1 outsourcing firms.

BFSI sector transforming to increase margins, strengthen operations and enhance capital efficiency; clients modernizing core banking, policy administration and brokerage platforms with cloud native architectures.
Upgrading enterprise data infrastructure is a critical enabler for AI adoption while facilitating compliance mandates (DORA, BCBS 239, ESG reporting).

Institutions integrating traditional payments and digital assets via real-time networks, blockchain settlements and tokenized real-world assets to improve liquidity and minimize counterparty friction.
Shift seen from business-as-usual programmes to transformation initiatives preparing clients for enterprise AI adoption.
Four principal client focus areas: AI-led software engineering, payments and digital assets, data infrastructure, and nonlinear cost transformation.
Case study: large US insurer migrated core policy lifecycle from decades-old COBOL-based platform directly onto Duck Creek using AI-augmented engineering approach.

Case study: cloud-native FedNow payment solution built for a large financial technology provider, covering customer credit transfers and merchant disbursement use cases end-to-end (architecture through integration and certification readiness).

Selected by one of the largest banks in the Nordic region to modernize payments platform, implement regulatory changes and augment core transaction capabilities, chosen against established incumbents owing to strong payments domain capability.
Case study: large European bank deployed iAURA to address hundreds of siloed systems creating regulatory exposure across BASEL, AML, KYC.
Case study: one of the largest life insurance providers in Australia selected Persistent to co-build a digital underwriting platform replacing fragmented manual processes.

subsections.label: Healthcare/hi-tech vertical commentary
points: Healthcare vertical grew strongly quarter on quarter despite some peer weakness in top payor accounts; management has been able to grow in same set of accounts despite sector headwinds, showing strength of offering and relationships.

Case study (pharma/diabetes/metabolic disorders): built disease-specific knowledge graph from proprietary dataset, using a fine-tuned open-weight foundation model on Google Cloud Platform with Google's MedGemma and TxGemma healthcare AI models for drug discovery.

Case study (global pharmaceutical company): joint solution with NVIDIA's BioNeMo toolkit for protein structure prediction, novel molecule generation, protein design and molecular interaction simulation, built via plug-and-play microservices with industry-standard APIs.
Hi-tech case study: engineering carve-out and offshore-led operations deal (Japan B2B industrial tech leader) across SAP, IT, and data analytics.

subsections.label: Next-year vertical growth expectations (directional, non-guidance)
points: Pecking order for growth next year expected to be between Healthcare Life Sciences and BFSI at the top (neck to neck), followed by tech — explicitly stated as directional view, not guidance.

subsections.label: AI strategy pillars
points: AI strategy anchored on three pillars: engineering hyperproductivity, business hyperproductivity, and enterprise data readiness, along with responsible AI.
Engineering hyperproductivity embeds AI across the software development lifecycle for faster delivery, improved code quality, doing more with less.
Business hyperproductivity applies AI to automate and optimize business processes, workflows and decision-making across enterprise functions.
Enterprise data readiness prepares an enterprise data foundation with right structure, governance and accessibility so AI can deliver accurate, contextual, trusted outcomes at scale.

subsections.label: Three enterprise-wide layers for AI delivery
points: Core foundation layer ensures secure, governed, interoperable, cost-controlled foundation for enterprise AI operation - vital for scalability, compliance and trust.

Governed grounding layer contextualizes and provides reliable, traceable access to enterprise-wide data, processes, knowledge and history, building trusted enterprise memory with domain awareness, lineage, business rules and compliance.
Work orchestration layer coordinates and integrates people, agents, applications, resources and systems in process-driven workflows with clear control, accountability and governance.
Platforms SASVA, iAURA, and GenAI Hub bring these together; methodologies and accelerators extend this into partner ecosystem.

subsections.label: SASVA platform progress
points: SASVA continues to be central driver for clients in engineering hyperproductivity; progression seen from individual productivity to team intelligence and enterprise-scale execution, bridging the last-mile gap of AI adoption.

Approach is now repeatable across verticals, converting enterprise technologies and AI assessment into a 90-day actionable roadmap, including for private equity due diligence and transformation at scale.

Case study: public safety system for law enforcement — SASVA brought organizational context from code repositories, ticket communication channels and planning tools; created purpose-built SLMs alongside Anthropic; unified agents and humans into a single execution loop; mapped dependencies/risks; modernized stack to cloud-native architecture without disrupting operations; embedded continuous security/privacy controls; accelerated engineering through governed releases and full observability.

SASVA expanded to run as a native layer on the core foundation, integrating with partner platforms like Claude, GitHub Copilot and OpenAI Codex, giving clients more choice in models/tools while SASVA adds enterprise value on top.
Partnership with DigitalOcean allows clients to access Anthropic and OpenAI among other models/tools, build/consume agentic solutions, with private cloud and sovereign deployment options.

subsections.label: Business hyperproductivity / GenAI Hub / Agent Studio
points: Upgraded GenAI Hub and Agent Studio with agent runtime, orchestration, evaluation and knowledge management abilities; expanded Agent Processing Unit for agent collaboration.
Agent portfolio built in-house and across partner ecosystems (Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, NVIDIA).

subsections.label: Enterprise data readiness / iAURA
points: Enterprise data readiness remains single most important driver for scaled AI adoption.
Expanded enterprise context, semantic layer and knowledge graph within iAURA to make enterprise data AI-consumable, not just AI-available.

Industrialized modernization using agentic accelerator to migrate legacy data stack into cloud-native platform, delivering outcomes including modernizing thousands of reports with significant automation and establishing data lineage for regulatory alignment.

subsections.label: AI capability building / talent
points: Persistent AI Huddle held in Pune with 1700+ team members (business leaders, delivery heads, delivery partners, technical architects, senior engineers), doing deep dive into AI offerings across the three pillars, with hands-on execution of end-to-end real-world use cases using AI stacks such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Copilot and SASVA.
Goal of huddle was to strengthen execution for expanded AI platform/offerings and enable GTM readiness across the organization.
Following the huddle, company conducting its annual flagship hackathon 'Semicolons' involving entire employee base, focused on building AI-native solutions.

Company intends to host an AI Investor Day in early June timeframe at Pune offices to showcase AI capabilities, partnerships, and marquee customer case studies, including a hands-on AI hackathon involving investors.

subsections.label: Ecosystem partnerships / recognitions
points: Significant AI roadmap announcements from ecosystem players (Anthropic, OpenAI, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Google, Snowflake, Databricks) expected to accelerate adoption pace, with tech companies leading the way.

Co-innovated solutions: full-stack NVIDIA AI platform for biopharma companies (production-grade agentic systems for molecular simulation/virtual screening); Databricks-based Merchant Risk Management Solution for financial institutions/payment providers.
Recognized as leader in Everest Group Private Equity Services PEAK Matrix Assessment 2026 and Everest Group Software Product Engineering PEAK Matrix Assessment 2026.

subsections.label: Geography commentary
points: India growth this quarter is an aberration: one IT customer's renewal in the erstwhile Accelerite business, billed in INR terms through their GCC, had to be classified as India revenue; North America revenue would have been even higher and India revenue lower otherwise; this is expected to correct in the next quarter.
Europe declined 1.8% sequentially; management wants to double down on Europe; there are some customer puts and takes contributing to this.
Both the India uptick and North America adjustment noted as one-off classification effects rather than underlying trend changes.

subsections.label: Demand environment / macro
points: Middle East war situation does not directly affect the company due to zero to very little exposure in the Middle East, but prolonged conflict could raise oil prices and inflation, affecting the entire sector.
Company confident of gaining market share within the sector given progress in AI and investments; remains 'cautiously optimistic'.

Enterprise AI adoption varies by sector: tech companies (fastest adopters, largest demand for AI-led SDLC), Healthcare Life Sciences and BFSI (regulated industries) adopting more slowly from POC/pilot to enterprise-wide scale.

subsections.label: Private equity (PE) channel
points: PE channel is a critical channel; PE-owned companies today outnumber public companies in the US; many enterprise software companies have been taken private by PE in the last 4-5 years, which does not imply they are small or financially weak.

'SaaS-apocalypse' viewed as an opportunity: partnering with PEs and portfolio companies to improve margins using platforms like SASVA (own tuned open-source LLMs or third-party models like Anthropic) is viewed as a big growth opportunity.
Company hired a senior leader (Hari Abhayankar, ex-McKinsey) with experience in enterprise software at scale to lead this PE/professional services opportunity.

subsections.label: Salesforce Headless 360 / competitive positioning
points: Headless 360 gives customers options to use agents via APIs, but also increases integration work; not every customer is tech-savvy enough to leverage this without SI help.
Company working closely with Salesforce and expects increased engagement time in current installed base and new customers as a result.

subsections.label: Revenue mix / billing model seasonality
points: Historical seasonality was partly due to outcome-based pricing with one top customer, which has since reduced as a percentage of revenue; company worked hard to reduce that seasonality.

Going forward, whether using own IP (SASVA, iAURA, GenAI Hub) or third-party platforms (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.) under the hood, these are part of services engagements and not expected to introduce significant seasonality.

Third-party platform token costs are paid either by company or by customers depending on business model; use of AI technology is expected to be margin neutral or margin accretive, as it enables doing more work with fewer people.

subsections.label: OPD (outsourced product development) / SDLC compression
points: Tech vertical is strong in Persistent's OPD; tech is a creator (not just consumer) of AI technologies and less regulated, hence faster adoption into production, with valuable learnings for the company.

Possible compression in tech-vertical SDLC business due to AI-led productivity gains may occur, and company may also cannibalize its own SDLC business, but there remains ample new outsourcing opportunity given the company's relatively small $1.7 billion size and expected market-share rotation among providers.

So far, the company has been able to deliver more value and get more business in return despite early cannibalization dynamics in tech; management declines to give forward guidance beyond directional commentary.

subsections.label: Leadership additions
points: Ruchi Kulhari joined as Executive Vice President, Enterprise Strategy and Execution, partnering with CEO and executive leadership to drive critical priorities across business units and functions into initiatives with measurable outcomes; prior experience at Infosys, EXL, Unisys.

Hari Abhayankar joined as Executive Vice President and Global Head of Private Equity and Professional Services, spearheading global strategy and growth across PE investors, portfolio companies and professional services organizations; prior significant time at McKinsey consulting with enterprise software companies.

subsections.label: Partnerships
points: Partnership with DigitalOcean to give clients access to Anthropic, OpenAI and other models/tools, with private cloud and sovereign deployment options.
Co-innovation with NVIDIA (full-stack AI platform for biopharma) and Databricks (Merchant Risk Management Solution).

subsections.label: Geopolitical/macro risk
points: Middle East war situation flagged; company has zero to very little direct exposure to Middle East, but prolonged conflict could push oil prices higher for longer, impacting inflation and affecting the entire sector (not company-specific).

Additional overhang noted for FY27 versus FY26 due to the war situation, on top of prior year's challenges of weak US macro, tariff uncertainty, and GenAI-related deflation; management hopes overhang settles in coming weeks.

subsections.label: AI-led SDLC compression / cannibalization risk
points: Possible compression in tech-vertical business due to AI-driven productivity gains (shorter SDLC), with the company potentially cannibalizing its own business; management uncertain how this will play out given rapid pace of AI tool announcements (e.g., Anthropic).

subsections.label: Cash flow related delays
points: Additional delays in receipt of tax refunds and annual payment towards insurance premium contributed to decline in OCF to PAT this quarter.

subsections.label: Revenue run-rate target
points: The $2 billion by FY27 target is a run rate, not FY27 full-year revenue; company is marching towards it steadily and expects to reach it 'plus minus a quarter at worst', contingent on macro conditions not worsening materially.
Clarified that this refers to a quarterly annualized run rate with Q4 FY27 exit run-rate expected to be in the range of $500 million or so.

subsections.label: Margin aspiration
points: Margin trajectory previously communicated has been achieved; this is described as an aspiration, not guidance, continuing to target 16-17% EBIT margin range.
First priority remains growth and investing back into the business/developing capabilities; margin maintenance or improvement is a secondary goal pursued along the way.

subsections.label: FY27 growth outlook (directional, not guidance)
points: Company declines to give explicit forward-looking guidance, but directionally expects decent growth in the coming year, building AI and other capabilities, and working closely with partners (NVIDIA, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Snowflake).
Directional vertical pecking order for FY27: Healthcare Life Sciences and BFSI expected to be close to neck-and-neck at top, followed by tech — explicitly caveated as not guidance.

Our aspiration continues to be in the 16 to 17% range... it's not a guidance, it's an aspiration.
between one and two will be healthcare life sciences, BFSI followed by tech... this is no guidance... just directionally what we are seeing.

key_takeaways: We achieved a healthy revenue growth of 3.2% quarter-on-quarter and 16.2% year-on-year, delivering USD 436 million in Q4 FY26. This marks our 24th sequential quarter of revenue growth.

quarters.summary: Q1 FY2027 revenue was weighted lower given order book execution cycle, with management expecting revenue and margin recovery through Q2/Q3 as order book execution ramps up; full-year FY2027 operational EBITDA margin guided to mid-30s. Order book stood at Rs.1239 Crores at quarter-end, with a further Rs.177.5 Crores simulator order received post quarter-end from Ministry of Defense; management expects order book to reach ~Rs.2500 Crores by year-end and reiterated the cumulative Rs.4000 Crores FY2027+FY2028 turnover target, with simulators expected to contribute ~Rs.2000 Crores of that and anti-drone systems expected to be a much larger multi-thousand-Crore opportunity over time. Management flagged demand-side (not supply-side) constraints on order inflow due to delayed government tenders, but expects fast-track tenders to convert soon across simulators and anti-drone systems, and highlighted large addressable markets in exports (US ~$10 billion), Navy/Army simulators (~Rs.25,000 Crores), robotics, drone propulsion (Vector Technics), integrated smart border suite, and continued interest in acquisitions.

subsections.label: Margin movement drivers
points: Margin lower than guidance of 35% at EBITDA level largely due to negative operating leverage; significant portion of cost base (standalone and group) is fixed in nature, so lower revenue base compresses margins.
As revenue picks up through the year in line with order book execution, the same operating leverage is expected to work favorably.

Gross margin of 72.9% broadly consistent sequentially and year-on-year, indicating no structural change in underlying business profitability; EBITDA-level compression is a function of fixed cost base spread over a lower revenue quarter.

Q1 FY2026 had benefited from reversal of provisions created in FY2025 (Rs.7.65 Crores) that were no longer required, giving Q1 FY2026 an additional ~5% margin measurement; adjusting for this, Q1 FY2026 margin would be ~35%.
Q1 FY2027 saw an increase in warranty provisions (Rs.2.88 Crores) and incremental R&D costs (Rs.4.25 Crores).
Sequential margin of 27.3% broadly in line with 28.6% in Q4 FY2026, reflecting a stable underlying run rate.

Management affirms margin this quarter is a function of revenue timing and operating leverage, not any structural change in business profitability; expects margins to recover and end FY2027 with full-year operational EBITDA margin in the mid-30s, in line with guidance.

Fire incident at a subsidiary damaged certain inventory (adequately insured), resulting in a one-off exceptional loss of Rs.3.4 Crores in Q1 FY2027; adjusted PAT excluding this item would be ~Rs.37 Crores at ~26.1% margin.

subsections.label: Balance sheet and working capital
points: Increase in working capital cycle over year-end position primarily driven by buildup in advances to suppliers and inventory, both reflecting procurement and production activity underway to execute the order book for delivery through FY2027; consolidated working capital cycle stood at 257 days as of June 30, 2026.
Debtor days remained stable at 122 days.
Liquidity position of the group remains strong with cash and bank balances of approximately Rs.1217 Crores as of June 30, 2026, and the group remains debt free.

subsections.label: Order book movement
points: Consolidated order book stood at Rs.1239 Crores as of June 30, 2026, comprising Rs.920.6 Crores equipment order book and Rs.318.4 Crores AMC order book.
During the quarter, executed Rs.141.6 Crores of orders and secured Rs.44.6 Crores of new orders, resulting in a net reduction over the March position.

Subsequent to quarter-end, received a further order of Rs.177.5 Crores from the Ministry of Defense for upgradation and integration of tank and crew gunnery simulators, taking the order book (per analyst) to roughly Rs.1400 Crores.
Pipeline of opportunities across counter and training systems remains strong.

subsections.label: Order book outlook
points: Management expects to end the year at around Rs.2500 Crores of order book after execution for the current year.
Pipeline of orders currently being evaluated is healthy; once government procurement starts, a healthy portion of pipeline expected to convert into order book by year-end.

Rs.177 Crores tank gunnery order was actually an integration of existing simulators (driving simulator and tank gunnery simulator combined with AI-based scenarios), not a new simulator order; considered a small part of overall requirement.

subsections.label: Demand drivers and rush
points: Cumulative Rs.4000 Crores turnover target for FY2027+FY2028 reiterated; simulator segment expected to contribute ~Rs.2000 Crores of this.
Rs.700-800 Crores worth of simulator orders in the pipeline expected to materialize soon.
Anti-drone system tenders expected to run into at least a couple of thousand Crores of rupees in scope, much larger than simulators.
Government has allocated thousands of Crores for anti-drone systems post Op Sindoor (~Rs.800 Crores placed already); many more tenders expected.

Geopolitical rush for training due to ongoing wars is driving simulator demand globally, as countries previously unprepared now seek compressed training (e.g., Agniveers' 100-week training program shrunk to 30 weeks using Zen's simulators).

Demand-side constraint flagged: no tenders currently floated for anti-drone systems or simulators by government; expected fast-track process to release tenders soon, with orders finalized within a few months once floated.
Recent tenders saw Zen as single/sole qualified vendor due to strict IDDM design/code/drawing requirements; competition disqualified technically.
Government moving toward more 12-month fast-track procurement (FTP) cycles in urgent cases, but very large orders still routed through regular (up to 3-year) procurement cycles.
Naval and Army simulator market estimated at upwards of $2.5 billion (~Rs.25,000 Crores) each over coming years, though exact timing uncertain.
Order lifecycle for simulators typically ~10 years, with AMC revenue generated from the third year onward through the lifecycle.

subsections.label: Simulators
points: Simulator market expanding; recent Rs.177.5 Crores order seen as the start, with more orders expected in coming months.
New flight simulator developed for C295 aircraft, marking Air Force market entry; related technologies including 3D motion platform already available, enabling full motion simulator capability.
Company shortlisted for future Air Force simulator programs.

Naval simulators cover a wide range: bridge simulators, engine room simulators, submarine tactical trainers, and weapon simulators for Navy ships; considered the most exhaustive naval simulator range available.
Drone and counter-drone simulators developed to train operators on neutralizing swarm attacks (e.g., simulating 100 drones attacking a ship or ground post) using hard-kill decision training.

subsections.label: Anti-drone systems
points: Company recently launched a man-portable anti-drone system, awaiting evaluation by armed forces.
Government building out anti-drone requirements across border, tank, and infantry applications.
Anti-drone order flow currently constrained by lack of floated tenders, not by supply capability.

subsections.label: HyperStrike (interceptor drone)
points: HyperStrike is an interceptor drone designed to neutralize incoming Shahed-class drones within a ~20 km range; travels very fast (flown comfortably at 300 km/hr in tests) and chases targets until destruction if it misses.
Payload integration ongoing; product already demonstrated.
At speeds up to 400 km/hr the threat can be handled; drones flying faster than 400 km/hr are rare but a solution is being developed for that scenario as well.
Detection typically occurs at a probable distance of ~100 km, giving roughly 20 minutes reaction time before interception is required; management believes interception is feasible within this window.

subsections.label: Vector Technics (drone propulsion)
points: Capacity expanded to almost 300,000 units.
Vector Technics sells propulsion stacks to all customers agnostically, not just Zen; roughly 50% of queries received are from overseas including Europe and America.
Drone segment in India has slowed down, limiting order inflow to Vector Technics currently; expected to be first beneficiary once orders come to Indian drone companies.

Illustrative revenue potential: if orders come in at scale (~Rs.10,000 per unit basis), could translate to roughly Rs.300 Crores of revenue contribution, though management stresses this is a rough estimate pending actual order flow.

subsections.label: Integrated Smart Border Suite
points: Solution fuses sensors and human intelligence from multiple units (BSF, state police, army) into a common operating picture for decision makers.
Currently being demonstrated to various security forces; considered a very large market expected to have multiple players, not serviceable by a single company.
Zen expects to be a beneficiary when orders are rolled out.

subsections.label: Robotics / Vrishabh UGV
points: New unmanned ground vehicle 'Vrishabh' launched around Kargil Vijay Diwas; internal trials completed; customer trials expected next, though maturation will take time.
Robotics considered a newly entered capability expected to take longer to mature and contribute meaningfully to order book.

subsections.label: Laser-based directed energy weapons and R&D
points: Laser-based direct energy weapon systems and other cutting-edge technologies are in R&D; details cannot be disclosed at this time but will be announced as they progress.

subsections.label: Anti-drone neutralization technology
points: Multiple methods to neutralize drones: jamming ground-to-drone communication (drone loses signal, lands or returns home); GPS spoofing (drone misled into thinking it is in a different location, leading to disorientation, landing, or return home); for autonomous AI-based drones using topographical mapping and live camera matching, jamming does not work, requiring hard-kill weapon systems.
Hard-kill options include interceptor drones (like HyperStrike), high power microwave (HPM)-based solutions being developed by others, and a laser solution being offered to armed forces by Zen.
At drone speeds above 600 km/hr, jamming becomes a challenge; company is developing solutions for this higher-speed threat.

Detection-to-interception process: radar detects drone, AI dictates speed and available solution options, but a human ('man in the loop') must authenticate any hard-kill action before UAV launch or weapon engagement.

subsections.label: Competitive positioning
points: In recent tenders, Zen was effectively single-vendor as competitors failed to qualify technically under IDDM requirements (codes, drawings, design scrutiny); management expects competition to increase going forward.
Market is expanding in multiple directions with varied, specific requirements across multiple verticals; Zen will not be able to cater to all requirements and may lose some while winning others.
Current order flow softness attributed to demand-side issue (lack of floated tenders), not Zen's supply capability.
Naval market considered a large growth opportunity given India's largely unguarded peninsular maritime borders and the strategic importance of the Indian Ocean.

subsections.label: Illustrative market sizing methodology (tank simulators)
points: Management provided illustrative calculation: assuming ~4000 tanks with 3 operators plus 3 backup operators each (24,000 soldiers), each requiring 200 hours of training (10% of 2000 duty hours), yields ~48 lakh hours of training demand; dividing by 2000 hours per simulator implies ~2400 simulators needed.
Actual procurement to date represents only a small slice of this total requirement; management suggests multiplying current orders by ~30-100x to estimate true market size.
This calculation used to illustrate that army/navy simulator markets are still in early/proving stages relative to true potential demand.

subsections.label: Comparable threat scale (competitive context)
points: Referenced example: China's infantry units reportedly equipped with ~1000 drones each, highlighting scale of drone swarm threats and corresponding large addressable market for interceptor drone solutions, particularly for Shahed-class threats.

subsections.label: Acquisition strategy
points: Management confirmed active search to acquire more companies, expecting them to add new dimensions to the company similar to the ARI acquisition and other past acquisitions, with huge revenue potential.
Most QIP funds have been deployed, but the company has built sufficient cash to invest in interesting acquisition targets.
Management characterizes upcoming acquisition news as very good news for investors, though specifics were not disclosed.

Increasing competition expected in tenders going forward as government IDDM qualification processes evolve, which may result in some disqualifications/losses for Zen in certain verticals.
Robotics and other new capability investments (autonomous vehicles) expected to take at least two to three years to mature and contribute to revenue.

quarters.summary: Q4/FY26 revenue and margins declined YoY due to order-timing shifts, with bulk of orders scheduled for execution from FY27 onwards; management reiterated long-term guidance of 35% operational EBITDA margin and 25% PAT margin, and a cumulative ~Rs.4000 Crores turnover target for FY2027-2028 combined, backed by a large order book (Rs.1336 Crores consolidated) and a multi-thousand-crore bidding pipeline skewed ~55:45 toward anti-drone systems over simulators.

subsections.label: Margin drivers for the quarter
points: Five factors weighed on margins: (1) lower Q4 revenue base vs strong Q4 FY2025 execution, causing margin compression given largely fixed cost base at standalone and group level; (2) year-end performance incentives recognized for certain employees, adding ~Rs.5 Crores sequential employee cost; (3) updated warranty provisioning percentages for anti-drone system products supplied in FY2025 based on actual expense data, adding ~Rs.3.1 crores incremental warranty expense; (4) ~Rs.2.7 Crores of post-supply expenses (on-ground installation support, logistics, external consultants) for an export order delivered in FY2026; (5) R&D expenses higher by ~Rs.3.3 Crores sequentially, reflecting investment in future product portfolio and expected to remain structurally elevated going forward.
Unlike the other four one-time/period-specific factors, the R&D increase is a structural commitment that will continue.
Despite quarterly margin volatility, long-term guidance of 35% operational EBITDA margin and 25% PAT margin remains intact.

subsections.label: Working capital and liquidity
points: Increase in working capital days primarily due to higher inventory days and advances to suppliers required for projects currently being executed for FY2027 deliveries.
Notable improvement in DSO position, improving by 42 days from Dec-25 to end of FY2026.
Liquidity position of the group remains strong; group remains debt-free.

Management (CFO) guided long-term working capital cycle to remain around 140-150 days; will stick to existing outsourced-manufacturing/assembler model even with the new manufacturing license, manufacturing only critical components in-house for arms.

key_figures.label: Order book expected to be dispatched in FY2027 (product)
Implied FY2028 revenue (per analyst math, confirmed reasonable by mgmt)

subsections.label: FY2027 revenue conversion from order book
points: Of the Rs.1336 Crores order book, ~Rs.1000 Crores of product is expected to be dispatched in FY2027, with most deliveries happening in Q2 and Q3 of FY2027; the balance ~Rs.326 Crores is AMC revenue spread over the AMC contract period.
Management confirmed essentially the entire order book will be recognized into revenue.

subsections.label: Order inflow sustainability and outlook
points: Management expects orders to accelerate in FY2027 across both the simulation segment and anti-drone segment, with demand far exceeding earlier estimates.

Management reiterated the cumulative Rs.4000 Crores turnover target for FY2027 and FY2028 combined, and agreed it is reasonable to expect the order book could touch Rs.3000 Crores at some point in time, even if FY2028 execution is around Rs.2500 Crores.
New arms-license-related sales may contribute partially to these figures but will not be significant in the first two years; more significant contribution expected from the third year onwards.
Orders were expected in Q1 FY2027, with management indicating confidence should build in Q1 and further visibility for the second year emerging as the year progresses.

Bottleneck for delayed orders explained: post Operation Sindoor, government went slow on regular simulator procurement and instead accelerated emergency procurement of anti-drone systems, delaying simulator orders which are now expected to come through soon.

subsections.label: Subsidiary order book detail
points: ARI and UTS combined are expected to generate ~Rs.365 Crores of revenue in the next 12 months.
Beyond FY2027, guided expectation (referred to as 'FY2022' in transcript, likely FY2028) is ARI to do around Rs.300 Crores and UTS between Rs.150-200 Crores.

subsections.label: Subsidiary contribution detail
points: Consolidated revenue Rs.688 Crores vs standalone Rs.423 Crores; subsidiaries contributed Rs.260 Crores in FY2026, majority from UTS and ARI.
ARI was acquired at end of FY2025, so full-year consolidation happened for the first time in FY2026.
Anticipated margins for both ARI and UTS expected to remain in similar range going forward.

subsections.label: Anti-drone system evolution
points: Focus areas of anti-drone systems and simulators have gained prominence following Israel-Iran, Armenia-Azerbaijan, and Ukraine-Russia wars; post-Israel-Iran war focus has at least doubled (2x) from original projections.
Hard kill options introduced in addition to pure software jamming, aiming to neutralize Shahed-type drones at a fraction of their cost.
AI has taken a major role in development at two levels: process-level (AI-driven software development) and embedded/product level (AI-native simulators and anti-drone systems).
Preemptively widened frequency dominance from 400MHz-6GHz to 70MHz-12GHz to counter bad actors making drones at unconventional frequencies (100MHz, 10MHz, 10GHz, 12GHz).
Neutralization capabilities include RF jamming, GNSS jamming, RCWS guns, and integration of L70 and ZU-23 air defence guns; radar is fully indigenized.
Latest anti-drone system launched at North Tech event in Prayagraj; considered future-proof with large addressable market in India and worldwide.

subsections.label: New product launches
points: Vrishabh: unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) capable of combat, logistics, and casualty evacuation; integrated with MMG, LMG, direct fire, AGS, indirect fire weapon systems with well-absorbed recoil; manual or autonomous operation with Ackermann steering; commercial launch planned in FY2027.

Cybersecurity suite (developed by ARI/ANAWAVE under Commodore Ahluwalia) integrable into control/command centers, ships, and aircraft; six layers - awareness/training, monitoring/intelligence, protection/prevention, encryption/data sovereignty, threat perception/investigation/response, and post-quantum readiness; zero foreign dependencies, positioned as an Atmanirbhar Bharat example.

Anti-drone simulator developed by ARI as an advanced training platform separate from the live anti-drone system, teaching detection, tracking, and neutralization of single-drone or swarm threats with configurable, adjustable threat-level scenarios.

30mm smart ammunition (with AI-Turing, an associate company) - RF-based programming, pre-fragmentation with tungsten ball core, usable on standard 30mm cannons without weapon modification, also usable as anti-drone ammunition; testing ongoing with certifying agency involved, manufacturing/supply expected to start next financial year.

CIWS (Close-In Weapon System) - gun-missile system developed with AiTuring Systems for naval forces, combining weapon system with shorter-range missile and built-in radar as a self-contained, lower-cost hard-kill solution.

HyperStrike interceptor drone: AI-enabled tracking/guidance with manual override capability; positioned as a low-cost counter to Shahed-type drones; production planned to start in FY2027; high-speed propulsion supplied by Vector Technics.

Management believes the interceptor drone (HyperStrike) could become the largest product in the portfolio within two years, potentially the most sought-after product worldwide given the cutting-edge research involved.

subsections.label: Arms and ammunition licensing
points: Company has received both weapon license and ammunition license (applied two years back); remote control weapon station developed as expansion of Hard Kill offering.
12.7mm, 20mm, and especially 30mm identified as caliber preferred for bringing down drones; weapon systems planned for launch this year, majority next year.

Ammunition manufacturing/supply targeted to start next financial year, with testing and certifying agency engagement ongoing; management expects a two-year period to be sufficient to get everything in order.
Company focused on developing 'smart' ammunition rather than 'dumb' ammunition to preserve margins.

subsections.label: Competitive positioning
points: Management believes its anti-drone system, used effectively in Operation Sindoor, is in the top three in the world, if not the absolute top, citing the wide 70MHz-12GHz detection/jamming range that surprises other vendors and customers at exhibitions.
Simulator market showing strong demand, particularly drone-related/anti-drone simulation and naval simulation (cited context: Hormuz Strait navigation, mine-handling training needs).

subsections.label: Export potential
points: Management factored exports into targets; expects export orders to play a major role given rising global demand from multiple wars.
ARI (100% subsidiary) has connections in South America and Europe being leveraged to push naval simulation and other solutions internationally.
Naval simulation and combat naval training centers expected to be a large revenue contributor going forward, with positive response not only in India.

subsections.label: Sector consolidation view
points: Management expects a consolidation phase in the defense industry over the next three to five years, where a few companies with strong indigenous R&D emerge as 'Googles or Amazons of the defense world'.
Government reportedly willing to consolidate vendor lists (e.g., narrowing ten vendors down to three) in indigenous procurement.

subsections.label: M&A / acquisition strategy
points: Company is looking at acquisitions in simulation, anti-drone systems, and 'Pareto Technologies' (key technologies determining disproportionate share of outcomes, akin to the 20% of technology determining 80% of war outcome).
Approach: identify smaller, resource-constrained companies dispersed across too many projects, help them focus resources on the most promising one, and provide capital plus ecosystem guidance.

subsections.label: Diversification and facilitator role
points: After ~25 years focused solely on army simulators, company diversified into anti-drone systems ahead of competitors, gaining a 4-5 year R&D lead.

Zen is positioning itself as a facilitator, working with a set of associate/subsidiary companies (ARI, ANAWAVE, AiTuring, Vector Technics) to unleash creativity and holistically address market demand.
Actively evaluating acquisitions in simulation, anti-drone systems, and Pareto Technologies for the future.

subsections.label: Policy and procurement risk
points: Draft DAP (Defence Acquisition Procedure) had an early provision that could equate foreign technology (via ToT) with IDDM (Indigenously Designed, Developed, Manufactured) status; management views this as dangerous since it could allow foreign counterparts to undercut Indian capabilities developed after years of R&D by transferring older tech and killing the indigenous product's commercialization.
Management flags a distinction needed between 'foreign design developed and Indian assembled/manufactured' versus true IDDM, and hopes wiser voices will prevail in the final DAP.

Foreign procurement (excluding Rafale) has risen even amid record indigenization push; channel checks suggest armed forces may prefer 'instant patch-up' foreign solutions over waiting for indigenized systems, posing a risk to near-term order inflow going to domestic players.
Domestic government ordering process viewed as slow and subject to delay across multiple rounds of approval.

subsections.label: Operational/one-time cost risk
points: Warranty provisioning for anti-drone products supplied in FY2025 was revised upward based on actual utilization data, indicating potential for further warranty cost adjustments.
Post-supply support costs (installation, logistics, consultants) incurred on export orders add to costs in period of delivery.

subsections.label: Order timing risk
points: Simulator orders were delayed because government procurement processes were diverted toward emergency anti-drone procurement following Operation Sindoor, illustrating order-timing volatility tied to external crisis events.
Regular tenders (as opposed to single-vendor tenders) may take longer, cited at ~18 months, adding timing uncertainty to pipeline conversion.

subsections.label: Forward guidance summary
points: Management reiterated the long-term guidance of 35% operational EBITDA margin and 25% PAT margin despite quarterly volatility from one-time cost items.

Cumulative turnover target of Rs.4000 Crores for FY2027 and FY2028 combined reiterated; implies order book could reasonably touch Rs.3000 Crores at some point, even if FY2028 execution comes in around Rs.2500 Crores.
Working capital cycle expected to normalize to 140-150 days over the long term despite near-term buildup from inventory and supplier advances tied to FY2027 execution.
Orders expected to come in Q1 FY2027 (not later than Q2), which should provide comfort on achieving current-year targets; visibility on the following year expected to build as FY2027 progresses.
Arms/ammunition-related revenue expected to be immaterial in the first two years, with meaningful contribution from the third year onwards.

key_takeaways: Consolidated revenues for Q4 FY2026 stood at Rs.178.1 crores, broadly in line with Rs.177.8 Crores reported in Q3 FY2026 and lower by 45.2% year-on-year compared to the Rs.325 Crores in Q4 FY2025.
The revenue trajectory in FY2026 has been impacted by the timing of order inflows with the bulk of the orders received over the past several months scheduled for execution from FY2027 onwards.

Operational EBITDA for the quarter stood at Rs.51 Crores, which translates to an operational EBITDA margin of 28.6% lower by approximately 900 basis points sequentially and 1390 basis points year-on-year.
While these factors are weighed in on the quarterly margins, our long-term guidance of 35% operational EBITDA and 25% PAT margins remain intact.
Consolidated revenues for FY2026 stood at Rs.687.7 Crores, lower by 29.4%, as against Rs.973.6 Crores in FY2025.

The consolidated order book stood at Rs.1336 Crores as on March 31, 2026. The standalone order book as on March 31, 2026, stood at Rs.1222.6 Crores. Majority of this order book is scheduled for execution from FY2027 onwards and provides clear revenue visibility for the next financial year.
Our Days Sales Outstanding at the end of FY2026 stood at approximately 119 days compared to 161 days on December 31, 2025, an improvement of 42 days.
The liquidity position of the group continues to remain strong. Cash and bank balances aggregated to Rs.1308 Crores as of March 31, 2026. The group remains debt-free.
We stick to that prediction of our projection of Rs.4000 Crores turnover in FY2027 and 2028 put together, so, we are very comfortable with those figures now.

ZENTEC.about: Zen Technologies Limited was incorporated in 1996. The company designs develop and manufacture combat training solutions and Counter-drone solutions for defense and security forces. It is actively involved in the indigenization of technologies, which are beneficial to Indian armed forces, state police forces, and paramilitary forces. Zen Technologies is headquartered in Hyderabad, India with offices in India, UAE, and the USA. [1] [2] [3]

quarters.summary: Smartworks reported another strong sequential quarter (Q1 FY27) with revenue up 44% YoY/5% QoQ to INR 546 crores, normalized EBITDA up 74% YoY/8% QoQ to INR 107 crores (margin 19.6%), and normalized PAT nearly tripling YoY to INR 39 crores. Management reaffirmed FY27 guidance of 28-30% revenue growth, 19-20% normalized EBITDA margin, and operational footprint over 13 million sq ft by March 2027, anchored by INR 5,400 crores of contracted revenue (87% of FY27 revenue already contracted). A fresh capex cycle (INR 550-600 crores for FY27) has begun to secure supply through FY28/29, with two marquee properties (Eastbridge Mumbai and Eastside Pune) landing in H2 FY27. ROCE held at 21.5% through the heaviest investment quarter, expected to expand meaningfully through FY28 as the capex cohort matures.

key_figures.label: Normalized operating cash flow growth YoY

subsections.label: Revenue drivers
points: Revenue increase driven by existing clients expanding, centres maturing, and new seats added.
Majority of revenue comes from core rental business which grows consistently every quarter.

Growth increasingly comes from existing clients expanding across the network even while winning new logos; expansion revenue is characterized as the lowest-risk revenue — low acquisition cost, low ramp risk.

subsections.label: Margin drivers
points: EBITDA margin improvement largely driven by centre maturity, cost excellence initiatives (particularly on energy), and operating leverage at both centre and corporate levels.

subsections.label: Cash flow
points: Negative working capital model with roughly six days debtors; OCF/EBITDA structurally runs above 1x.
Dip in OCF/EBITDA this quarter largely due to INR 33 crores of security deposit paid to landlords to book buildings through FY28 and partially FY29 — 'paying today to own tomorrow's growth.'
Fair amount of float income from security deposits received from tenants also noted.

subsections.label: Capital allocation / balance sheet
points: Balance sheet remains virtually debt-free with net debt of INR 5.6 crores and borrowing cost under 9%.
Credit rating upgraded earlier this year.
Growth at Smartworks is self-funded by design — negative working capital and durable cash flows mean growth funded primarily from internally generated cash.
International growth (Singapore) funds itself from international cash flows with no risk taken on the Indian balance sheet, while India cash flows are deployed into the domestic platform.

subsections.label: Capital efficiency / ROCE
points: ROCE held at 21.5% despite INR 151 crores of fresh capital deployed into capex, through the heaviest investment quarter in company history.
Gap between EBITDA and PAT narrowing every quarter as centres mature and complete payback — reflects how much operating profit converts to bottom line, improving mechanically as portfolio ages.
As the capex cohort matures and completes payback, ROCE expected to expand meaningfully through FY28.

subsections.label: Capex guidance/composition
points: FY27 capex estimated between INR 550-600 crores, comprising refurbishment capex (done every three years) and fresh capex for new assets already signed.
New fit-out capex at INR 1,350 per sq ft, increasing ~5% every year due to cost inflation.
Refurbishment capex is closer to about 15% of the initial capex value, done every three years (~5% per year equivalent).
More than 3.5 million sq ft of space already signed, under construction or coming up for construction within first two quarters of the year.
FY25 operational footprint was 8.1 million sq ft, matured to 10.1 million sq ft by March FY26; guiding 2.5-3 million sq ft of operational addition this year.

subsections.label: VAS / non-lease revenue
points: Non-lease rental revenue (largely value-added services) grew from INR 22 crores to INR 68 crores YoY (nearly tripled) even as overall revenue grew ~30%, due to increasing base of occupied seats.
VAS focus started only about three quarters back with limited services currently; opportunity to increase further but not factored into current-year projections as most are in pilot stage.
VAS is largely on a take-rate basis with third-party suppliers — no expense on books, hence margin accretive; magnitude for this year difficult to predict as verticals are still being launched.

subsections.label: Client concentration & lock-in
points: No client typically takes more than 30% of a campus.
Through every cycle since inception, the company has not surrendered a single campus.
Committed client lock-ins cover landlord rental commitments roughly two times over at the portfolio level.

subsections.label: Retention nuance
points: Seat retention of 74% should be read alongside committed occupancy of mature centres at 92%; occupied seats actually rose during the quarter despite lower client count — reflects deliberate portfolio rebalancing and mark-to-market repricing at renewal.
Client count is down while occupied seats and revenue are up — 'fewer, bigger, longer-duration clients' by design.

Retention pattern is seasonal — most churn happens in H1 (decisions to move offices happen in Q1-Q2), with churn shrinking in Q3-Q4, as seen in FY26 (Q2 retention 74% but full-year retention ended at 80-88%).
Clients being churned came in at a lower base 4-5 years ago; markets have corrected and Smartworks has already found replacement customers, keeping mature committed occupancy at 92%.

subsections.label: Occupancy trajectory
points: Occupancy dip to 81% from 82% purely due to newly opened buildings still filling up, not demand weakness.
Mature centres running at 89% occupancy on 9.1 million sq ft with 92% committed occupancy — indicates where newer cohort is headed.

Expect occupancy to range 80-85% over next three quarters despite high growth, due to new centre ramp-up; not expected to significantly impact margins since older mature centres are approaching 90%+ occupancy.

subsections.label: Pricing power
points: Realization for mature footprint incremental seats rose from INR 170/sq ft (previous fiscal) to INR 181/sq ft (Q1 FY27), an increase of INR 11/sq ft.
Closest competitor prices almost 10-15% higher than Smartworks' price points, indicating room to price up further.
Company believes both volume (2.5-3 million sq ft addition) and value/pricing will help achieve the year's projected numbers.

subsections.label: Landlord terms
points: Preferred terms from institutional landlords are a function of the volume of deals Smartworks is doing (e.g., Vikhroli/Bombay acquisition — one of the top 10 largest office space deals in the country).
Institutional landlords gaining confidence from Smartworks' track record and ability to fill buildings quickly.
Non-institutional to institutional landlord mix currently ~65:35 and expected to remain similar over the next few quarters/years.

key_figures.label: Additional Singapore seats available to sell post-acquisition

subsections.label: Cohort mix strategy
points: 1,000+ seat cohort is the primary engine of growth, up from 12% in FY22 to 41% now, driven by network effect — leasing large campuses and filling them quickly with large, long-duration clients.
GCC is seen as a primary growth driver with significant headroom; sub-100 seat cohort expected to shrink by design as focus shifts to larger clients and annuity revenue.
Target is to reduce IT/ITES dependency to 25-30/35% range while diversifying into manufacturing, engineering, and professional services/business consultancy clients.

subsections.label: GCC / SmartVantage detail
points: GCC clients include Switzerland's largest financial institution, a global CX and digital services leader, and (this quarter) the subsidiary of a leading Japanese NBFC at the Mumbai campus.
GCC demand is diversifying beyond US to Europe and Japan; recent handovers include one of the largest Swiss banks and one large manufacturing GCC.

SmartVantage platform (soft-launched a couple of quarters ago) has already won two large contracts for additional services beyond seat revenue; management expects this revenue to meaningfully double over the next two years.

GCC/SmartVantage revenue upside has not yet hit the books — most GCC spaces are still under fit-out or just handed over; value accretion from additional services expected to build over the next two to three quarters.
Any client segment (not just GCC) that comes into the ecosystem is seen as ROCE accretive given the pricing/value proposition Smartworks offers.

subsections.label: Singapore / international expansion
points: Acquired Work Studio in Singapore, funded entirely from Smartworks' own generated cash flows over the last year, at cost-of-construction pricing (building ~14,000-17,000 sq ft in Singapore costs the same).

Not looking to scale up Singapore meaningfully beyond current ~80,000 sq ft; may add one or two more centres opportunistically depending on performance of new centres and pre-filled demand for a third new centre.
Singapore market is meaningfully more profitable given cost efficiency and the Indian operating structure brought in, but strategic capital focus remains on India (17 million sq ft platform).

Singapore existing centre occupancy pre-acquisition was ~88%, while Work Studio was acquired at ~60% occupancy; combined seat count now 1,500+ with 400-450 additional seats available to sell post-acquisition.

subsections.label: Client sector mix
points: Call centres are not separately classified below IT/ITES and are not believed to be a significant number within that category; retention within IT/ITES-type clients that had the option to leave stood at 74%, and non-retained clients were largely backfilled given 92% committed occupancy.

subsections.label: Supply security
points: Every building needed for the next two years is already secured; work on FY29 has begun.
Long-term rights acquired to properties in prime locations gives uninterrupted access to quality buildings for the next 10-15 years.

Eastbridge (Vikhroli, Mumbai, 8.15 lakh sq ft) declared the world's largest standalone managed campus, surpassing the company's own prior record; Eastside in Pune also coming — both land in H2 FY27 with strong pre-fills.
Asset-liability mismatch is eliminated up to FY29.

subsections.label: Supply risk mitigation
points: Even with a delay of a quarter or two on any project, enough supply is locked in that it will not derail the business plan; buffer of 700,000-800,000 sq ft added versus the 2.5-3 million sq ft guided range allows another asset to compensate for any delay.
Company builds in a buffer of at least one or two quarters into its planning in case of handover delays.

Over the last 12-18 months the platform has attracted marquee institutional-grade developers (DLF, Hiranandani, Tata, Panchshil, Salarpuria) who deliver on schedule, serving as a hedge against completion risk, versus the earlier varied mix of unorganized/non-institutional developers.

subsections.label: Scale economics
points: At 10.4 million sq ft operational, Smartworks is the largest platform in the industry; scale earns preferred terms from landlords and lower unit costs across leasing and operations.
Green initiatives including solar adoption across campuses are cutting energy costs and improving economics for the company and its clients.
New investment cycles land on a larger, mature near-fixed-cost base, so each new cohort's ramp-up drag on margins keeps shrinking; at current scale, adding new centres/capex is not margin dilutive.
Once a centre crosses breakeven, incremental revenue flows disproportionately to EBITDA.

subsections.label: Market positioning
points: Office market is at a record high; Flex is its biggest buyer and is consolidating fast towards Smartworks.
Widening gap in Flex market — top 10 operators' share climbing every year (67% in 2024, 72% in 2025, 74% in H1 current year), with the long tail below 5% and shrinking.
Scale, balance sheet strength, and developer relations are now the 'price of entry'; smaller players cannot add buildings the way large platforms can.
Smartworks' lead over the next largest operator in area is expected to keep expanding.
AI and GCCs are expanding office demand; AI workforce inside India's GCCs set to grow fourfold by 2030, landing in premium collaboration-rich campuses that Smartworks builds.
Smartworks growing at 44% versus commercial real estate >6% and Flex market 23% — roughly seven times the office market and twice the Flex market.

subsections.label: Regional diversification of new supply
points: New supply/upcoming centres are diversified across multiple cities — West, South, North all hold significant portions of upcoming supply (per Slide 15 of investor presentation).

key_figures.label: Refurbishment capex as percentage of initial capex

subsections.label: Work Studio acquisition (Singapore)
points: Acquisition completed via cash flows Smartworks generated from its centres over the last year, at cost-of-construction pricing.
Doubled Singapore seat count to 1,500+ seats.

No risk taken on the Indian balance sheet; capital allocation philosophy is that international growth funds itself from international cash flows while India cash flows are deployed into the domestic platform.

subsections.label: One-year listing anniversary
points: This month marks one year since Smartworks listed on NSE and BSE.
Management states it has delivered the fastest growth in the industry in area, revenue and EBITDA, with steadily rising market share quarter after quarter.
Every durable metric — revenue, EBITDA, margins, PAT, ROCE — has continued to move up for 5 consecutive quarters post listing.

subsections.label: Supply/completion risk
points: Reports of completion delays among developers were raised by an analyst; management maintains supply-side visibility is very high and any one/two quarter delay would not derail the business plan given the buffer of locked-in supply and multiple compensating assets.

Shift towards institutional-grade developers (DLF, Hiranandani, Tata, Panchshil, Salarpuria) seen as a hedge against completion risk versus earlier reliance on unorganized/non-institutional developers.

subsections.label: Occupancy volatility risk
points: New centres and base effect can cause a quarter or two of occupancy volatility as newly added seats take time to ramp up, though this is not expected to significantly impact margins given mature centre occupancy trending toward 90%+.

subsections.label: Client concentration/churn risk
points: Deliberate churn of certain longer-tenure customers who signed at a lower base 4-5 years ago as markets have corrected; company proactively manages this by finding replacement customers, keeping committed occupancy healthy.
No client is allowed to take more than 30% of a campus, limiting concentration risk.

subsections.label: Reaffirmed guidance
points: Reaffirmed guidance of 28-30% revenue growth, normalized EBITDA margins between 19-20%, and operational footprint of over 13 million sq ft by March 2027, anchored by INR 5,400 crores of contracted revenue and a ready pipeline of signed buildings already under construction.
ROCE held at 21.5% through the heaviest investment quarter in company history; expected to expand meaningfully through FY28 as capex cohort matures and completes payback.

subsections.label: Revenue growth confidence
points: 28-30% guidance range reflects the fact that new centres take about 12 months to ramp up and there might be delays on property handovers; existing committed occupancy is already at 92% so there isn't much to sell on the existing base — growth will predominantly come from new centres ramping through Q3/Q4.

subsections.label: VAS / SmartVantage outlook
points: SmartVantage platform revenue (beyond seat revenue) expected to meaningfully double over the next two years.
VAS revenue growth from the current INR 68 crores base not specifically guided for this year as most services remain in pilot stage.

risk_register.note: New centres take time to fill; occupancy may see quarter-to-quarter volatility (guided 80-85% over next three quarters) but not expected to materially affect margins.
Seat retention at 74% due to deliberate proactive churn of older, lower-base clients as markets corrected; largely backfilled, keeping committed occupancy at 92%.

themes.label: Margin expansion / operating leverage
themes.note: EBITDA margin expanded to 19.6% from 16.2% YoY driven by centre maturity, cost excellence (energy) and operating leverage; margins continue expanding irrespective of capex cycle.

themes.label: Contracted revenue visibility / annuity model
themes.note: INR 5,400 crores contracted revenue covers 87% of FY27; enterprise annuity demand at 92% of rental revenue with long tenure contracts.

themes.label: Capex cycle / capacity expansion
themes.note: Fresh capex cycle started this quarter (INR 550-600 crores FY27 guidance) to secure buildings for FY28/29; capex step-up drove negative free cash flow this quarter but is ROCE-accretive by design.

themes.label: GCC / AI-driven demand tailwind
themes.note: GCC contribution rose to 21% of revenue from 15% in FY26, with AI workforce in GCCs expected to grow fourfold by 2030; significant headroom flagged.

themes.label: Market share consolidation in Flex
themes.note: Top 10 Flex operators' share of leasing rose from 67% (2024) to 74% (H1 current year); Smartworks growing at 44% vs Flex market growth of 23% and office market >6%.

themes.label: Client mix diversification away from IT/ITES
themes.note: IT/ITES share of client mix fell from 44% (FY24) to 35% (Q1 FY27) as company diversifies into manufacturing, engineering and professional services.

themes.label: Retention vs committed occupancy divergence
themes.note: Seat retention at 74% (down) reflects deliberate churn of lower-value legacy clients, while committed occupancy of mature centres remains healthy at 92%.

key_takeaways: This month marks one year since Smartworks listed on the NSE and BSE.
Revenues stood at INR 546 crores, up 44% year-on-year and 5% quarter-on-quarter.
Normalized EBITDA of INR 107 crores, up 74% year-on-year and 8% quarter-on-quarter, with the margin expanding from 19% in the last quarter to 19.6% this quarter.
Normalized PAT stood at INR 39 crores, which nearly tripled from INR 13 crores in the same quarter last year.
Committed contracted revenue today stands at approximately INR 5,400 crores, and 87% of our FY27 revenue is already contracted for.
A fresh capex cycle has started this quarter.
We reaffirm our guidance of 28% to 30% revenue growth, normalized EBITDA margins between 19% to 20%, and an operational footprint of over 13 million square foot by March 2027.
Our ROCE held at 21.5% through the heaviest investment quarter in our history, and as this capex cohort matures and completes payback, we expect ROCE to expand meaningfully through FY28.

SMARTWORKS.about: Incorporated in 2015, Smartworks Coworking Spaces Limited is engaged in the business of customized managed workspace solutions, offering fully serviced, tech-enabled office environments.[1]

quarters.summary: Management framed FY27 as "a year of rebuilding earnings strength" after a difficult MFI cycle, with priorities on franchise quality, collections, balance-sheet strength, mix-shift to secured, and liability franchise improvement. Net loss narrowed to ₹34cr, down more than 80% both YoY and sequentially, indicating a clear normalization trajectory though profitability is not yet restored. Disbursements re-accelerated (+49% YoY) with mix shifting toward non-JLG, and asset quality metrics (collections, SMA, GNPA) improved meaningfully. The bank continues its structural rebalance toward secured lending, is ramping CGFMU credit-guarantee coverage to mitigate credit costs, and is pursuing an ARC sale of stressed assets, a reverse merger (pending NCLT), and a new core banking system, while guiding to FY28 targets of 15% ROE, ~8% NIM, 55% secured mix and 25-30% loan growth, and a path to double-digit ROE by FY27 exit.

subsections.label: Q1 FY27 framing
points: Management framed FY27 as "a year of rebuilding earnings strength" after a difficult MFI cycle, with priorities: franchise quality, collections, balance-sheet strength, mix-shift to secured, and liability franchise improvement.
Reported metrics indicate a clear normalization trajectory, though profitability is not yet restored.
Net loss of ₹34cr in Q1 FY27, reduced by more than 80% both YoY (vs Q1 FY26) and QoQ (vs Q4 FY26).

subsections.label: Capital, Liquidity, and Funding Actions
points: Funding plan: raise ~₹500cr Tier-2 NCDs in FY27; expected to add ~250 bps CRAR (back-of-envelope).
Liability optimization: premature redemption of ₹200cr debt tranche at 12.5% coupon (mid-August), expected savings ~₹20cr; intention is not to carry incremental net expensive debt.
Equity raise: management stated no equity issuance anticipated through FY27.
Surplus liquidity of ₹3,200cr with LCR at 227%.
CD ratio at 83.8% and CRAR at 17.4% as of Q1 FY27.

subsections.label: Funding cost trend
points: Funding cost: cost of funds 7.7%, down ~40 bps YoY and ~50 bps QoQ; management expects repricing benefits to continue in coming quarters.

subsections.label: Business Momentum
points: Disbursements re-accelerated with total disbursements up 49% YoY, driven by JLG +5% YoY and Non-JLG +93% YoY.
Management emphasized calibrated growth and underwriting discipline: "grow assets to the right quality and risk profile rather than forcing growth for its own sake."

subsections.label: Portfolio growth guidance / mix

Micro/JLG: management expects JLG to remain ~25% of the portfolio over "next two to three years," with JLG + microbanking targeted growth 15–20%, i.e., below 20%.
Strategic mix trajectory reiterated: move from unsecured to secured; keep micro/JLG capped while the overall balance sheet grows.

subsections.label: Structural Portfolio Rebalance
points: Micro concentration down: GSG (microfinance) portfolio now 26% of gross loan book (incl. BC exposure also cited at 26%), down from 88–90% in Mar-2020.
Secured lending 51% of gross loan book (vs 45% a year ago), with a stated aim of 55% secured share.
Management claims this reduces margin volatility and improves risk resilience.
JLG X-bucket collection efficiency improved to 99.7% in Q1 FY27 from 98.6% in Q1 FY26.
Microbanking SMA pool improved to 1.2% in Jun-26 from 1.3% in Mar-26 and 5.1% in Jun-25.

subsections.label: Microbanking Business Loan (MBBL/MBPL)
points: Product positioned as a graduation path: "serves customers who have demonstrated repayment discipline and are ready to graduate beyond traditional group lending."
MBPL portfolio grew 147% YoY and 11% QoQ, now >30% of the microbanking portfolio.
Penetration still <20% of customer base (management sees large runway).
Customer sourcing: currently almost entirely existing customers with 2–3 cycles; new-to-bank is only a "pilot… may not be even 100 or 200."
Underwriting: handled by a separate underwriting team with "complete underwriting as is the norm in all other unsecured loan business," plus dedicated collection team.
Post-Apr'25 MBBL pool outstanding ₹1,042cr out of total MBBL outstanding of ₹1,250cr, with delinquency/NPA on the post-Apr'25 pool at ~0.4%.

subsections.label: Non-Micro / Diversified Assets
points: MSME portfolio at ₹4,482cr, up 12% YoY; micro-led segment disbursement yield ~18%; MSME GNPA ₹169cr (~3.8% ratio).
Housing loans portfolio at ₹1,005cr, up 8% YoY.
Business banking portfolio (BBD/BBG) up 40% YoY.
CV/Construction equipment: composition refined; used vehicle ~30% of disbursements to balance growth with risk.
Gold loans: pushing penetration via digital LOS to improve TAT/controls/efficiency; current scale small (~₹300cr mentioned by CEO in Q&A).

MSME secured: ₹168cr
"CBC": ₹62cr

subsections.label: Liability Franchise
points: Deposits mix improvement led by CASA and retail term deposit growth; deposits grew 3% YoY overall, with CASA up 15% YoY and retail term deposits up 15% YoY.
CASA + retail term deposits reached 83% of deposits, up from 74% a year ago.
CASA ratio at 22% as of Jun-26.

subsections.label: Technology & Process Transformation

Bank "about to launch new CBS."
Objective: scale without commensurate cost growth (workflow automation, digitized journeys, reduced manual intervention).

subsections.label: Balance Sheet Cleanup + Corporate Actions + Operating Model Changes
points: ARC sale strategy: bank will pursue ARC sale of stressed JLG and "wheels" portfolio to accelerate cleanup and focus on forward growth; management: "accelerating balance sheet cleanup… focused on future growth opportunities rather than legacy stress."

Reverse merger / amalgamation update: NCLT hearing July 23, 2026; additional 10 days granted for pending replies; next hearing scheduled August 2026; expected completion "in the next few months" subject to proceedings.
Workforce rationalization: headcount reduced by ~1,700, with strategy centered on productivity over branch expansion.
Collections infrastructure: specialized call center for overdue accounts, enhanced monitoring and training; collections workforce >1,200 (JLG+MBBL context).

subsections.label: Recovery redeployment plan
points: For micro/JLG recoveries, management expects improvement in Q2/Q3 and plans to redeploy excess collection capacity toward legacy NPA/write-off recoveries: collection headcount ~1,100 in JLG, and "we would obviously shift some of this headcount for recovery of the NPA and write-offs."

subsections.label: Recoveries commentary (key investor concern)
points: Some recoveries/upgradations were slower than expected. Management attributed this largely to retail/secured legal recovery timelines, noting SARFAESI/auction processes can take 6–7 months; also suggested many cases cure once notices are initiated.

Risk weight benefit: CGFMU allows 0% RW on a capped portion—management stated on incremental ₹100 MFI lending, ₹15 gets zero risk weight, balance normal RW.

quarters.summary: Q4 FY'26 showed green shoots — improved disbursements, contracting SMA pools, sharply lower fresh NPA slippages and improved collection efficiency — though FY'26 net loss reflected legacy stress provisioning. subsections.label: Income & Profitability
points: Income compression led to elevated cost-income ratio for the financial year which impacted the PPoP; if adjusted for interest reversals due to fresh NPA slippages, PPoP would be ~INR140 crores for the full year.
Net loss of INR188 crores for the quarter was driven by provisioning for legacy stress.
Steady state interest income should find revival in coming quarters as reversals reduce with improved collection efficiency and new-guardrail disbursements.

subsections.label: Capital & Liquidity
points: Capital adequacy ratio comfortably above regulatory thresholds at 17.7% as on March 31, 2026.
Rights issue of INR950 crores completed in November 2025 to strengthen Tier 1 base and support future growth.
Proactively addressed legacy stress through ARC sale of stressed JLG portfolio — a value-enhancing decision improving balance sheet strength.
No immediate plans for equity capital raise; if needed, would consider Tier-2 capital or offloading balance sheet items rather than going to capital markets.
Maintained prudent liquidity buffers; CD ratio declined and surplus liquidity/LCR provide flexibility to support calibrated disbursements while preserving resilience.

subsections.label: Provisioning & Asset Quality Coverage
points: PCR breakdown provided at overall, secured, unsecured, and JLG/MBBL levels; JLG and MBBL provisioned similarly.
Some provisioning still remaining for MBBL and JLG (85% provisioning bucket and portion of 70% bucket still to be recognized) over next 2 quarters.

SFBs exempted from Ind AS/ECL implementation from April 1, 2027; bank runs pro-forma Ind AS but ECL provisioning may be equal to or higher than current provisioning given last year's slippage-driven provisioning.
Net NPA target of below 1% by FY28, from ~3.3% in FY26, via recovery of past NPAs and continued provisioning over next few quarters.

subsections.label: Write-off Recovery
points: Back-of-envelope calculation of write-off recovery (credit in P&L for write-off vs write-off number on inventory) works out to 12-14% recovery, unchanged from prior range.

Collection headcount ramped up primarily to arrest slippages from X-bucket to SMA; once normalization completes (expected in ~1 quarter more), ~30% of that headcount will be reallocated to collecting write-off/NPA pool.
Last quarter, ~INR50 crores collected from NPA/write-off pool with ~900 people in the field, ~20% of collected value from this pool; expected to remain stable for next couple of quarters.

subsections.label: Opex vs Growth
points: Management expects to achieve 20-30% portfolio growth largely with the same cost base as collection machinery is already built.
For the ~1,200-1,300 hardcore collection people, cost is estimated at ~25-30% of amount recovered (illustrative: recovering INR1 lakh costs ~INR30,000).
Case load per collection person has come down significantly to a range of 330-350, supporting expectation of ~25-30% additional portfolio growth with the same cost base.

subsections.label: Disbursement Recovery Drivers
points: Disbursements improved across both JLG and non-JLG segments in Q4 FY26, reflecting a calibrated return to lending activity.
Guardrails implemented in April'25 caused a sudden increase in PAR, shifting focus to collections; by Q3 (Oct-Nov) collections had nearly stabilized, after which trust was placed back on sales.
Industry-wide also saw an upward trend in disbursements; FY25-26 portfolio post-guardrails is behaving well with respect to collections.
Bank is currently at only ~70% of optimum disbursal capacity and expects to stabilize in similar ranges going forward.
Fresh NPA slippages declined sharply versus year-ago levels, a direct outcome of tightened underwriting, stabilized collections and targeted collection initiatives.
