subsections.label: TruBridge acquisition rationale
points: Deal aims to build the only integrated system of record and system of action for the rural healthcare market ($162 billion TAM, 2,200+ hospitals); TruBridge's EHR covers 700-800 hospitals with 15+ million patients' data.

True ownership of EHR data (not just transactional/partial access) is viewed as the real moat, enabling a longitudinal, action-aware AI training corpus linking clinical context to actions and outcomes for more effective agentic orchestration.

Since 60-70% of rural hospital care is outpatient, much of IKS's existing physician-group platform technology and future SLMs built for rural healthcare are expected to be applicable to its traditional large physician group market too, despite zero current customer overlap.
Transaction still awaiting regulatory approval/close; described as equal-size deal financed by debt.

Migration of TruBridge's EHR from legacy COBOL to PostgreS is critical to move to a cloud-native, AI-first system; AI now assists significantly in reverse-engineering embedded business logic from COBOL's database/UI layers, making migration easier than in the past, though still a significant, modular, multi-year effort (COBOL-to-PostgreS migration and full agentic integration estimated at 18-24 months before a fully integrated system of action/record is achieved).

RCM improvement opportunity at TruBridge (growing gross 15-16%, net only ~10% pre-IKS due to manual processes) is independent of and can proceed in parallel with the COBOL migration; plan includes proliferating RCM beyond the current 250-300 EHR customers already on RCM to TruBridge's broader base.
Post-close, cross-leverage expected: SLMs built for rural healthcare applicable to physician group market and vice versa.

subsections.label: ARAI acquihire
points: Acquihire of ARAI, founded by Dr. Roland Haas and Dr. Asoke Talukdar, for $1.2 million upfront cash for IP acquisition, plus ESOP-based incentives as they become IKS employees.

ARAI brings proprietary knowledge graphs and clinical decision support IP directly relevant to accelerating neuro-symbolic 'Glass Box AI' capability and provides a scalable R&D talent pipeline given the founders' reputations as 'talent magnets.'
ARAI's value is expected to increase further if TruBridge closes, given the AI training corpus opportunity.

subsections.label: AQuity integration progress (second strategic pillar)
points: First two dimensions of AQuity integration (organizational/cultural integration and margin transformation from human-led US-based to tech-led offshore-enabled model) are largely complete, reflected in recent margin expansion.

Third vector — cross-sell into the large AQuity customer install base — took longer than planned due to an initial mistake pitching the full platform to point-solution-focused buyers (not C-suite decision-makers) within large health-system-owned groups; strategy has since been revised to a land-and-expand, point-solution entry approach for large health systems while retaining full-platform GTM for mid-sized systems.

subsections.label: Future M&A strategy
points: Management does not anticipate another transformative acquisition like TruBridge in the near term; post-TruBridge close, focus will be on deleveraging via internal accruals and combined cash flows rather than pursuing similarly large deals.

Continued appetite for smaller, highly accretive 'tuck-in' deals (like ARAI) that accelerate AI capability, and potential tuck-ins of point-solution vendors that have hit growth ceilings due to commoditization.

subsections.label: Five strategic pillars of execution
points: Pillar 1: Progression to AI-native agentic platform manifest (see Product & Technology section for detail).
Pillar 2: AQuity acquisition integration (organizational, margin, and cross-sell dimensions).

Pillar 3: Achieving top-3 rankings in key point solutions (RCM, coding, patient access) to support the large-health-system land-and-expand motion, alongside maintaining unique full-platform positioning for other segments.
Pillar 4: Differentiated stratified go-to-market strategy across customer segments.

Pillar 5: Building a moat via outcomes-alignment with providers (e.g., outcomes-based deals like the $3 million NEVA earnings from Palomar in 2025), positioning IKS to demonstrate transformative financial outcomes.
A likely sixth pillar — TruBridge integration and the rural healthcare opportunity — will be added if the transaction closes, with cross-leverage benefits for the core physician group market.

subsections.label: Seasonality
points: Q1 calendar (which is Q4 FY26 for IKS) is seasonally the weakest quarter for US healthcare providers due to insurance plan resets, patients needing to work through deductibles, and reduced patient footfall; this was compounded by a fairly intense winter. Improvement expected in coming quarters.

subsections.label: TruBridge transaction execution risk
points: Transaction has not yet closed; regulatory approvals are still work in progress, and additional transaction-related expenses are expected in Q1.
COBOL-to-PostgreS migration, while eased by AI-assisted reverse engineering, remains a significant, multi-year (18-24 month) undertaking before full agentic integration is achieved.
Post-close leverage expected to rise to ~3x EBITDA, requiring disciplined deleveraging.

subsections.label: Pricing/margin deflation risk
points: Minor pricing deflation on a percentage-of-revenue basis expected over time as features become more easily autonomizable, particularly for point-solution features purchased individually by large health systems (already observed in the Ambient AI scribing product); platform pricing is comparatively less exposed to commoditization.

subsections.label: Rising competitive intensity
points: Large TAM and rapid growth in the outsourced segment are attracting significant capital (~$50 billion invested in US healthcare IT over the last four years) and rising competitive intensity, especially in the point-solution systems-of-action category with low entry barriers, alongside ongoing industry consolidation (e.g., recent PE acquisitions of RCM players).

subsections.label: AI/technology risk framed as tailwind, not headwind
points: Management does not view AI making coding cheaper/more prevalent as a risk since IKS builds its own proprietary AI/technology rather than being paid to write code for others; cheaper, more reliable AI is framed as a tailwind for IKS's own automation.

subsections.label: AQuity cross-sell execution challenges (resolved/evolving)
points: Initial cross-sell strategy into the AQuity customer base underperformed expectations because the platform pitch was directed at non-decision-making point-solution users rather than C-suite buyers within large health systems; strategy has since been revised.

subsections.label: No formal quarterly/annual growth guidance
points: Management reiterated it does not give quarter-on-quarter or specific growth-rate guidance, citing the non-linear nature of the business, but points to a 10-year historical track record as directional support.
Management is not in a position to predict exactly when growth might taper given a rising base; growth trajectory will depend on execution against the large outsourced TAM growing at 12%.

subsections.label: True North vision
points: Target to grow EBITDA from ~INR1,000 crores (LTM Dec 2025) to ~INR3,000 crores by FY30, driven by the confluence of the core physician-group platform business and the rural healthcare opportunity via TruBridge, aided by the AI training corpus/data moat.
Target to return to near-zero net debt by FY30 (having been close to that level this year before the TruBridge-related leverage increase).

subsections.label: ETR guidance
points: ETR guided at ~22% for FY27, applicable only to the standalone IKS business (not a pro forma consolidated IKS+TruBridge figure); consolidated guidance to be provided after the TruBridge transaction closes.

That has resulted in an EBITDA of about INR300 crores, which is about 35% EBITDA... on an 18.5% year-on-year revenue growth, our EBITDA growth is nearly 33% year-on-year.
Profit after tax for the INR857 crores came in at about INR206 crores, which is about 24%... a growth of 39% year-on-year and 12 odd percent quarter-on-quarter.

Revenue came in at INR3,193 crores, which is nearly a 20% year-on-year growth... EBITDA coming in at INR1,091 crores or 34 odd percent... a 48% year-on-year growth in PAT, where PAT came in at about INR721 crores.
We believe that it will take our EBITDA from that INR1,000 crore odd mark LTM December 2025 to about INR3,000 crores in FY30 and take us back close to zero net debt.
Today we are number one in AI-driven RCM as recognized by Black Book. We're a top performer in ambulatory RCM as recognized by KLAS.
We're very excited about announcing this additional acqui-hire ... a company called ARAI ... paying about $1.2 million in upfront cash for acquiring the IP.

We are awaiting the close of that transaction even after we signed the agreement [TruBridge]... the idea there is to build the absolute leader, the only integrated system of record and system of action for the rural healthcare market, which is a $162 billion market with 2,200 plus hospitals.

quarters.summary: Q1 FY27 delivered 28% operating revenue growth and 41% operating EBITDA growth despite temporary international travel disruption from the West Asia conflict; management reiterated confidence in double-digit RevPAR growth and mid-to-high teens EBITDA growth for FY27, continued portfolio expansion (Tadoba added), progress on the Dubai asset, and a long-term FY30 EBITDA target of INR20 billion (10x FY20 EBITDA of INR19.3 billion) which management says remains on track.

key_figures.label: ROCE trajectory
key_figures.value: double digit currently, mid-to-high teens in coming years

subsections.label: Profitability drivers
points: Strength of operating performance combined with lower finance cost following debt reduction through IPO translated into significant profitability growth.
Consolidated PAT increase was after a INR156 million loss booked due to share of profit of JV, mainly on account of the Dubai JV.

Dubai SPV financials do not get consolidated into P&L line-by-line as Leela holds 25% ownership with Brookfield holding the remainder; hence no impact on consolidated revenue or EBITDA, but 25% of Dubai SPV profit/loss reflected under share of profit of JV/associates.
Interest on asset-level debt and depreciation for the Dubai asset is expensed as per accounting standard, leading to an accounting loss in the Dubai SPV presently.

subsections.label: EBITDA margin management
points: Margin expansion driven by disciplined cost management, effective vendor rate renegotiation on AMCs and central procurement, and renewable energy share of around 67% (intended to rise to 75%).

Management expects EBITDA margin to continue at similar levels or grow marginally quarter-on-quarter; on a full-year basis margins are close to 50%, with Q1 being a summer (seasonally weaker) quarter at 41%.
No specific new margin target set beyond maintaining ~50% and growing marginally year-on-year as RevPAR grows.
EBITDA flow-through excluding Coorg was over 60%, and EBITDA margin nearly doubled two-year comparison from 31% (Q1 FY25) to 41% (Q1 FY27).

subsections.label: Balance sheet / leverage
points: Balance sheet remains growth-ready with 1.6x net debt to EBITDA maintained even while continuing to invest in the development pipeline.

Company has given guidance that it is comfortable with average net debt/EBITDA up to 2.5x in coming years (moving up and down in some quarters), even if debt is taken for capex or value-accretive acquisitions.
Existing same-store hotel cash flows are expected to fund capex over the next three years.
Gross debt stood at INR1,600 crores and net debt at INR1,332 crores in Q1 FY27.

subsections.label: Revenue mix contributors
points: F&B revenue of INR132-133 crores grew 25% YoY, contributing 38% of operating revenue.
Non-room revenue contributed over 50% of operating revenue.
HMA fees grew 86% YoY to INR262 million, with annualized run-rate approaching INR100 crores; other operational service revenues grew 26%.
Retail segment revenue grew more than 20% in Q1 FY27.

subsections.label: Long-term EBITDA target bridge (FY30)
points: Management reiterated it is on track to achieve the FY30 EBITDA target (INR20 billion, versus FY20 base of INR19.3 billion) based on same-store performance (achieved/overachieved targets quarter-on-quarter), five new deals signed in the last five quarters (owned and managed), development pipeline hotels all under construction with financing and approvals in place, at least double-digit RevPAR growth endeavor, and IPO-committed value drivers now operational and stabilized contributing to EBITDA.
ROCE is currently double digit and is expected to move to mid-to-high teens in coming years.
Resort occupancy target is mid-60s and city hotel occupancy target is to cross the 75% threshold, potentially close to 80%, over the next 3-4 years.

subsections.label: Occupancy and RevPAR drivers
points: Occupancy across six owned hotels rose to 67.5% from 63.6% a year earlier; RevPAR growth of 17% driven by 10% ADR increase coupled with 4 percentage point occupancy improvement on an expanded portfolio including Coorg.

Growth is broad-based across city hotels (14%) and resorts (24%), and comes on top of a 20% RevPAR growth base in Q1 FY26, reflecting compounding gains; same-store RevPAR growth excluding Coorg was 15%.
RevPAR index versus competitive set improved to 1.4x from 1.3x a year earlier.
Occupancy growth reflects ability to capitalize on growing domestic leisure and MICE demand.
Jaipur and New Delhi specifically had great performance but growth was broad-based and spread across the entire portfolio.
Leela RevPAR growth has outpaced luxury hospitality RevPAR by 1.4x and India hospitality sector RevPAR by 1.6x over FY20-FY26.

subsections.label: Domestic vs international mix
points: Domestic demand was mined proactively through event-led business, long stay offers, and digital activations in response to West Asia conflict travel disruptions; domestic room revenue growth at five owned palace hotels was 25% YoY, with occupancy at those hotels nearly 70%.
International room revenue mix recovered progressively through the quarter, moving from a 10% YoY decline in March to a 1% YoY increase by June, demonstrating dynamic rebalancing ability.

Both international and domestic segments have been equally important (50-50 mix) even before geopolitical issues; since June, international demand has recovered to FY26 level for the same period and is expected to grow from here.
October to March are peak months for international travellers, with November-February busiest for international FTOs, tourists, MICE and incentives; no change expected in this pattern.

Once international business is fully actualized in H2, it is expected to create further inventory compression and pricing/yield opportunity during high-demand dates; domestic growth is expected to continue at high double-digit across all hotels.

subsections.label: Non-room revenue diversification
points: Non-room revenues contribute over 50% of overall operating revenue, strengthening resilience and diversity of earnings.
F&B contributed 38% of operating revenue; curated specialty restaurants, bars and experiential dining attract a diverse customer base.
More than half of F&B revenue at city hotels was driven by non-resident guests, highlighting Leela's growing position as a dining/lifestyle destination beyond traditional hospitality.
HMA fees grew 86% driven by ramp-up of managed properties, including higher fees in some contracts linked to performance and past key money investment.

subsections.label: Direct distribution economics
points: Branded website booking contribution doubled to 16% versus Q1 FY26, reducing reliance on higher-cost third-party channels and enhancing distribution economics; total direct channel bookings reached 64%, with a full-year target of two-thirds.

Investment in revenue management tools and AI overlay has optimized brand.com/website business; company is enhancing business channels and creating AI-based content for LLM discovery to drive more direct business.
Cost of direct acquisition is almost one-third the cost of third-party/OTA channels, contributing to industry-leading EBITDA margins.

subsections.label: Coorg ramp-up detail
points: Unveiled as The Leela Coorg Forest Sanctuary on 8 July, ahead of schedule; ADR nearly doubled post-acquisition and the asset broke even operationally in the quarter even before rebranding.
Customer response has been strong per social media/TripAdvisor feedback; occupancy and ADR improved to nearly 2x levels versus pre-acquisition.

EBITDA contribution in Q1 was negligible/not significant to overall EBITDA but positive; ramp-up will be driven by integration into Leela's distribution network, loyalty ecosystem, direct channels, and focus on wellness/leisure travellers ahead of a planned phase two.

subsections.label: Resort demand drivers
points: Resorts RevPAR growth of 24% attributed to growing FIT share (not just events/celebrations) and prior-year investments in Kids Club, wellness offerings, renovated F&B venues (e.g., Amber Terrace in Jaipur) targeting multi-generational travellers.

Growth trend is not attributable to a low base effect from Operation Sindoor, as last year's resorts also grew high double-digit; growth is linked to increasing numbers of travellers able to drive to these destinations.

Domestic room revenue growth (25%) attributed to repurposing of resort hotels (new restaurants in Jaipur, renovated Aujasya Spa, unique dining/programming in Udaipur) to enhance length of stay for multi-generational travellers; longer length of stay driven by more travellers taking higher room categories (suites/villas), traveling in small/multi-generational groups - trends considered durable, not one-off.

subsections.label: City hotel dynamics
points: Bengaluru and Chennai city hotels have a large share of GDS business, high-profile corporate business, and global CEO/C-suite delegations.

Delhi hotel hosts heads of state and global delegations from conferences; Udaipur, Jaipur and now Coorg are becoming destinations for high-quality celebrations and luxury experiences; Delhi keys represent 20% of total five owned palace keys.

Management does not target a specific occupancy ceiling for city hotels (industry luxury peers operate near 80%) but focuses more on ADR positioning and growth than pure occupancy growth; occupancy could cross 75% threshold.

subsections.label: Resort occupancy trajectory
points: Resort programming (joined villas for multi-generational travel, Kids Club in all resorts for year-round occupancy) is expected to drive resort occupancy from 59% (FY26 blended) towards mid-60s over the growth trajectory; city hotels occupancy blended at 72% in FY26.

Green power share of electricity (palace hotels)

subsections.label: Pipeline additions and status
points: Signed concession agreement to develop a premium 30-luxury-key resort in Tadoba, Maharashtra (62-acre site, ~INR1,200 million project cost), an underserved premium wildlife tourism location, under a 60-year concession agreement (extendable 30 years), targeted for completion in CY30.
Tadoba adds to a potential wildlife tourism trail along with Ranthambore and Bandhavgarh; concession obtained at attractive terms with expected 15-17% YOC.
Following Tadoba, portfolio stands at 25 properties with 5,257 keys across 15 operational hotels and 10 in the pipeline, with development pipeline totaling more than 1,000 keys.

Progress across pipeline: villa construction started at Bandhavgarh; room walling and landscaping in progress at Srinagar; piling work advancing in Agra; test piling completed in Ayodhya; main piling work at Ayodhya to commence mid-to-end August; Sikkim main block and civil work started; Ranthambore wall stabilization (400-year-old fortress) completed, delayed by a couple of quarters as a one-time activity, now catching up; Mumbai BKC in final site preparation and design development stage.

On track for FY27 openings: Jaisalmer (interiors finished, pre-opening team in place) and Leela Residences Mumbai (63 keys, 200 bays; pre-opening teams in place, interior fit-outs at advanced stage, show-arounds starting toward year-end, residents/tenants to move in early next year).
Srinagar and Bandhavgarh openings targeted for CY27, specifically towards Q4 (October-December 2027); overall CY27 delays versus prior disclosure are only about a quarter.
Agra, Ayodhya, Sikkim, Ranthambore targeted for CY28 opening.
Coorg brownfield expansion of 19 keys planned after stabilizing the existing operating asset; company presently focused on stabilization before expansion.
Owned:managed keys split is roughly half/half currently.

subsections.label: Talent and leadership development
points: Launched The Leela Centre of Excellence (LCOE), a purpose-built 9,600 square foot learning hub in partnership with Le Cordon Bleu, to institutionalize service standards at scale and support a future-ready talent pipeline as the company scales from 15 to well over 25 hotels; expected to train more than 3,000 associates over the next three years.

Conducted the LEAD leadership development program at IIM Ahmedabad with 20 executive committee members to strengthen leadership effectiveness, decision-making, and expose leaders to global best practices.

subsections.label: ESG / sustainability
points: Company remains on track towards Net Zero 2050 ambition; all owned hotels, including Coorg, have Platinum green building certification.
Almost two-thirds (67%) of electricity consumed across five palace hotels is sourced from green power, with intent to raise this to 75%.
Renewable energy projects planned at Coorg and Chennai to lower fixed costs.

subsections.label: Value-driver / asset productivity initiatives
points: Expanded ultra-premium club offering Arq by The Leela to Delhi, enhancing the luxury ecosystem for Leela loyalists.
Opened Azulian House, a signature 3,300 square foot restaurant with 74 covers in Bengaluru, to strong reviews and occupancies.
Progressed on upcoming Arq Chennai launch and a world-class wellness facility in Bengaluru.
Nearly all value drivers outlined at IPO have been delivered through disciplined execution and are now fully operational/stabilized, contributing to EBITDA.

Dubai H1 2026 home sales above USD10 million

subsections.label: Domestic vs international demand rebalancing
points: Nearly 40% of India's international air traffic transits through West Asia; disruptions since March impacted both inbound and outbound travel demand.
Company demonstrated ability to dynamically rebalance business mix toward domestic demand around periods of external disruption.

subsections.label: Dubai real estate market context
points: Dubai residential market has largely been resilient in the last quarter with stable prices, though overall transaction volumes moderated as expected; luxury market continues to see strong volumes with large trophy transactions.

H1 2026 recorded 296 home sales above USD10 million, a record for the first half despite the regional conflict; Palm Jumeirah and a few other sub-markets accounted for a disproportionate share of transactions.

subsections.label: Brand strength and guest loyalty
points: The Leela ranked world's second-best hotel brand in Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards 2026 among global luxury hospitality brands; fifth time since 2020 among top three globally in these guest-voted awards.

Guest experience remains the most important differentiator and source of competitive advantage and ADR premium; NPS of 86 is 12 points above the luxury hospitality average in APAC, delivering stronger guest loyalty, repeat visitation and pricing power.
Consistent global recognition acts as a strong pull factor supporting both domestic and international demand.

subsections.label: Structural demand-supply imbalance
points: Macro backdrop for luxury hospitality remains very favourable given rapid growth in HNI households, expanding airport infrastructure, and double-digit domestic air travel growth supporting premium travel demand.

Luxury segment remains significantly undersupplied — 12% of room nights but nearly 24% of industry room revenues — providing a strong foundation for sustained growth combined with India's rising attractiveness as a global destination.
Hotels are located in iconic, hard-to-replicate locations; new competing luxury supply is not really entering Leela's specific micro-markets.

subsections.label: Event-driven demand catalysts
points: Marquee events in New Delhi (e.g., BRICS Summit scheduled 12-13 September, prior AI conference) create outsized demand compression that Leela Palace New Delhi and other hotels are well-poised to capture, including pre- and post-event demand; management declined to disclose further specifics due to sensitivity.
August festive weekend demand expected to benefit resorts; historically second half of year (Oct-March) brings stronger international/tourist/incentive/conference-linked business.

subsections.label: Dubai JV / asset development
points: Leela holds 25% ownership in the Dubai SPV with sponsor Brookfield holding the remainder; Dubai hotel continues to be operated by the existing operator, with Leela taking over in CY27, after which the property will undergo about a year of renovation.

Reduced travel flows due to the West Asia conflict impacted occupancy and ADR at the Dubai asset, but it remains operationally break-even during this off-peak period on the back of local business/leisure demand including MICE and staycation.

Once operational under The Leela brand, the asset will generate management fee income and royalty from planned sale of branded residences, flowing into HMA revenue and EBITDA and getting consolidated.

Company had factored a two-to-three year period for the sale of Dubai residences with no change to the business plan presently; conditions are seen improving as travel activity normalizes, and management expects a strong recovery given the asset's iconic positioning and Dubai real estate/hospitality market resilience.

On track with plan: handover from current operator and start of rehab early next year, with intent to complete renovation in ~12 months and rebrand to Leela; no re-evaluation/postponement of capex due to Middle East situation.

subsections.label: Active asset management initiatives
points: Continued expansion of high-margin, experience-led value drivers including Arq by The Leela (Delhi expansion, upcoming Chennai launch), Azulian House restaurant, a wellness facility in Bengaluru, and renewable energy projects at Coorg and Chennai to lower fixed costs and unlock incremental revenue/asset productivity.

subsections.label: Portfolio deal-making
points: Five new deals signed in the last five quarters across both HMA and acquisition structures, continuing a consistent pattern of portfolio addition every quarter since listing.
Company continues to look for value-accretive deals on both HMA and acquisition side.

subsections.label: Geopolitical disruption
points: West Asia conflict caused a temporary slowdown in international tourist arrivals due to travel disruptions since March, given ~40% of India's international air traffic transits through West Asia, impacting both inbound and outbound demand.
Impact on international business is viewed as temporary, with progressive recovery through the quarter (from -10% YoY in March to +1% YoY in June).

subsections.label: Dubai asset headwinds
points: Reduced travel flows from the West Asia conflict impacted occupancy and ADR at the Dubai hotel; asset booked an accounting loss due to required expensing of interest on asset-level debt and depreciation, despite being operationally break-even.
Dubai transaction volumes have moderated as expected amid regional conflict, though luxury trophy transactions remain resilient.

subsections.label: Construction/approval risk
points: Ranthambore development delayed by a couple of quarters due to the need to stabilize walls of the 400-year-old fortress structure, described as a one-time activity now largely resolved.

subsections.label: Leverage risk tolerance
points: Company has guided it is comfortable with average net debt/EBITDA up to 2.5x in coming years even if debt is taken for capex or value-accretive acquisitions.

subsections.label: FY27 outlook
points: Management reiterated confidence in delivering double-digit RevPAR growth and mid-to-high-teens EBITDA growth for FY27 based on current operating environment and momentum, with no real headwinds foreseen for the next quarter or balance of the year.
July trends positive with international business share increasing marginally versus last year and domestic remaining very strong; August expected to benefit from festive weekend demand for resorts.
H2 FY27 expected to be as strong as historically, driven by major events, international tourist/incentive/conference business normalizing (Oct-Mar peak period).

subsections.label: Long-term FY30 target
points: Management reiterated it remains on track toward the FY30 EBITDA target (INR20 billion, a 10x increase over FY20 EBITDA of INR19.3 billion), citing same-store outperformance, five new deals signed in five quarters, development pipeline hotels all under construction with financing/approvals in place, at least double-digit RevPAR growth endeavor, and fully operational/stabilized IPO value drivers.
ROCE is currently double-digit and expected to reach mid-to-high teens in the coming years as new hotels become operational and value drivers stabilize.

key_takeaways: We delivered 28% operating revenue growth and a 41% rise in operating EBITDA.

The Leela was ranked the world's second-best hotel brand in the Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards 2026 survey among global luxury hospitality brands. This is the fifth time since 2020 that The Leela has featured among the top three brands in the world in these elite guest-voted awards.
During Q1 FY27, our Net Promoter Score stood at an industry-leading 86, remaining 12 points above the luxury hospitality average in the APAC region.
Domestic room revenue increased by 25% year-on-year at our five palace hotels.
The international room revenue mix for our five owned palace hotels recovered progressively through the quarter, moving from a 10% Y-o-Y decline in March to a 1% Y-o-Y increase by June.

Occupancy recovered strongly to 67.5% for Q1, compared to 63.6% in the corresponding period last year... We delivered a robust RevPAR growth of 17%, driven by 10% increase in ADR, coupled with a four percentage point improvement in occupancy on an expanded portfolio which now includes Coorg.
Operating EBITDA grew 41% year-on-year to INR143 crores, highlighting the strong operating leverage of our business model and resulting in a record first quarter EBITDA margin of 41%.

We signed a concession agreement to develop a premium resort in Tadoba in Maharashtra... The INR1,200 million project is to be developed under a 60-year concession agreement with an opportunity to extend for another 30 years and is targeted for completion in CY30.
Following this addition, our portfolio now stands at 25 properties with 5,257 keys across 15 operational hotels and 10 in the pipeline.
Consolidated PAT increased five-fold year-on-year to INR488 million.

We reiterate that based on the current operating environment and the momentum that we are seeing in our business, we remain very confident on delivering double-digit RevPAR growth and mid-to-high teens EBITDA growth for FY27.

quarters.summary: FY26 was a transformational year for The Leela with double-digit growth in operating revenue and EBITDA in Q4 despite geopolitical disruption (Middle East conflict) impacting international travel and occupancy in March; domestic demand offset this and ADR growth remained strong (15% YoY in Q4). Management expects double-digit revenue and EBITDA growth to continue into Q1 FY27 (May-June exceptional), with occupancy recovering to prior-year levels by April, and guided FY27 occupancy in early 70s, net debt/EBITDA to stay ~1.6x before declining toward 1.4x and eventually below 1x. Expansion continues via Coorg acquisition, Jaisalmer and Mumbai Luxury Residences openings in FY27, ARQ club rollout, and greenfield projects across Bandhavgarh, Srinagar, Sikkim, Agra, Ayodhya and Ranthambore (Ayodhya, Agra, Ranthambore now targeted CY28).

subsections.label: P&L Drivers
points: Q4 FY26 operating revenue and EBITDA growth driven by strong ADR momentum despite occupancy drop from geopolitical disruption.
FY26 double-digit RevPAR growth across city hotels and resort properties driven by improvement in both ADR and occupancy, and strong momentum in retail and group segments.
Over 60% of incremental revenue converted to operating EBITDA in FY26, reflecting robust operating leverage and disciplined cost management.
PAT turnaround to record INR 403 crores in FY26 (8.5x increase) driven by sustained same-store RevPAR growth, targeted asset enhancements, key portfolio additions, and reduction in finance costs.

subsections.label: Cost Structure Commentary
points: Most costs grew broadly in line with inflation; sales & marketing and sales commission costs rose because OTAs (Expedia, Agoda) started charging on a gross basis rather than net basis, and GHA revenue share and sales commissions increased.
Payroll cost increase in Q4 FY26 included an exceptional item for accrual impact of the new labour code affecting leave encashment and gratuity; excluding this, payroll cost grew only 8% to 8.5%.
Additional employees were hired ahead of new value driver initiatives (e.g., ARQ club, refurbishments) for training/simulation, adding to cost before associated revenue ramps up.

All costs except sales & marketing/commissions were a lower percentage of GOR versus last year; management expects costs as % of revenue to decline going forward as new value drivers begin generating revenue.

subsections.label: Balance Sheet & Capital Allocation
points: Net debt reduced by 50% in FY26; net debt to EBITDA at a conservative 1.6x, supported by strong AA credit rating and strong cash conversion, providing financial headroom to fund expansion and manage future capex while maintaining flexibility across cycles.

Debt is expected to increase in FY27 for pipeline capex, but net debt/EBITDA should remain at similar 1.6x level due to EBITDA growth, before declining to 1.4x and eventually closer to/below 1x as new assets generate EBITDA (unless more acquisitions are made, which could push it higher temporarily).
Depreciation to remain around INR 100 crores over next two-three years, with only marginal increase once new hotels become operational.

subsections.label: Demand Resilience
points: Domestic demand has not been impacted by the West Asia conflict, while some international business from key source markets (US, UK) was impacted.
Despite March disruption, Q4 achieved 15% ADR growth and 6% RevPAR growth YoY.
April occupancy recovered to similar levels as last year with healthy RevPAR growth; May and June expected to be exceptionally good months with double-digit revenue and EBITDA growth for the quarter.
H1 (next six months) is typically only about one-third the size of H2 in terms of impact on overall business plan, underscoring resilience.
In past disruptions (e.g., Operation Sindoor), occupancy bounced back quickly; management expects similar mitigation once situation normalizes.
Structural drivers of luxury hospitality demand in India remain intact: rising aspirational spending, wealth creation, growing cohort of experiential luxury consumers.
New luxury supply in The Leela's key micro-markets remains constrained, enabling consistent outperformance, market share gains, and improvements in occupancy and pricing.

subsections.label: Sales & Distribution
points: Strengthened domestic customer base supported occupancy recovery in April.
Robust sales and distribution channels in India: over 300 person sales associates, nine regional sales offices, and revenue members controlling nearly two-thirds of revenue via direct channels.

subsections.label: MICE / Weddings
points: Cancellations of MICE events booked across the portfolio occurred in March due to geopolitical tensions; company issued credit notes and deferred bookings by 6-9 months, expecting high percentage to return in coming quarters.

Some weddings originally booked in the Middle East shifted to India; three such weddings were hosted in Leela hotels in March, with queries continuing in April and May, expected to drive incremental revenue in the wedding segment.

subsections.label: Occupancy/RevPAR Breakdown
points: Occupancy drop in Q4 FY26 was concentrated in city hotels, which have a larger share of international business; resorts were relatively insulated.
If not for war-related cancellations, Q4 FY26 occupancy would have been similar to or slightly better than Q4 FY25.

Domestic travelers stay for about 2 to 2.5 nights versus 3.5 to 4 nights for international (long-haul) travelers, but spending on F&B and ancillary revenue is similar between domestic and international guests.

subsections.label: F&B Performance
points: F&B revenue growth driven by strong performance across both restaurants and banqueting.
Growth supported by approximately 13% increase in non-resident footfalls across city hotels, reflecting increasing relevance of Leela as a dining/events destination beyond resident guests.
F&B is nearly 40% of business; Leela emphasizes food and beverage experiences and dining programs as a key differentiator alongside rooms.

subsections.label: Managed Hotels / HMA Fees
points: Management fees for FY26 at INR 95 crores; growth expected next year as managed hotels ramp up, particularly Hyderabad which reached ~62% occupancy.
HMA fees benefited from contract terms allowing additional fees, and from ability to charge higher fees in some cases where key money was invested in the past.
The Leela Hyderabad, opened FY2025, achieved healthy margin within first year, operating at 62% occupancy with ADR 1.24x versus peer set.

subsections.label: Portfolio Expansion
points: FY26 marked fastest pace of expansion ever with 23% growth in keys (966 additional keys) across Mumbai BKC, Dubai, Jaisalmer, and Coorg.
Portfolio now over 5,200 luxury keys across 24 properties, spanning 15 operational hotels and nine in the pipeline; balanced mix of owned and managed keys enables disciplined capital deployment.

Q4 FY26 acquisition of 71-key ultra-luxury all-villa operational resort in Coorg (to be unveiled as The Leela Coorg Forest Sanctuary), marking entry into nature-immersive and wellness-anchored hospitality; built to Leela standards on 76 acres with 25 rooms with heated pools, offering multi-day experiences for multi-generational families.
Coorg rebranding expected end of this quarter or early next quarter, at which point full Leela distribution (loyalty programs, key customers) will kick in.
Coorg initial guest feedback positive; touchpoints designed for next-generation travelers, MICE, wellness-seeking travelers, and longer-itinerary guests.
Only 20 of 76 acres at Coorg currently utilized, presenting future expansion opportunity once hotel stabilizes.
Coorg Phase 1 includes 19 villa expansion at INR 38 crores capex, contributing to stabilized revenue target of INR 165-175 crores achieved in Year 4.
The Leela Jaisalmer and The Leela Luxury Residences Mumbai set to open in FY27.
ARQ BY THE LEELA (invite-only ultra-luxury membership club) launched at The Leela Palace Bengaluru in FY26; slated to open in New Delhi in Q1 FY27, Chennai in Q2 FY27, and Mumbai later in the year.

subsections.label: Asset Management Initiatives
points: Refurbished and added seven F&B outlets across The Leela Palace New Delhi, Jaipur, and other locations.
Relaunched approximately 34,000 sq ft of high-end retail space at Leela Palace Bengaluru, 100% occupied.
Reimagined spa and wellness offering at The Leela Palace Jaipur, being expanded to Bengaluru.
Introduced exclusive kids club at Leela Palace Jaipur and Udaipur.
Converted select villas into premium private villas catering to multi-generational travel at The Leela Palace Jaipur.
These initiatives targeted to deliver a projected yield on cost of approximately 25%.

subsections.label: Greenfield Development
points: Construction and execution milestones progressing on plan across Bandhavgarh, Srinagar, Sikkim, Agra, Ayodhya, and Ranthambore, with progress across design development, demolition, excavation, piling, site preparation and structural works.

Ayodhya, Agra, and Ranthambore now targeted for CY28 rather than FY28; management clarified this is only a one-to-two quarter shift due to approval-related timing risk that always exists when opening hotels, not a delay, since all approvals are already in place, funding is in place, and construction has started; capex numbers remain the same with no cost escalation.

subsections.label: ESG / Sustainability
points: Commissioned 2.25 MW of solar capacity at The Leela Palace Chennai, increasing green energy usage to 67% of total consumption.
Power and fuel cost reduced to 3% of operating revenues in FY26 from 3.3% in FY25, enhancing long-term operating efficiency.
Supported livelihoods of 1,000+ women through upcycling 3 metric tons of floral waste.
Sourced 45% of tea from carbon-neutral estates.
Transitioned to 100% artisan-made jute bags.

subsections.label: Domestic vs International Mix
points: Leela's business mix has shifted from a normal 50%-50% international-domestic split to approximately 40% international and 60% domestic due to the geopolitical disruption impacting international inbound travel.
Domestic demand remains robust and has been leveraged to offset impact on international inbounds; domestic market expected to remain a strong growth opportunity approaching the holiday season.

subsections.label: Dubai Market
points: The Leela is a 25% shareholder in the Dubai Palm Jumeirah asset, with Brookfield holding the remaining 75%; physical asset and personnel unaffected by regional conflict, and impact to the larger business plan is minimal.
New hotel supply in Dubai expected to be muted in the near and long term, creating a positive fundamental for the market long-term despite headlines of hotel shutdowns/refurbishments.
Plan remains unchanged: refurbishment to start by end of this calendar year, handover expected 1 January 2027, hotel to be rebranded and relaunched under The Leela brand by 2028.
Residential sales component of the Dubai business plan was budgeted with sufficient time (2-3 years) to execute; management hopeful market will have recovered regarding residential sales by then.
No cost overrun expected on Dubai refurbishment/rebranding plan; existing operator continues managing the hotel until handover.

subsections.label: Brand Positioning
points: The Leela recorded highest-ever Net Promoter Score of 86 in FY26, maintaining position as highest-rated luxury hospitality brand in India, 12 points above Asia Pacific Luxury Industry average.
Voted India's Best Hotel Group at Travel + Leisure India Best Awards 2025 for sixth consecutive year.
Received Michelin Keys 2025 for The Leela Palace New Delhi, The Leela Palace Jaipur, and The Leela Palace Chennai.
ZLB23 at The Leela Palace Bengaluru featured across 30 Best Bars in India and Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025; Le Cirque, The Library Bar, and Megu also recognized.

The Leela completed 40 years of operations in the new financial year, positioned as a platform to reinforce brand leadership, deepen guest engagement, strengthen brand visibility, and accelerate premiumization through curated experiences and storytelling.

subsections.label: ARQ Membership Model
points: ARQ is an invite-only ultra-luxury membership club creating a compounding impact for the rest of the business and providing lifetime access to ultra-HNI and HNI customers.
Revenue model includes an initiation fee (currently INR 45 lakh plus GST) plus an annual run-rate fee; memberships currently structured for 10 years or lifetime for founding members.
Company plans to evaluate other membership models over time to scale membership base while maintaining quality of real estate, privileges, and programming.
ARQ clubs planned across Bengaluru (opened), New Delhi (Q1 FY27), Chennai (Q2 FY27), Mumbai (later in year), with additional consideration for a Mumbai club based on guest feedback.
Overall stabilized target of 2,000 members across all clubs, viewed as the right fit to serve members with the intended luxury experience.

subsections.label: People & Talent
points: Onboarded 45 future leaders through Leela Leadership Development Programs during FY26.
Achieved Great Place to Work recognition in FY26.
Preparing for the launch of The Leela Centre of Excellence, dedicated learning infrastructure.

subsections.label: 40th Anniversary Platform
points: FY27 marks The Leela's 40th year, serving as a strategic platform to reinforce brand leadership in true Indian luxury, leveraging heritage and excellence.
Company to deepen guest engagement, strengthen brand visibility, and accelerate premiumization through curated experiences and differentiated storytelling across the portfolio.

subsections.label: Geopolitical / Macro Risk
points: FY26 saw the Indian hotel industry navigate multiple headwinds including aviation disruptions and geopolitical events, notably the Middle East conflict, which disrupted international inbound and outbound travel and impacted occupancy in March, particularly in city hotels with larger international mix.
Impact is expected to be temporary based on historical precedent (e.g., Operation Sindoor), with occupancy bouncing back once situations normalize.
MICE event cancellations occurred in March due to geopolitical tensions; deferred via credit notes over 6-9 months with high expected recovery.

subsections.label: Dubai Asset Risk
points: Real estate prices in Dubai have been under pressure; management evaluating situation daily but does not currently foresee a write-off risk given conservative underwriting basis for the asset.
Uncertainty remains regarding pace of market recovery and residential sales execution timeline in Dubai, though company has budgeted 2-3 years of flexibility for this.

subsections.label: Cost Inflation Risk
points: Sales and marketing/commission costs increased due to OTAs (Expedia, Agoda) shifting to gross billing basis, and increased GHA revenue share and sales commissions.
One-time exceptional payroll cost impact from new labour code accrual (leave encashment and gratuity) in Q4 FY26.
Additional headcount added ahead of new revenue-generating initiatives (e.g., ARQ), adding near-term cost before associated revenue materializes.

subsections.label: Near-Term Outlook
points: May and June expected to be exceptionally good months, with double-digit revenue and EBITDA growth for the quarter overall.

Domestic market expected to remain a strong growth opportunity as the holiday season approaches; inbound recovery presents a future opportunity once source markets stabilize given strong brand recall.
Ayodhya, Agra, and Ranthambore openings retimed to CY28 (from FY28), attributed to normal one-to-two-quarter construction/approval timing risk, not cost escalation; capex numbers unchanged.

guidance_ledger.statement: For the quarter we will do a double-digit growth in revenues and EBITDA; May and June will be very exceptional good performance months for us.
We definitely expect maybe a high single digit or early double-digit growth in the month of April.
Occupancy for FY27 will be in early 70s for sure. The city hotel will do in mid-70s and resorts will be doing in mid-60s to late 60s.
Our net debt to EBITDA will remain in the similar levels of 1.6x, and moving forward it will come down to lower to 1.4, and then come to closer to one... even below one.

Depreciation will almost INR 100 crores will remain in the same line in the next two, three years. Only when we have the new hotels operating, then only the depreciation numbers will start to increase marginally.
We are looking towards the next year, we'll have a growth again because our managed hotels will have ramped up... that will have a double-digit growth in our management fees as well moving forward.
We'll do somewhere around INR 65 crores to INR 70 crores will be the first year of revenue, and very healthy EBITDA margins we'll do, almost 50-55% (stabilized).
Will be doing the occupancy in early 40s for the first full year.
INR 165 crores to INR 175 crores stabilized revenues... will be achieved in the year four when those 19 villas will also come into play.
The capex that we have planned for those additional villas are around INR 38 crores that we would spend to make those 19 villas.

We have just put CY, basis one or two quarters of construction risk always moves because of the approval when you open the hotel... All the approvals of all these three hotels are already in place; the funding is already in place, the construction has started.
Our plan is to start a refurbishment work by the end of this calendar year, which we would then accelerate and reopen and launch the property in 2028 under The Leela brand.
Costs as a percentage of revenue should go down going forward.
We are looking at an overall stabilized number of 2,000 members.

key_takeaways: In Q4 FY26, The Leela delivered double-digit growth in operating revenue and operating EBITDA, underpinned by a 15% year-on-year increase in ADR.
In FY26, The Leela achieved 11 points increase in market share, with our RevPAR index strengthening to 150.
Overall, in FY26, our same-store RevPAR increased 14%, supported by double-digit growth across all five owned palaces, and an overall 13% increase in ADR.
This operating momentum culminated in a record profit after tax of INR 403 crores in FY26, representing a decisive turnaround from a PAT of INR 48 crores in FY25.
From an expansion standpoint, FY26 marked Leela's fastest pace of expansion ever with 23% growth in keys, totalling to a visibility of 966 additional keys.
Our net debt reduced by 50%, with net debt to EBITDA now at a conservative 1.6x in FY26.

During fourth quarter of FY26, The Leela strengthened its leisure portfolio with the acquisition of 71 key ultra-luxury all-villa operational resort in Coorg, to be unveiled as The Leela Coorg Forest Sanctuary.
The continued expansion of The Leela footprint takes our portfolio to over 5,200 luxury keys across 24 properties, spanning 15 operational hotels and nine in the pipeline.
pressing_questions: Could you throw a bit more light on how were trends in March, because we see quite a sharp drop in occupancy, whereas, the war impact could have been only there for one month? So, could you specifically share some trends on March and how is April, May also trending?

Have you seen any meaningful cancellations or postponements in MICE Events due to the evolving geopolitical environment, and are these events getting deferred into upcoming quarters, or are being lost altogether?

On the Coorg acquisition, how's been the initial response, and when you say INR 170 crores of stabilized revenue, what kind of ARRs are you pencilling in for that number, and also does that include the 19 villa expansion in Phase 1?

For Ayodhya, Agra, and Ranthambore, we are now looking at CY28 instead of FY28, so is there a slight delay here? And also if you could talk a bit about the cost inflation that you might be seeing in terms of construction cost, and then how are you looking at the capex number for FY27 and '28?

On the Dubai side... do we have any plans in terms of fast-forwarding or delaying, what's the status there in terms of taking it over and upgrading it to a Leela brand? Is there any change compared to where we were earlier?

Since current environment is uncertain, and we have seen real estate prices plummeting in Dubai market itself, is there a possibility that we may have to take any write-offs on our investment in Dubai in the near-term if the situation persists for a longer period?

Basically in this Q4, I think most of the costs were quite inflated... what's the reason? Is it like only impact on March revenue had such a big impact? And then going forward, are you thinking about taking any steps to cut down your cost to protect your margins?
Depreciation was 1.8% versus FY25 and '26 was block, whereas, last year this was 2.5%. Is there a reason for this, and do we see any spike in this going forward?

THELEELA.about: Established in 2019, Schloss Bangalore Limited is a luxury hospitality company operating under "The Leela" brand in India.[1]

quarters.summary: Q1 FY27 was a strong start with broad-based growth across India, Indonesia and GAUM. Consolidated revenue grew 19% YoY with 9% underlying volume growth; EBITDA grew 14% at 19% margin; net profit grew 11%. Management guided that FY27 revenue growth will exceed original guidance significantly, EBITDA growth (originally double-digit) may exceed a little, volume growth may be in-line or exceed a little, while cash may get a little squeezed; India margins expected to return to normative 22%-26% band by H2 FY27 as LPG/kerosene/LABSA costs normalize, and Africa (GAUM) mid-teens EBITDA and mid-to-high-teens constant currency growth seen as sustainable for the rest of FY27.

subsections.label: India margin drivers
points: Sharp India gross margin decline driven by three commodities that more than trebled in cost: LPG, kerosene and LABSA (used in detergents); packaging and palm oil had only minor impact.

GCPL was among the companies most impacted by LPG cost as it is among the largest FMCG users of LPG and kerosene (kerosene used in household insecticide products) and a reasonable, though not largest, user of LABSA.
LPG was both a cost and availability issue in the quarter; government temporarily banned LPG for commercial use for a period.
No amount of price increase could fully offset the short-term crisis-driven cost spike (e.g., West Asia-linked commodity shock); company took a short-term margin hit instead of over-pricing.

Margin hit was concentrated in home care/PAKS, air care, laundry and household insecticide categories — not soaps, which are at normative margins this quarter (contrast to last year when soap margins were hit by palm oil).
Two consecutive years of below-normative H1 margins (last year palm oil volatility, this year crude oil volatility) considered unlikely to recur a third year.
Target of 22%-26% India EBITDA margin (widened from previously stated 24%-26%) reflects ongoing commodity volatility; company still aims to get close to this on a full-year basis.

Cost recovery from current LPG/kerosene/LABSA cost trends: normative margins to be restored 'in the next couple of quarters'; a good part of the ~500 bps margin hit expected to recover as costs stabilize, contingent on limited further pricing.
Q2 will still not be fully favorable due to a consumption/replacement lag; full normalization only expected by Q3.
Pricing decision remains cautious given crude volatility; company has 'broadly priced for' Brent staying in an 80-85 range.

Total cost increase of 9-10% over the planning exercise, of which 6% was an unforeseen war-linked delta over plan; company had planned a 2-3% price increase pre-crisis and took an additional 2-3% in Q1 FY27.
India second-half FY26 EBITDA growth was 17-18%, providing context for the base against which current margin pressure is measured.

subsections.label: Advertising/media spend
points: Media spend cut ~7-8% this quarter, but media reach down only ~3% YoY due to deflation in conventional media and superior technology/planning.
Share of voice has been broadly maintained versus competitors, who faced similar inflation pressures across categories.
If costs were lower, company would have been more aggressive on new launches; some launches were pushed to this quarter from the last.

subsections.label: Revenue segment reconciliation change
points: Domestic segment reporting changed: unbranded exports now folded into home care and personal care categories rather than reported separately, since unbranded exports are virtually nil; historical numbers restated accordingly to ensure both categories tie to the total.

subsections.label: Speedboats/new growth engines
points: Speedboats, Godrej Fab, GK Incense Sticks and Godrej Air globally continue to grow strongly and are becoming increasingly meaningful contributors to overall company.
New entries in toilet cleaners, body wash, face wash and pet care are showing strong progress and meeting stated milestones, though still early stage relative to long-term potential.

Speedboat salience target of going from 15% to 20% contribution for the year is on track broadly, though Q1 increase was ~3 points; salience expected to rise ~100-150 bps each quarter as the business scales, not evenly to 20% in one quarter.
Softness in Air in India attributed to LPG-related fill rate issues (aerosols have large LPG component), not underlying demand weakness.

subsections.label: Dishwash launch - Godrej Rizz
points: Launch of Godrej Rizz marks entry into liquid dishwash, a INR2,500-3,000 crore category growing in strong double digits as consumers upgrade from bars to liquids.
Launching in select states initially; company declined to give specifics pre-launch citing competitive sensitivity.
Home care strategy of differentiated product + good pricing has worked in Fab and Spic and is expected to work in Rizz.
Increased media spend versus earlier home care launches (e.g., Godrej Protect) and more fundamentally differentiated products distinguish current approach from past attempts.

subsections.label: Spic (detergent) brand
points: Spic taken pan-India; company declined to share specific market share numbers but expansion signals satisfaction with test-market results.
Spic has relatively high urban penetration but low rural penetration, growing reasonably fast; category creation opportunity remains given low penetration outside SEC A.

subsections.label: Household insecticide (HI) share gain
points: Gained overall market share in HI category in Q1 FY27 for the first time in almost a decade; HI incense stick market share is now 16%, with a ~45% share of incense stick handlers, after losing 15-20 share points over the last decade.

Share gain driven by two reasons: sharp share gain in incense sticks, and 'deinfluencing' of illegal incense sticks which slowed the incense stick category (reducing the negative mix headwind from fast-growing but low-share segment); incense stick category growth has slowed from ~30% last year to high single-digit to early double-digit currently.
No share gain occurred in premium segments where GCPL already holds high share.
Management views the share gain as structural given historical share loss and current incense-stick handler share position, though cautions one quarter does not constitute a trend.

subsections.label: Africa (GAUM) turnaround
points: Outstanding quarter with 25% constant-currency growth, led by FMCG portfolio where media investment was doubled, alongside continued strength in hair fashion across markets.

Successfully scaled air fresheners across GAUM region, achieving double-digit market share in South Africa air care in the last 6 months; initial pilot of incense sticks in Nigeria received strong consumer feedback.
Structural improvement in EBITDA from high single digit to consistent mid-teens level, expected to hold going forward.

Performance driven by three factors: favorable Africa macro tailwinds, improved core hair-extension operations (governance, cost discipline), and FMCG/air care progress (South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, and now Argentina, Chile, US).
Business benefiting from portfolio simplification, stronger execution, improved cost discipline, and increased investment behind priority brands/categories.

Currency appreciation in African currencies boosted reported top-line growth but pressures bottom-line/margins; despite this, margins held steady due to FMCG scaling and increased ad spend efficiency.
GAUM FMCG:dry hair portfolio salience started FY26 at a 50-50 split; going forward, 75% of GAUM growth is expected to come from FMCG.

subsections.label: Indonesia performance
points: Better-than-expected 10% growth attributed to four factors: favorable macro, easier base (last year unduly weak), El Nino tailwind (more of the benefit expected in Q2), and structural pickup in the Stellar (air) business after years of being a laggard, following a stepped-up global air-model investment approach.
Air business media investment significantly stepped up, viewed as sustainable growth driver.

subsections.label: Muuchstac / M&A learnings
points: Muuchstac acquisition working strongly, growing 70-80% from run-rate since acquisition; profitable and EPS-accretive from day one as a digital-first brand.
Management views right acquisition size and target profitability confidence as key learnings, especially in smaller DTC space; still early days (6-8 months).
Exploring applying Muuchstac capabilities to other brands.

subsections.label: Pet care
points: INR500 crore total capital committed to pet care as a long-gestation business requiring new supply chain and sales force; losses expected for a few years.
Product-market fit was not achieved for first six-seven months in Tamil Nadu pilot; fit now achieved and expansion into rest of South India underway.
Additional INR200 crore investment via rights issue reflects continued commitment.

subsections.label: Soaps
points: Soap volumes grew positively in the quarter (early single digits) and are expected to grow faster in this quarter and next after a few quarters of decline; no major weather-driven negative effect like HI.

subsections.label: Hair color and shampoo
points: Hair color had a very good quarter; the INR15 cream (small pack) has seen explosive volume growth over the years and its growth curve has now intersected with the declining large cream, leading to overall volume and value growth in hair color category.

Small INR15 cream is now the largest and widest-distributed hair color pack by volume, bigger than the market leader's henna, and is not solely a male product - widely used by women, especially rural, for partial grey coverage.
Hair color has been one of the fastest-growing categories in terms of penetration.
No plans disclosed for entering mass-market shampoo despite competitor and hair-oil companies' strong bets on the category; Godrej Professional remains a small niche presence.

subsections.label: Regional performance drivers
points: Broad-based growth reported across India, Indonesia and GAUM (Africa, US, Middle East) geographies.
Africa currency tailwind (on constant currency growth) expected to persist for another 4-5 months, reducing towards the latter end of H2.

subsections.label: Competitive dynamics in dishwash
points: A large multinational player has reportedly vacated/reduced presence in the liquid dishwash category; management stated this was not the major factor behind entering dishwash — their focus is on long-term category growth potential and differentiated products.

Market entry strategy for home care remains: enter with differentiated products backed by strong pricing and, increasingly, higher media investment than in past launches (e.g., contrasted with Godrej Protect).

subsections.label: Category growth dynamics
points: Category penetration in India for several segments (liquid dishwash, liquid detergent) remains low, providing room for category creation; competitor actions in general help expand the category, as seen with Fab's success in growing the liquid detergent market.

subsections.label: Commodity/input cost volatility

Brent crude on a consumption basis was ~USD90/bbl in Q1 FY27, having peaked near USD100/bbl during the crisis and troughed near USD70/bbl post-crisis, with current replacement-basis price around USD84/bbl.
Going ahead, volatility expected to remain with both crude and palm being unstable.
LPG availability was also an issue — temporarily banned by government for commercial use for a period.
Pricing decisions complicated by rapid swings in crude (Brent from ~100 to ~70 back to ~84), making it hard to price definitively for a moving cost base.
It typically takes three to four weeks for downstream commodity prices to adjust after crude price moves.

In Indonesia, El Nino is expected to be a positive factor for household insecticide demand (hotter, more rain).

key_takeaways: Q1 FY27 has been a strong start to the year for Godrej Consumer Products Limited. We delivered broad-based growth across India, Indonesia and GAUM.
At a consolidated level, revenues grew 19% year-on-year with underlying volume growth of 9%. EBITDA grew 14% with margins at 19%. Net profit grew 11%.
We are pleased to announce the launch of Godrej Rizz, our entry into liquid dishwash. Liquid dishwash is a INR2,500 crores to INR3,000 crore category, which is growing in strong double digits.
After almost a decade, we gained overall market share in the household insecticide category in Q1 FY27.
There has been a structural improvement in EBITDA from high single digit to a consistent mid-teens level [in GAUM/Africa], and we are confident of holding this going forward.

In Q1, we experienced significant input cost inflation and instability with LPG prices going up 3x and similar increases in other costs. This especially impacted India, where the cost impact was close to 6% on the business. Despite this, we delivered a double-digit EBITDA growth.
We remain firmly on track to deliver our guidance for the full year with the confidence to exceed the same in select areas.

quarters.summary: Q4 FY26 saw broad-based, profitable growth (consolidated revenue +11%, EBITDA +10%, PAT +10%) with a standalone India business delivering 8% UVG and 18% EBITDA growth at 24.7% margin. Management flagged near-term margin pressure in Q1/Q2 FY27 from crude/middle-distillate inflation (Brent at $100-110, palm oil at 4,500 MYR) but expects pricing actions and category momentum (soaps, detergents, HI) to offset this; Indonesia is expected to see a meaningful step-up as pricing pressure abates from FY27, and Africa/US/ME plus Latin America are expected to sustain double-digit growth over the medium term. The company also announced a presentational change (netting customer-related spend against revenue per ICAI EAC opinion) with no impact on absolute EBITDA, PAT or cash flow.

subsections.label: Presentational Change in Revenue Reporting
points: From quarter ended 31 March 2026, GCPL is changing how it presents revenue: certain customer-related spend (in-store visibility, display arrangements, mailers, channel-level spend) previously shown as operating expense will now be netted off against revenue, per an Expert Advisory Committee (EAC) opinion of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) issued in February 2026.

GCPL's prior position (till 2025) was that these spends did not have a direct correlation with sales, pricing remained unchanged regardless, and fair value for services received could be reasonably demonstrated — hence presented as opex similar to other marketing/promotional efforts.

The EAC examined multiple customer-related arrangement instances in the consumer goods sector and concluded such spend should be netted off from revenue rather than shown separately as operating expense.

Impact: revenue from operations and the corresponding 'other expenses' line both reduce by the same amount, period after period; there is no impact on absolute EBITDA, PAT, total liquidity, or cash flow.

Margin percentages will be optically higher under the new presentation because the denominator (revenue) is smaller while the absolute profit pool is unchanged; underlying business economics, pricing, competitive position and cash generation remain unchanged.
A&P expenses look optically lower for the quarter, but restated Y-o-Y comparisons are broadly similar.
Restated revenue for the last 8 quarters and last 5 years under the new presentation has been provided in the investor communication accompanying results.
Management stated there is no material impact on growth or profit metrics, and welcomed the EAC opinion for enabling better consistency and comparability across FMCG players.

subsections.label: Profit Growth Trajectory
points: Profit growth has been weaker over the last 2 years, driven by significantly stepped-up investments to ignite growth and expand into new categories.

Management expects parts of the portfolio that have started to significantly outstrip growth (driven by investments) to also deliver profitability driven by scale benefits, and expects this to happen across the portfolio.

subsections.label: Margin Outlook / Inflation Impact
points: Management expects some pressure on EBITDA percentage margin in Q1 and Q2 FY27 due to crude oil at USD100-110, but expects higher revenue via pricing actions to largely net out at reasonably good absolute EBITDA levels.

Crude oil inflation affects all categories evenly (spread out), unlike a typical palm-oil-driven inflation which concentrates in one category (e.g., soaps) and is harder to price up; hence the current situation is viewed as less alarming than a typical palm oil crisis.

Current palm oil increase (~10%) is much smaller than the FY22 episode (20-25%), and soaps' relative salience in the portfolio is now lower as the company scales up Home Care — both cited as reasons the current margin impact should be less severe than the FY22 ~200bps contraction.
Management expects a dip in percentage margins for 3-4 months but expects recovery to come back sooner than during a palm oil crisis.
Absolute EBITDA growth is expected to be relatively less impacted than percentage margins, since India (which gets hit most) is offset at the consolidated level.
Tax effective tax rate (ETR) for FY27 is expected to remain similar to FY26's level, aside from clarified one-offs.

FY26 performance builds on a depleted FY25 base; management expects strong performance to continue in FY27 as underlying FMCG growth drivers continue to compound.

subsections.label: Godrej Fab (Detergent) Portfolio
points: Fab ARR is tracking near the INR500 crore exit aspiration (GSV terms; ~INR450 crore NSV terms) and broke even in Q4.

Every quarter Fab has performed better than the previous quarter; management sees a good/solid path to profitability, viewing the ~INR4,000 crore India detergent liquid market as a hypergrowth opportunity with 'a lot to gain and very little to lose.'
Fab is no longer purely a South India business — it is now a national player performing extremely well across most states including North and Maharashtra, though South still leads in absolute size.
Q1 FY27 may see some issues for Fab because laundry is affected by crude/input cost inflation.

Pricing strategy for Fab: company will lead pricing when it is a market leader in a category, and follow pricing when it is a follower — in detergents specifically, since GCPL is not yet market leader, pricing will be led by the market leader.

subsections.label: Soaps Category Dynamics
points: Soap category volumes have been a bit muted, potentially due to a colder-than-usual year; management is uncertain whether this reflects a structural shift or weather effect, but does not see it as an alarming change.
There is also a category shift/movement from soaps (bars) toward liquid formats.

Grammage on small soap packs remains ~15-20% lower than the prior year due to earlier sharp grammage cuts made between Q4 FY25 and Q2 FY26 when palm prices spiked; this is cited as a reason volumes on small packs remain more muted than large packs.

Management is shifting its strategic lens from 'soaps' to the broader 'skin cleansing' category, citing green shoots in Cinthol body wash, strong growth in Magic handwash, and a promising face wash entry via the Muuchstac acquisition.

On competitor's new soap formulation (in response to palm oil inflation), management declined to comment specifically but reiterated it is comfortable with its own margins in soaps and views the category as 'wait and watch' for FY27, not expected to be a major swing factor either way.

Regarding future soap pricing, since GST cut prices from 18% to 5% while palm oil rose ~10%, the company may not need to pass on the full cost hike — meaning post-price-hike MRPs may still be at or below pre-GST-cut levels, with realization improving even though consumer-facing prices may not rise net.

subsections.label: Pet Food
points: Company is still in pursuit of product-market fit but is increasingly convinced it has found it.
A state-of-the-art plant has been set up in Nashik, and volumes have begun shipping from there.

Management expects this to be a long-burn category requiring sustained investment, but believes there is good potential to build a large business in a few years; further detail to be shared at the Monday Investor Meet.

subsections.label: West Asia / Crude-driven Input Cost Inflation
points: Middle distillate costs (kerosene, linear alkyl benzene, which compete with jet fuel) have more than doubled, affecting laundry and household insecticide inputs.

Crude/geopolitical (West Asia) inflation affects all categories broadly rather than being concentrated in one, making it comparatively easier to absorb via cross-category pricing versus a palm-oil-specific inflation shock.
Management expects this to cause a temporary dip in percentage margins for roughly 3-4 months before recovering, given the price cannot be passed through immediately.

On the positive side, rising middle distillate costs are pressuring local/unorganized competitors' ability to source kerosene for making local products (e.g., incense sticks), which could benefit GCPL's market share versus locals in categories like household insecticide and laundry.

key_takeaways: Q4 FY26 has been a quarter of strong broad-based performance for Godrej Consumer Products Limited fully aligned with our expectations and strategic priorities.

In Q4, at a consolidated level, revenues grew 11% in INR terms on the back of 6% underlying volume growth. EBITDA grew by 10%, with operating margin at 21.7%, and net profit after tax grew by 10% on a reported basis.
Our standalone business delivered an excellent quarter, driven by 8% underlying volume growth and 10% sales growth. EBITDA grew 18%, with margins at a healthy 24.7%.

Within the standalone business, Home Care delivered 12% value growth with strong momentum across household insecticide, air fresheners and fabric care and consistent market share gains in our key categories. Personal Care grew 3% with Personal Wash continuing gaining market share.
In Indonesia, the pricing pressures we have been calling out over the last several quarters have now largely bottomed out, and we are seeing increasingly clear signs of stabilization.

Our Africa, U.S.A. and Middle East business delivered another strong quarter with top line growth of 20%. EBITDA grew 2%, reflecting a deliberate doubling of media spend behind our FMCG categories to build a long-term franchise.
Our Latin America and others business delivered 26% sales growth. EBITDA was impacted by one-time costs in the quarter. We expect this to normalize over the coming quarters.

GCPL is adopting an important presentational change in reporting revenue from Q4 FY26 onwards, netting customer-related spend against revenue per an ICAI Expert Advisory Committee opinion, with no impact on absolute EBITDA, PAT, liquidity, or cash flow.

Or do you think you will be able to sort of manage what you had in mind before the war started out? (Management deferred full detail to the Monday, 11th May Investor Meet.)
