key_takeaways: Greaves Cotton delivered another quarter of steady and all-round performance in Q4 FY '26, with consolidated revenue growth of 22% YoY and improved profitability, recording the highest annual revenue on a consolidated as well as standalone basis in the last 10-year period.

Energy Solutions business registered 18% growth in Q4 (aftermarket up 23%) and 20% growth for full year FY26 (aftermarket up 35%), including securing the single largest institutional order worth INR 35 crores and launching a new 650 kVA genset.

Mobility Solutions (automotive engines, aftermarket, Engineered Components/Excel) delivered 16% YoY growth for FY26, with Q4 automotive business growth of 48% YoY driven by domestic 3-wheeler diesel demand and Euro V+ export momentum; company exited non-core segments (two-wheeler parts, construction equipment, select battery/digital platforms) as part of GREAVES.NEXT.
Industrial Solutions delivered 15% YoY growth for the quarter, with execution commenced on the defense order (engine to repower army trucks) and new OEM customers onboarded in agriculture.

International revenues increased from approximately 9% of total in FY25 to 13% in FY26, driven by Euro V+ engine export partnerships such as Ligier and expansion across Europe, Middle East and other markets.

Greaves Electric Mobility (GEML) logged its strongest quarter yet in Q4, with FY26 volume growth of 51% YoY (Vahan data), market share expansion from 3.6% to 4.4%, and GEML EBITDA margin improving from -30% to -20% YoY with loss per unit falling by almost half.

Consolidated Q4 FY26 revenue stood at INR 1,000 crores with EBITDA of INR 68 crores and PBT before exceptional items of INR 44 crores; FY26 consolidated revenue was INR 3,437 crores (+18% YoY) with EBITDA of INR 239 crores (+76% YoY) and PBT before exceptional items of INR 154 crores (+118% YoY).

Management reiterated medium-term core business growth guidance of 16%-18% with EBITDA margins of 13%-15%, and CAPEX plan of INR 500-700 crores over the next 4-5 years, while an impairment of ~INR 16 crores was taken on ePowertrain technology assets under development.

quarters.summary: Q1FY27 was a solid start to the year despite chronic labor shortages, election/weather disruptions and geopolitical uncertainty-led fuel/input inflation. Revenue grew ~28% YoY to ~Rs.3000 Cr and EBITDA grew ~5% YoY to Rs.156 Cr; margins were impacted by fuel and minimum-wage inflation and by ramp-up costs in two new large SCS contracts, but management expects the fuel/wage pass-through to normalize through Q2/early Q3 and reiterated no material change to FY27 or medium/long-term margin trajectory. Express volumes and PTL yields set records; Delhivery Direct/Local (new initiatives) are running ahead of plan and full-year investment guidance has been revised upward though absolute spend ceiling is maintained.

subsections.label: Margin drivers
points: Profitability affected by chronic labour shortages, election and weather disruptions, geopolitical uncertainty-led inflation in fuel/input costs, and changes to statutory labour codes.

Company chose to prioritize network service quality over profitability in Q1, incurring additional staffing and network investment costs to support fleet partners amid rising fuel costs and maintain service levels.
Of the ~37 paisa PTL yield improvement, only ~6 paisa came from fuel inflation pass-through; the rest is organic yield improvement from network quality and scale.

Fuel cost has a direct impact (~20% i.e. ~0.6 percentage points) on the margin impact, but overall impact is higher due to consumables cost, airline charges and last-mile rider payout expectations rising with fuel prices.

Minimum wage cost impact is larger than fuel because there is no contractual pass-through clause for minimum wages, unlike fuel which has a monthly-indexed contractual pass-through providing some cushion.
Fuel pass-through full benefit will be visible in Q2 numbers; minimum wage pass-through negotiation is ongoing and expected to continue as more states revise wages (e.g., Karnataka pending).

Diesel Price Hike (DPH) contractual coverage is now ~97-98% of relevant volumes (very low-volume exceptions); DPH is a lookback average of the previous month's price, so escalation that happened gradually through May means July/August impact could exceed the April-May-June average impact if prices stay the same.
Normalized EBITDA (excluding fuel delay pass-through and extra service-quality investments) would have been about Rs.30-35 Cr higher than reported Q1 EBITDA.
Fuel has a more significant relative cost impact on PTL/freight than on Express, where labour cost is more important.

No structural change anticipated to margin trajectory for FY27 or beyond despite Q1 softness; some planned investments (staffing/network expansion) were brought forward and will be absorbed as H2 volumes typically grow significantly.

subsections.label: SCS margin decline explanation
points: Sequential margin decline in SCS is not due to any structural change in existing contracts from the previous financial year; those legacy contracts remain as profitable as before.

Decline driven by the start of two new large contracts (one industrials player, one consumer durables player) where fulfilment centres are being commissioned across multiple sites, inventory is rolling in but billing is on inventory outbound, creating a temporary buildup phase with negative margins that is factored into project NPV/IRR calculations.
Margins typically start scaling up ~45-60 days after inventory starts rolling in as clients move to full potential outbound volumes; no complications anticipated with the two new contracts.

E-commerce client contracts in SCS are typically profitable almost from the start because systems are often pre-integrated and transportation runs through the existing network, unlike the newer industrial/consumer durables contracts.

subsections.label: PAT reconciliation
points: The Rs.15 Cr difference between the Rs.17 Cr cash e-commerce integration cost and the ~Rs.30 Cr statutory P&L impact is due to depreciation on tangible assets and depreciation on ROU (right-of-use) assets (rent) that show up on the statutory P&L but not in the cash-cost/management estimate figure.

key_figures.label: Delhivery Local/Direct combined new-initiatives investment envelope

subsections.label: Express volume drivers
points: Record volumes delivered in Q1, historically the industry's slowest quarter, reflecting sustained trust of tens of thousands of e-commerce shippers/clients.
Growth partly reflects base effect since Ecom Express acquisition was fully reported from Q2 of prior year onward, but even adjusting for that, organic volume growth remains robust.

New customer growth seen across the board, with the majority of new customer count (self sign-ups via DelhiveryOne portal or consumer app) coming from D2C and SME businesses, which also carry a disproportionate share of heavier packages.

Faster delivery speed programmes (SDD/NDD) launched in a more structured fashion over the last 5-6 months and better integrated with SCS business, becoming a meaningful part of overall express volumes.

Q4-to-Q1 sequential e-commerce growth of ~5-6% is unusual for the industry; attributed more to share shift toward Delhivery (flight to quality/reliable network in an uncertain environment) than to underlying market growth, given market commentary of guarded overall e-commerce volumes.

subsections.label: PTL yield drivers
points: PTL yield improvement is a planned, sustainable structural gain from improving network quality and scale, not seasonal; occurring across all distance bands, not just long-haul.

Sequential yield increase into subsequent quarters (e.g., Q3) will partly reflect mix shift (higher proportion of heavies, longer intercity distances from tier 3/4 cities) rather than pure pricing changes.

subsections.label: B2C realization/yield mix explanation
points: Yield decline from Q1FY26 to Q1FY27 (67.5 to ~58) is explained by mix: Ecom Express network (acquired) was a small-parcel delivery network with no heavy delivery services, diluting the proportion of heavy consignments in the combined Delhivery network versus the standalone network a year ago, even as combined volumes were 55% higher YoY.

No pricing pressure or price cuts anticipated structurally going forward; yields expected to hold at minimum given reduced competitive intensity post-industry consolidation and inflationary cost environment allowing pass-through.

subsections.label: New initiatives - Delhivery Local/Direct
points: Delhivery Direct (consumer application for inter-city shipping) growing faster than planned; original FY27 GMV target of ~Rs.250 Cr revised upward as current run-rate is already ~Rs.150 Cr GMV (reported alternately as ARR context in Local discussion), expected to close FY27 higher than originally planned.
Contribution margins for Delhivery Direct have expanded versus original expectations, so anticipated investment for the year will be somewhat lower than planned.

Delhivery Local provides light commercial vehicles on hire/on-demand for intra-city, point-to-point movement (e.g., trader-to-trader shipments within a city) and does not use much physical infrastructure; fleet owners participating are often the same providers used across express/PTL/gateway movements.

Delhivery Local is the largest and fastest-growing new-initiative opportunity and receives the largest portion of new-initiatives investment; original FY27 exit target was Rs.250 Cr ARR, but already at ~Rs.150 Cr ARR as of July, prompting an upward revision to the target.

Full-year investment envelope for new initiatives (previously guided ~130-160 Cr) is now expected to be well within the higher band of ~160-175 Cr given current trajectory, since contribution margins have been better than expected.
Financial services (NBFC) is a very new business, having just received NBFC approval in July.

subsections.label: Small parcel mix and network architecture
points: As small-parcel volumes rise as a proportion of the mix, average last-mile delivery centre sizes are expected to reduce structurally, since heavy/freight loads get withdrawn into centralized gateways/service centers rather than being handled by forward delivery centers.
Example: loads over 200 kgs are being withdrawn wherever possible into gateways rather than delivered from forward service stations (e.g., in Chennai, gateway now delivers all LRs above 200 kgs).
This reduction in average delivery centre size lowers rental costs, changes supervisory costs, storage costs and delivery architecture over time.

subsections.label: Delhivery Maps launch
points: Launched Delhivery Maps, based on proprietary GIS information; has been deployed internally for a while and will now also be made available to external customers going forward.

subsections.label: Serviceability and demand-shaping engines
points: Improved serviceability engines and demand-shaping tools over the last year determine which DCs receive which volumes and enable redirecting traffic within the network toward underutilised nodes, expected to have its biggest impact during peak season.

Company has matured systems to make many demand/serviceability decisions in real time (which packages to accept, which node should service which form factor), described as 'orchestration' -- a core software focus area alongside mid-mile automation.

Serviceability decisions account for granular differences: e.g., a 300kg vs 50kg freight LR, a 98%-utilized DC vs a 72%-utilized nearby DC, or a 140g parcel yielding ~21% gross margin vs a 370g parcel yielding ~27% gross margin, are all treated differently by the system.

subsections.label: Automation and engineering investment
points: Continued investment in industrial automation systems across key transportation facilities (in-facility movement) and automated storage and retrieval systems across fulfilment centers, expected to be key to sustaining market share growth amid a challenging labor environment over the next couple of years.

subsections.label: Market share and 1P vs 3P shift
points: Management believes share gains have occurred both relative to other 3PLs and relative to customers' in-house (1P) logistics operations, based on volume growth from customers who have in-house logistics being large enough to suggest share gain from insourced players.
Uncertain/inflationary environments historically favor Delhivery due to a 'flight to quality' toward long-term sustainable players with structural cost and service advantages.

Company invested in additional staffing and network support during Q1 (at some cost to profitability) specifically to maintain service quality through the uncertain environment, which management believes contributed to volume/share gains.

Management is cautious about calling this 'evidence' of a structural insourcing-to-outsourcing shift, noting individual client strategies vary, but notes three consecutive strong quarters (Q3, Q4, Q1) as an encouraging pattern.

subsections.label: Quick Commerce positioning
points: Delhivery participates in Quick Commerce only where brands (via SCS or PTL network) supply into mother warehouses/dark stores of large QC players, viewing this as strategically aligned with margin profile and differentiated capability (appointment deliveries, hold requests, multi-channel shipping from same inventory pool).

Company deliberately stays away from running dark stores for QC players (no multiplayer dark store model has emerged; every QC player wants dedicated dark stores) and from last-mile delivery from dark stores to consumers.

Rationale: dark-store operation is viewed as undifferentiated contract logistics ('renting a shop and racking it up'), a segment that has historically struggled to generate returns in India; last-mile QC delivery is viewed as non-differentiated and likely to be kept captive by QC platforms who will compress rates over time (as seen in food delivery).
QC point-to-point delivery is structurally more expensive than consolidated delivery (directionality-of-load economics), limiting network benefits and efficiency gains achievable by third parties.

Management observed many 'dark store specialist' startups exiting within 12 months as underlying economics fail to scale, reinforcing skepticism about durability of third-party dark-store outsourcing.
Company remains focused on the goods-to-mother-warehouse/dark-store reliability problem, which it sees as enduring regardless of QC's own last-mile economics evolution.

subsections.label: Pricing environment
points: No significant structural pricing pressure currently seen in e-commerce, contrasting with poor pricing environment ~2 years ago that enabled industry consolidation.
Yields expected to hold at minimum, with quarterly fluctuations driven by weight/distance/client mix (e.g., H2 yields typically higher than H1 due to heavier mix).

Industry-wide cost inflation (fuel, wages) is being passed through to customers via relatively smooth negotiations since all providers (3PL or in-house) face the same inflation; reduced number of market players lowers the need to respond to irrational pricing.

subsections.label: NBFC/financial services strategy
points: Company received NBFC approval in July; intends an asset-light model rather than lending heavily off Delhivery's own balance sheet.

Plans to work with high-quality lending partners (discussions already underway) leveraging Delhivery's demand-side and supply-side data/information advantage, effectively underwriting demand for fleet owners.

Goal is to facilitate fleet owners in obtaining insurance and fleet financing to expand their fleet, benefiting Delhivery through a larger, more stable supply pool and reduced cost of service over time.

subsections.label: Management focus and organizational allocation
points: Sahil Barua indicated more senior management time (including his own) will be spent on fundamental competitive advantages -- network structure, technology, product and engineering -- as the company approaches what he describes as a periodic (~4-5 year) fundamental technology/engineering inflection point in logistics.

This follows prior phases: introducing basic industrial automation, then designing complex automation suited to Delhivery's needs, then integrating two networks technologically to deliver current cost/service structure.

Renewed focus aims to mitigate rising risks: labour availability constraints, changing statutory labour codes (for both fixed employees and gig workers), sustained wage inflation, and an increasingly difficult operating climate.

subsections.label: Rider/gig-worker engagement philosophy
points: Company philosophically avoids 'multiplexing' rider time across multiple platforms/jobs, preferring riders work a defined workday with a defined load for Delhivery, citing superior delivery metrics for regular, retained staff versus new or intermittent workers.

This approach is influenced by anticipated regulatory direction on gig worker laws and statutory wage changes, and reflects observation that incentive structures across the industry already implicitly require full-day/full-week commitment.

Company's software focus is on maximizing efficiency of riders within already-dedicated hours (e.g., via Delhivery Maps for precise location/preferred delivery time identification) rather than building tools to flash short/part-time jobs.
A significant portion of Delhivery's supervisory layer has historically been built from field staff who progress internally, supporting the retention-focused strategy.

subsections.label: Reverse logistics strategy
points: Delhivery's relative share in reverse logistics is lower than in forward logistics by design, due to conservative approach toward volumes with uncertain SOPs that generate claims (which mature slowly, e.g., ~20 days at seller level before claims are raised to the platform and then to Delhivery).

Company does a large absolute volume of reverse logistics but keeps it a lower percentage of total volume, preferring to carry high-quality volume to preserve service quality; approach differs by specific client.

subsections.label: Approach to emerging logistics trends ('try and buy' example)
points: Company evaluates emerging demand patterns (e.g., historical 'try and buy' delivery concept promoted by others years ago) case by case and is willing to stay out of trends it judges non-enduring, while remaining willing to be a 'second mover' where execution capability and customer relationships allow fast scale-up if a trend proves durable.

subsections.label: Operating environment headwinds in Q1
points: Chronic labor shortages across the industry throughout April, May and June.
Significant disruptions due to elections and weather during the quarter; some weather-related challenges have continued into Q2.
Geopolitical uncertainty leading to inflation in input costs, fuel, and changes to statutory labour codes.
Diesel price hikes occurred gradually through May, creating a lagged and evolving cost impact into subsequent months.

Minimum wage increases across states lack a contractual pass-through mechanism (unlike fuel), creating margin pressure until pricing renegotiation with customers is completed; further states (e.g., Karnataka) still pending changes.
Gig worker regulatory changes in a couple of states flagged as a potential further cost-structure change for the industry and company, implementation status still being monitored.

key_figures.label: PTL service EBITDA margin FY27 internal exit objective
PTL long-term service EBITDA margin target

subsections.label: Overall outlook
points: Management anticipates a more benign overall environment going forward and sees no major changes to FY27 or medium/long-term growth and profitability targets.

Express volume growth is currently trending toward the mid-to-upper end of the 20-30% guided range based on Q1 and early Q2 trends; range kept wide because visibility will improve over the next month as festive season sales ramp (August is typically a high-watermark month).

Fuel cost pass-through impact will be fully evident in Q2 numbers; minimum wage-related pricing renegotiations with customers are ongoing and expected to continue as more states revise wages, without anticipated major delay.
No significant structural change anticipated to margin trajectory for FY27 or beyond, despite Q1 softness, as investments brought forward will be absorbed during typically stronger H2 volumes.

Delhivery Direct GMV target revised upward from original ~Rs.250 Cr FY27 plan given current run-rate of ~Rs.150 Cr GMV already exceeding plan; expected to close FY27 higher than originally planned, with lower-than-planned investment due to margin expansion.
Delhivery Local ARR target revised upward from original Rs.250 Cr FY27 exit target given ~Rs.150 Cr ARR already achieved by July.
New initiatives investment for FY27, previously guided ~130-160 Cr, is now expected to be within the ~160-175 Cr envelope based on current trajectory and better-than-expected contribution margins.
No anticipated need for pricing/yield reduction in e-commerce express business; yields expected to hold at minimum given reduced competitive intensity and ability to pass through inflation.

guidance_ledger.statement: Overall growth guidance of 20-30% YoY for express volumes; currently trending towards the mid-to-upper/better end of that range based on Q1 and early Q2 trends.
Target remains 16-18% service EBITDA range; confident of being in that range, closer to the higher end in H2FY27.
Internal objective to exit FY27 closer to 15-15.5% service EBITDA margins, versus 13.4% exited in FY26 (targeting ~1.5-2 percentage points improvement as in prior years).
Long-term target for PTL also remains 16-18% service EBITDA margin.
Original plan was to reach GMV of close to Rs.250 Cr in FY27; currently ahead of plan at ~Rs.150 Cr GMV and expect to close the year higher than originally planned.
Was expecting to exit the financial year at a Rs.250 Cr ARR; already hitting ~Rs.150 Cr ARR in July, so revising this target upwards.
Amount earmarked was up to about Rs.160-175 Cr for the financial year; looking at current trajectory, should be well within that (previously guided ~130-160 Cr).
Contribution margins have expanded compared to original plan, so anticipated investments this year will be somewhat lower.

guidance_ledger.metric: Overall FY27 growth and profitability targets
guidance_ledger.statement: Anticipate the overall environment to be more benign going forward and see no major changes to either FY27 or medium/long-term growth and profitability targets.

Do not anticipate any structural change to margins for the year or beyond; expect the ~Rs.30-35 Cr Q1 shortfall to normalize as fuel pass-through fully reflects in Q2 and wage pass-through negotiations complete.
No anticipated need for pricing or yields to come down structurally; yields expected to hold at minimum, with potential sequential increases from mix shift or wage-driven repricing.
Margins on the two new large SCS contracts expected to scale up to full potential roughly 45-60 days after inventory starts rolling in; no complications anticipated.
The express business remains firmly at the upper end of our normative margin guidance of 16 to 18%.
We will get to our 4% target [from current 4.7%]; at the moment, we're motoring a little ahead of the original plan.
The steady state ROICs, currently we are at 16%, but in a steady state, this number for our transport business can certainly go to 25% plus.
The adjusted EBITDA, which is today at 6.3%, has a potential to go all the way up to at least 10%... that takes the adjusted EBITDA to about 11% of revenue from the current 6%.
Corporate overheads going down to, say, 7% of revenue.
Today that capital invested is about 21.5% of revenue... this easily at least has a 2-3% points improvement potential.

guidance_ledger.metric: FY27 investment in new initiatives (Delhivery Direct/intracity etc.)
guidance_ledger.statement: Our anticipation of the investment for fiscal 27 is broadly between about 130 and 160 crores that we've guided to in our shareholder letter as well.
I think this gets us to north of about a 200-crore run rate in terms of on-demand intracity logistics... purely the external GMV.
We anticipate that they should see nothing less than 20% kind of growth rate, 15 to 20% growth rates for the industry as a whole... e-commerce as a whole growing at 15-20% into the medium term.
I think 11 days is sustainable... we are confident that it's quite sustainable... hopefully, we continue to figure out ways of reducing NWC.

guidance_ledger.metric: Overall CapEx intensity vs. volume growth
guidance_ledger.statement: We do not anticipate that because we are seeing larger volumes, there'll be a very big change in our capital intensity.

guidance_ledger.metric: Single largest customer revenue concentration ceiling
guidance_ledger.statement: If any single customer were to cross 35% of revenues [that would be a concern]... at the moment we are absolutely nowhere close to even my made up 35% threshold.
The SCS pipeline margin accretive? The answer is yes... the pipeline and the sectors that we look at are going to be margin accretive.
I don't think that's very likely... are we going to see irrational pricing the way we saw three years ago or four years ago? I think the short answer to that is no.

guidance_ledger.metric: AGV rollout to other mega gateways
guidance_ledger.statement: This is going to be expanded to other mega gateways within this year.

risk_register.risk: Chronic labor shortages across the logistics industry
risk_register.note: Persisted through April, May, June (Q1FY27) and flagged as an ongoing structural challenge requiring automation investment.
Impacted Q1; weather-related challenges have continued somewhat into Q2.

risk_register.risk: Geopolitical uncertainty driving input cost/fuel inflation
risk_register.note: Cited as a Q1 headwind with continuing uncertainty ('your guess is as good as mine' on future fuel moves).

risk_register.risk: Statutory labour code / minimum wage changes
risk_register.note: No contractual pass-through clause for minimum wages (unlike fuel), creating margin pressure until repriced with customers; more states expected to revise (e.g., Karnataka pending).

risk_register.risk: Gig worker regulatory changes in certain states
risk_register.note: Changes to gig worker laws in a couple of states flagged as a potential further cost-structure change; implementation status being monitored.
Diesel price hikes escalated gradually through May; DPH contractual pass-through coverage now ~97-98%, but timing lag exists; future fuel cost trajectory uncertain.
Two new large contracts (industrials, consumer durables) created temporary negative-margin buildup phase due to inventory inbound/outbound billing mismatch.
Claims take time to mature (e.g., ~20 days) before being raised, creating cost uncertainty; company stays conservative on volumes with uncertain SOPs.

Management views QC dark-store and last-mile delivery as structurally low-margin/undifferentiated with expected future rate compression, similar to food delivery; company deliberately avoids this segment.

risk_register.risk: Fuel/diesel price inflation impacting cost and consumer consumption
risk_register.note: Pump prices up ~3 rupees; PTL more sensitive via diesel-indexed contracts; DPH clauses and air surcharges provide partial pass-through; impact on consumption uncertain and being monitored over the current quarter.

risk_register.risk: Competitive intensity from first-party (1P) logistics networks (Amazon, Flipkart opening 3PL)
risk_register.note: Management views this as low-impact strategically ('old product in a new wrapper') given scale mismatch, last-mile prioritization of 1P orders, and higher fully-loaded cost of 1P vs 3P.
Largest customer share above last year's 16% but well below informal 35% comfort ceiling; actively managed via volume caps to protect network-wide service levels.

risk_register.risk: Labor market tightening and rising regulatory/labor costs
risk_register.note: Minimum wages rising, gig worker laws coming into effect; expected to tighten further, raising productivity-adjusted labor costs industry-wide, including for 1P networks previously relying on gray-area outsourcing; driving investment in industrial automation (AGVs).

risk_register.risk: Volatile fuel/macro environment impact on demand
risk_register.note: Management views a more volatile, expensive environment as generally favorable for the market leader (Delhivery) as customers shift volumes to reduce shipping costs.
Integration expenses reduced OCF/free cash flow in FY26; absent these, core free cash flow would have been meaningfully higher than the reported ₹89 crores.

themes.label: Fuel cost pass-through
themes.note: PTL yield gain includes only ~6 paisa from fuel (of ~37 paisa total); DPH contractual coverage now ~97-98%, with full pass-through benefit expected in Q2 due to monthly lookback lag.

themes.label: 1P to 3P share shift
themes.note: Management believes it has gained share both from other 3PLs and from customers' in-house logistics, driven by service-quality investments in an uncertain environment, though calls it encouraging rather than conclusive evidence of structural shift.

themes.label: New growth pillar investment (Delhivery Direct/intracity)
themes.note: Delhivery Direct/Local GMV/ARR running ahead of plan (~Rs.150 Cr vs original ~Rs.250 Cr FY27 target), with expanding contribution margins and an upwardly revised investment envelope of Rs.160-175 Cr.

themes.label: SCS turnaround
themes.note: SCS revenue grew to ~Rs.200 Cr but margins dipped sequentially due to ramp-up costs of two new large contracts (industrials, consumer durables); pipeline remains strong with new e-commerce, auto and consumer durables client starts expected.

themes.label: AI & automation moat
themes.note: Continued investment in industrial automation, automated storage/retrieval systems, Delhivery Maps launch, and maturing real-time serviceability/demand-shaping ('orchestration') systems seen as key to sustaining market share amid labour constraints.

themes.label: Margin expansion & capital efficiency
themes.note: Q1 margins hit by fuel/wage inflation and service-quality investments (~Rs.30-35 Cr normalized shortfall), but management reiterates no structural change to FY27 or long-term margin targets (Express 16-18%, PTL 15-15.5% FY27 exit).

themes.label: Quick Commerce stance
themes.note: Company reaffirms it stays out of QC dark-store operations and last-mile delivery, viewing them as undifferentiated, low-return businesses likely to face future margin compression similar to food delivery.

key_takeaways: Overall revenues for Q1FY27 came in at nearly Rs.3000 Cr, up about 28% year-on-year compared to Q1FY26 and EBITDA came in at Rs.156 Cr, which is about a 5% growth year-on-year.
Despite a challenging external environment, the company delivered record volumes in Q1: express business delivered 322 million packages in Q1, a growth of 55% year-on-year.

PTL network delivered close to about 542,000 tonnes of freight in Q1, a growth of 18% year-on-year, with yield rising to close to nearly Rs.12 for Q1FY27, leading to revenue growth of over 20% year-on-year.

Supply chain services business came in at nearly Rs.200 Cr of revenue for Q1; profitability was affected by the start of two new large contracts, expected to stabilize over a combination of Q2 and early Q3.

Delhivery Direct is growing faster than initially expected; original FY27 GMV plan of ~Rs.250 Cr is now tracking ahead at ~Rs.150 Cr GMV, expected to close the year higher than originally planned, with lower anticipated investments due to expanded contribution margins.

Launched Delhivery Maps, based on proprietary GIS information, to be made available to external customers going forward, alongside continued investment in industrial automation and automated storage/retrieval systems.
Management anticipates a more benign overall environment going forward and sees no major changes to either FY27 or medium/long-term growth and profitability targets.

Express margin target remains 16-18% service EBITDA (confident of being closer to the higher end in H2); PTL service EBITDA margin internal FY27 exit objective is 15-15.5%, up from 13.4% exited in FY26.

quarters.summary: FY26 closed as a record year for Delhivery with revenue crossing ₹10,400 crores, over a billion packages delivered, and ~2 million metric tons of PTL freight; margins expanded, PTL margins expanded successively, capital intensity fell below 5% of revenue, and the company turned free cash flow positive one year ahead of guided plan. Management guided to continued express margins at the upper end of the 16-18% normative range, a CapEx/revenue target of 4%, transport ROIC potential of 25%+ over time (from 16% currently), adjusted EBITDA potential of ~10-11% of revenue for the transport business, and FY27 investment of ₹130-160 crores in new initiatives (mainly Delhivery Direct intracity), with e-commerce industry growth expected at 15-20% into the medium term.

subsections.label: Capital efficiency & ROIC drivers
points: Net working capital days came down to 11 days, driven by sharp drop in receivables via disciplined and timely collections, including leveraging AI and automation.
CapEx as % of revenue reduced from 7.8% in FY23 to 4.7% now via disciplined capital efficiency.
Margin expansion plus reduction in capital intensity resulted in ROIC rising to 16% from 5.2% earlier.
Free cash flow turned positive at ₹89 crores, one year ahead of plan, despite integration expenses being factored in.
Ecom Express integration costs actually reduced OCF; absent those costs, core business free cash flow would have been meaningfully higher than ₹89 crores (per CFO Vivek Pabari).

subsections.label: NWC drivers (management commentary)
points: Original internal projections suggested free cash breakeven would be reached only towards end of FY27; achieved a year early.

Drivers include faster and more accurate billing (counter begins from moment parcel is delivered), improved client selection (avoiding certain large RFQs/customers with mismatched payment philosophies), and arrangements to bill some clients more than once a month in exchange for preferential pricing.

In SCS, key call was to not participate in mother warehousing for quick commerce; renegotiated contracts with a couple of existing clients improved profitability; billing accuracy improved as integration with customer backend/billing systems matured.

Management believes 11 days NWC is sustainable; further improvement possible via faster billing, more prepaid mix, and potential shift to weekly billing cycles with certain customers, though administrative costs limit how far this can go.

Security deposits are indirectly linked to sales (network facilities); some large items linked to corporate overheads; capital invested as % of revenue (currently 21.5%) has 2-3 percentage point improvement potential.

subsections.label: Steady-state ROIC pathway
points: CFO Vivek Pabari: steady-state ROIC for transport business could reach 25%+ from current 16%.
A small contribution from capital intensity improvement (21.5% capital invested as % of revenue could fall by a couple of percentage points).

Biggest driver will be overall profitability improvement: adjusted EBITDA (currently 6.3% for transport) has potential to reach at least 10%, driven by Express and PTL service EBITDA getting closer to 18% (Express already there, PTL still moving there), and corporate overheads declining to ~7% of revenue.

subsections.label: Express & PTL performance drivers
points: Express business remains firmly at the upper end of normative margin guidance of 16-18%.
PTL margins expanded successively on the back of reduction in capital intensity to less than 5% of revenue and a massive reduction in net working capital days.
Express volumes in Q4 (306 million) showed a sequential increase even versus the prior peak quarter.
Both Express and PTL delivered solid, robust full-year growth, aided by structural cost advantages and operating leverage.

PTL has gone from sub-300,000/~280,000-290,000 tons of freight two-plus years back to ~550,000 tons in this quarter, with gross margins doubling from 14% to 28% over roughly 2.5-3 years; management attributes this to a repeatable BD playbook of growing wallet share with each customer across geographies.

subsections.label: Supply Chain Solutions (SCS) turnaround
points: SCS turned the corner decisively this year with margin model now established and pipeline healthy; two mandates signed and activated in the last quarter.
Turnaround attributed to sharp calls on which businesses to stay in vs exit to ensure a viable, scalable model — notably the decision not to participate in mother warehousing for quick commerce.
Renegotiated contracts with a couple of existing clients improved profitability; billing accuracy improved as integration with customer backend/billing systems matured over time.

SCS pipeline is expected to remain margin accretive: an internal hurdle rate is applied to every SCS project and projects not meeting it are not taken up; pricing accuracy has improved with experience in sectors like consumer durables, auto, e-commerce and lifestyle.

Short-term profitability impact possible when starting up a new customer (e.g., building a 140,000 sqft site vs an immediate 80,000 sqft need in anticipation of pipeline conversion), but each client individually is expected to meet its hurdle rate.

subsections.label: Delhivery Direct / intracity
points: Delhivery Direct intracity on-demand logistics service is now live in six cities; intercity service (essentially the parcel service targeted at very small businesses/consumers) has been live for a while and is margin accretive and reported within the Express vertical.
Combined intercity + intracity Delhivery Direct business is, as a whole, probably profitable.

Rationale for building intracity: Delhivery itself is a large consumer of on-demand logistics (across distribution centers, service centers, fulfillment centers, SCS deliveries); once critical internal demand is proven, the service is externalized to customers — same playbook used previously for PTL and FTL.

FY26 investment in on-demand intracity was ~₹76 crores, a large portion of new-initiative spend; FY27 investment guided at ₹130-160 crores, targeting a run-rate north of ₹200 crores in on-demand intracity logistics (external GMV only, excluding internal Delhivery usage).

subsections.label: Fleet composition
points: Daily average vendor fleet count declined from ~21,000 to ~20,000, but this reflects only the contracted monthly fleet category, not the variablized per-kilo fleet where partners bring their own vehicles.

The decline is due to a shift in mix toward the per-kilo variablized fleet (varies by geographic/client mix of volumes), not a reduction in tractor-trailers; tractor-trailer count has actually increased QoQ.

subsections.label: AI & automation deployment
points: LLMs and multimodal AI deployed across all dimensions of operations — voice, vision, local intelligence, real-time transaction processing — embedded from order manifestation to mid-mile to last-mile to post-delivery.
AI embedding in product development process has reduced time and cost to deploy new tech.
Primary AI focus: making technology teams more productive internally — features that used to take 3-5 sprint cycles can now be done in 1-2 sprint cycles, increasing agility.

AI used strategically in: (1) reducing PTL documentation/paperwork for consignment manifestation, now largely automated; (2) automating communication with end consignees for scheduled deliveries/purchase orders between carrier and consignee; (3) claims handling, improving both efficiency/accuracy and reducing reliance on human review, allowing team size reduction in claims handling and parts of customer service.
No significant/unusual increase in OpEx from AI initiatives — no material increase in technology team size or inference costs reported.
AI has also enabled extremely fast, accurate billing (billing counter begins the moment a parcel is delivered), contributing to NWC reduction.

subsections.label: Robotics & industrial automation
points: Continued investment in robotics and industrial automation: in-facility automation (autonomous mobile robots, automated storage and retrieval systems, 3D sorters), delivery drones, and new trucking form factors.
Delhivery was first to launch a road train in India, following its earlier successful 46-feet tractor-trailer launch.

Key highlighted investment area: AGVs (automated guided vehicles) within mega gateways, driven by anticipated further tightening of India's labor market; AGVs address in-facility load movement (not driverless line-haul vehicles).
AGV pilots, developed in-house via Delhivery Labs (launched ~a year ago), have progressed from prototype to scale-up readiness in Mumbai and will expand to other mega gateways within this year.

Neither AI nor robotics/AGV initiatives are expected to materially alter the company's overall CapEx trajectory; CapEx/revenue is at 4.7% and targeted to reach 4%, and the company is running slightly ahead of the original plan.

subsections.label: Delhivery Labs
points: Continued investment in Delhivery Labs to sustain the tech moat and differentiate/stay ahead on cost and service leadership.

subsections.label: Market share & competitive positioning
points: Post-Ecom Express acquisition, management believes overall market structure is better and more settled, with more stable long-term competitive dynamics vs. the short-term price gouging seen for a two-year period prior to this financial year.

Share of 1P (first-party) logistics has declined a little bit over the last year per a listed marketplace's own commentary; management maintains 1P costs are structurally higher than 3P when fully loaded.

Regulatory changes (minimum wages rising, gig worker laws) are inflating productivity-adjusted labor costs and reducing the gray-area outsourcing advantage 1P networks previously had, supporting a gradual shift toward 3P.

In the long-tail segment (excluding the three large marketplaces), Delhivery's market share is stable to slightly up YoY and management considers Delhivery dominant, including in categories like heavy shipping.

Within the three large marketplaces, Delhivery's share is more or less stable; a competitor's strong Q4 growth is attributed to large growth in a single account where Delhivery manages caps on client concentration to protect service levels across the network.

Managing client concentration has been effective in Q3 and Q4, contributing to strong PTL volume growth as maintaining stable service levels rewards Delhivery with more business from PTL, heavy, and smaller customers.
In the D2C/SME long tail, share gains have come both via direct customers and aggregators; Delhivery Direct app has also helped gain share among very small SMEs shipping directly.

Largest single-customer revenue concentration was 16% last year and is higher this year but still well below management's informal 35% comfort ceiling; viewed at the overall company level, not segmented.
Management does not view customer relationships as zero-sum; believes rational financial decision-making will gradually shift more volume to 3P over time as 1P remains structurally costlier.

Amazon opening its 3PL to new customers viewed as strategically limited value ('old product in a new wrapper') given relative scale mismatch, first-party order prioritization at last mile, and higher cost of captive/first-party logistics versus third-party.

Market structure viewed as sensible with three listed players (Delhivery, Blue Dart, ShadowFax); management does not see structural advantages for Xpressbees or a reason for further consolidation/new entrants.

No expectation of a return to irrational pricing seen 3-4 years ago, as 'everybody's seen that movie and knows how it ends'; no material threat anticipated from Amazon becoming aggressive based on press releases alone.

subsections.label: TAM commentary
points: On-demand intracity logistics TAM not precisely quantified by management ('nobody really knows what all these TAMs actually are'), but described as very large — potentially a single or low double-digit billion-dollar market, estimated loosely by multiplying millions of commercial vehicles (LCVs) across Indian cities by roughly ₹2,000/day.

subsections.label: Board reconstitution
points: Neelam Dhawan welcomed as Chairperson of the Delhivery Board, with a long career in technology and technology services.
Kabir Ahmed Shakir joins the Board of Directors; formerly CFO of Tata Communications, prior stints at Unilever and Microsoft.
Romesh Sobti stepping down from the Board after five years (joined 2021), having played a role in Delhivery's IPO and strategy shaping.
Board reconstitution exercise is now formally complete.

subsections.label: Ecom Express acquisition
points: FY26 headlined by the completion of the Ecom Express acquisition earlier in the financial year.
Ecom Express-related integration costs reduced FY26 OCF/free cash flow; absent these costs, core business free cash flow would have been meaningfully higher than the reported ₹89 crores.

subsections.label: New growth pillars
points: Cash flows from core transport are being deployed with discipline into next growth pillars: local (intracity/Delhivery Direct), cross-border, rapid, and financial services — described as long-cycle bets now funded from a position of strength.
Company positions itself as having 'the balance sheet and the conviction to build our next chapter' after establishing profitable, cash-generative core (Express, PTL) and a pivoted SCS business.

subsections.label: Other transport modes exploration
points: Management believes road remains the predominant and largest untapped opportunity in India given relatively short trucking distances (e.g., sub-20-hour Delhi-Mumbai) reducing the relative advantage of rail or air.

Rail seen as unattractive for Delhivery's business given Indian railheads are designed for passenger, not cargo, traffic (captive rail could work for commodities/agri, which is not Delhivery's business).

Air: Delhivery has sufficient baseload to make a larger air network viable but continues to rely on commercial passenger belly capacity; running a subscale owned air freight fleet (e.g., 4-6 planes) would not be cost-effective; management will explore partnerships with airline companies for strategic ventures in air cargo over time, though not an immediate priority given challenges in the airline industry.

subsections.label: Fuel price inflation
points: PTL business has a natural pass-through mechanism — prices indexed to diesel prices at the pumps (industry standard since inception of the PTL business); PTL is more sensitive to fuel price increases than Express.

Express/e-commerce business has relatively lower sensitivity to fuel price increases; company covered via diesel price hike (DPH) clauses evaluated customer-by-customer based on margins and volume share.
Air shipping network saw a fuel surcharge introduced due to rising ATF costs, passed through to customers — likely explains the observed 1-2 rupee increase noted by an analyst.
Pump prices have risen ~3 rupees; this will be passed on to customers per existing contractual mechanisms, but there is no broad, unplanned pricing increase at the moment.

Fuel price increases had already begun showing up in Q4 margins, but the company offset this via further cost improvements elsewhere in the network, resulting in Q4 margins actually rising over Q3 — an unusual outcome.

Impact on consumer consumption from fuel price increase is uncertain; management wants to observe how this plays out over the current quarter before commenting further, though generally believes a more volatile/expensive environment favors the market leader as customers shift volumes to lower-cost providers like Delhivery to manage shipping bills.

subsections.label: Competitive intensity from first-party logistics
points: Media reports of Amazon opening its 3PL/Amazon Logistics to new customers viewed by management as unlikely to create meaningful competitive intensity, given scale mismatch, last-mile prioritization of first-party orders, and the inherently higher cost structure of captive/first-party logistics versus third-party.

subsections.label: Client concentration risk
points: Company actively manages client concentration to avoid overexposure to any single large marketplace customer's volume swings, both to protect service levels for all customers and to avoid dependence risk.
Largest customer's revenue share is above last year's 16% but management states it remains well below an informal internal comfort ceiling of ~35% and is not currently a concern.

subsections.label: Labor market tightening
points: India's labor situation is expected to continue tightening, increasing productivity-adjusted labor costs; this is a driver behind investment in industrial automation (e.g., AGVs) to maintain service reliability across the industry, not specific to Delhivery alone.
Regulatory changes such as rising minimum wages and new gig worker laws are adding cost pressure, including to 1P networks that previously benefited from outsourcing in gray regulatory areas.

subsections.label: Forward guidance summary
points: Express margins expected to remain at the upper end of normative 16-18% guidance range.
Original internal plan projected free cash breakeven towards end of FY27; achieved a year early in FY26 — management hopes to sustain and continue improving NWC and cash generation into next FY.
CapEx/revenue expected to continue trending toward a 4% target; AI and robotics/AGV investments are not expected to materially alter this trajectory.

Transport business ROIC guided to potentially exceed 25%, up from current 16%, driven mainly by profitability improvement (adjusted EBITDA rising from 6.3% to at least 10%) with a smaller contribution from further capital intensity improvement (21.5% capital invested/revenue could fall by 2-3 points).
FY27 investment of ₹130-160 crores guided for new initiatives (primarily on-demand intracity Delhivery Direct), aiming for an external GMV run-rate north of ₹200 crores (excluding internal usage).

Management expects e-commerce industry growth of 15-20% into the medium term, based on their own customer data, while noting a newly listed e-commerce company is better positioned to comment on industry growth specifically.
No major change anticipated in overall capital intensity despite growth in PTL/heavy Express tonnage; more mega gateways may be needed over time but as a shrinking percentage of base capacity.
Management does not expect further industry consolidation or irrational pricing to return, viewing the three-listed-player market structure (Delhivery, Blue Dart, ShadowFax) as sensible and stable.

PTL getting closer to 18% [service EBITDA, Express already there].
Corporate overheads going down to, say, 7% of revenue.
Today that capital invested is about 21.5% of revenue... this easily at least has a 2-3% points improvement potential.

risk_register.risk: Labor market tightening and rising regulatory/labor costs
risk_register.note: Minimum wages rising, gig worker laws coming into effect; expected to tighten further, raising productivity-adjusted labor costs industry-wide, including for 1P networks previously relying on gray-area outsourcing; driving investment in industrial automation (AGVs).

risk_register.risk: Volatile fuel/macro environment impact on demand
risk_register.note: Management views a more volatile, expensive environment as generally favorable for the market leader (Delhivery) as customers shift volumes to reduce shipping costs.
Integration expenses reduced OCF/free cash flow in FY26; absent these, core free cash flow would have been meaningfully higher than the reported ₹89 crores.

themes.note: Service EBITDA up 220bps to 15.6% in core transport+PTL; ROIC up to 16% from 5.2%; CapEx/revenue down to 4.7% from 7.8%.

themes.label: Fuel cost pass-through
themes.note: Diesel/ATF price increases are being passed through via DPH clauses and surcharges, with Q4 margins actually improving over Q3 despite cost pressure via offsetting productivity gains.

themes.label: AI & automation moat
themes.note: LLM/multimodal AI and AGV robotics deployed across operations to improve productivity, billing speed, claims handling and address tightening labor market, without materially raising OpEx or CapEx.

themes.note: FY27 investment of ₹130-160 crores guided for on-demand intracity and other new initiatives, targeting a 200+ crore external GMV run-rate.

key_takeaways: FY26 has been a bellwether year for Delhivery in many ways. Of course, the headline was our completion of the acquisition of Ecom Express earlier in this financial year.
We closed the year with over 10,400 crores in revenue, delivered over a billion packages in the financial year.
Margins continue to expand. The express business remains firmly at the upper end of our normative margin guidance of 16 to 18%.
PTL margins expanded again successively... on the back of a reduction in capital intensity to less than 5% of revenue and a massive reduction in net working capital days.
The company continues to be extremely well capitalized with over 4,500 crores of cash on the balance sheet.
Supply chain solutions again turned the corner pretty decisively this year. We expanded our service EBITDA about four times to 79 crores.
This profitable growth helped us turn free cash flow positive this year at about 89 crores... this is one year ahead of plan.
We're at 16% [ROIC]. This is up from 5.2% earlier.
pressing_questions: Would be great to understand what kind of an impact we could expect from an increase in fuel prices, both on consumption as well as cost.
There are media articles about Amazon opening up its 3PL to get new customers... should we see an increased competitive intensity, especially with smaller customers like D2C brands and others?
Would you be able to quantify how big would be the TAMs in this segment [on-demand intracity]?
Is there a chance of the CapEx intensity again increasing for the industry [given the current growth phase]?

DELHIVERY.about: Delhivery provides a full range of Logistics services, including delivery of express parcels and heavy goods, PTL freight, TL freight, warehousing, supply chain solutions, cross-border Express, freight services, and supply chain software. The company also offers value-added services such as e-commerce return services, payment collection and processing, installation & assembly services, and fraud detection.[1]

quarters.summary: Strong volume-led Q1 FY27 for Tata Motors CV, with wholesales +26% YoY vs industry +18% YoY, broad-based across product lines. Margins compressed on commodity inflation but were largely offset by realization and operating leverage. Cash flow inflected sharply positive, aided by a one-off Indonesia order advance. EV momentum accelerated (SCV pickup EV penetration hit double digits in May/June) though battery cell lead times remain a near-term constraint. Two major corporate actions: IVECO transaction nearing final regulatory clearance (one approval pending, expected end-Aug '26) and Freight Tiger becoming a subsidiary (~63.6% stake) to build an end-to-end logistics digital ecosystem. Management is cautious on H2 visibility, expects Q2 double-digit YoY growth, with commodity cost pressure expected to persist.

key_takeaways: Strong volume-led quarter despite “heightened geopolitical tensions,” with industry wholesales +18% YoY vs Tata Motors CV +26% YoY. Growth was broad-based across every product line (all double-digit).

Margins compressed on commodities, but realization + operating leverage largely offset inflation: “operating leverage and improved realization have absorbed almost all of the significant commodity headwind.”
Cash flow inflected sharply positive on working-capital discipline and an Indonesia-order advance (explicitly flagged as a one-off contributor).
EV momentum accelerated materially (CV EVs and SCV pickup EV penetration hitting double digits in May/June), but battery cell supply lead times are the near-term constraint.

Two material corporate actions: IVECO transaction nearing final regulatory clearance (one approval pending) and Freight Tiger becomes subsidiary (stake up to ~63.6%) to build an end-to-end logistics digital ecosystem.

quarters.summary: FY26 was a record year for Tata Motors CV business with record profitability, cash generation and balance-sheet strength; management exceeded most prior guidance metrics (margin at 13.2% a year ahead of plan, investment intensity held at 2.4%, FCF above guidance) while market share remains work in progress (35.7% vs 40% aspiration). Forward guidance includes sustaining double-digit EBITDA through the cycle (teens in upcycle), investment intensity of 2-4% of revenue, FCF target of 7-9% of post-tax revenue, ROCE moderating to 30-35% as Iveco increases capital employed, non-cyclical revenue growing ~1.5x domestic business growth, Iveco acquisition completion targeted by Q2 FY27, and FY27 industry volume growth expected higher single-digit for the full year despite a strong Q1.

subsections.label: Key structural shifts (CFO framing)
points: Customer value creation: shift from 'supply push/channel loading' to demand-pull anchored on retail (VAHAN) market share, with value-based pricing and improved mix.
Financial fitness: shift from subscale/levered to resilient margins across the cycle, net cash, consistent FCF.
Revenue diversification: increased mix from digital + downstream services + international; CFO noted international business grew ~54% in FY26 and that the 'anchor has shifted.'

subsections.label: Guidance scorecard vs prior commitments
points: Management stated they exceeded most metrics: margin reached 13.2% 'a year ahead' of plan; investment intensity held at 2.4%; FCF above guidance.
Market share is 'work in progress' (overall 35.7% vs 40% aspiration).

subsections.label: Returns commentary
points: CFO highlighted ROCE ~72% in FY26, calling it 'probably… globally among the CV players the best.'

subsections.label: Trucks (Rajesh Kal): premiumization, payload/fuel economics, and contracted services
points: Market position: truck share 47%+; HCV VAHAN share 55.2% (decade-high), ILMCV 38% (management wants higher).
Major MY26 launches (~17 trucks): multi-axle high payload, broad EV range (7T/9T/12T/28T tipper/55T prime mover), mining tipper Prima 400 hp with 8.5L engine, Azura range incl. 19T with 3.6L engine.
Mix/premiumization: shift from 'CX bottom of pyramid' toward higher-end; cited LX ~59% in HCV; Prima ramp from 100–150/month to 4,000+ FY26, recently 600+/month.
High payload upgrades (28→30T, 35→37T, etc.) adding up to 1.8T extra payload, claimed ~30% better profitability for customers and payback reduction 'up to six months.'
Powertrain step-up 300→320 hp positioned as improving turnaround time and earnings.
Mileage Sarthi: worked with 40,000+ customers; claimed ~7% better fuel efficiency in targeted deployments.

Service industrialization: Customer Success Centers designed with 25 customers, delivered 98.8% uptime across ~20,000 trucks; push toward AMC/FMS/onsite support and 'service on wheels' as annuity-like downstream revenue.
Safety positioning: cabin safety aligned to ECE R29.03; management indicated safety is now a purchase decision driver.

subsections.label: Buses/Vans + Smart City Mobility (Anand): disciplined tendering, service charter, and GCC scaling model
points: Growth & mix: bus market growth cited as structurally strong; business mix ~82–84% private, ~18% government/tender (tender-driven 95–98%).
Customer metrics: NPS up three straight years; FY26 saw NPS rise across buses, Winger, Magic.
Project Swabhiman (Magic): last-mile connectivity; expectation of further scaling (2x→3x/4x over time).
MCV buses: volumes doubled in two years; benefits from in-house body-building capacity (Dharwad plant rolled out 15,000th body).
Winger: segment creation in vans; Winger Plus won award within six months.
Service Charter ('Project Vishwas'): reach breakdown within 2 hours and restore within 4 hours (if not major); claimed 95%+ achievement across 3,500+ buses covered.
Government business turnaround: order book moved from ~1,000 to ~6,000 by Q4 after three-quarter cost reduction drive; now entering FY27 with ~6,000 backlog at 'reasonable profits.'
Smart City Mobility (GCC model): footprint of e-buses in 23 cities; portfolio includes school/staff/intercity EV buses plus displayed diesel/CNG/EV/hydrogen fuel cell.
Operating scale: 3,800 buses deployed, 53 crore km cumulative; EBITDA improving via power consumption, parts cost, penalties reduction.
Bidding discipline: emphasis on payment security + asset-light and consortium model (OEM + financier/investor + operator) to avoid asset-heavy scaling; uptime expectations 96–97% over 144 months.

subsections.label: SCV & Pickups (Pinaki): turnaround flywheel, alt-fuel skew, distribution & finance ecosystem
points: FY26 framed as 'start of turnaround' after 3 years of decline.
Share trajectory: FY26 full-year 26.8%, exited 27.2%; FY27 Apr–May 27.9%.
Growth sequence explained: dealer confidence → offtakes (Q2) → retail (Q3) → share (Q4 onward).
Alt-fuel salience: FY26 29% vs industry 19%; FY27 YTD 32% vs industry 21% (alt fuel = CNG + EV).

Network and GTM strengthening: service touchpoints +43%, dealer 'feet on street' sales executives +26%, financier participation +52% ('TM series books… one of the healthiest'), rural financing push with 22 Gramin banks added, Gramin bank count +300%.

Portfolio observations: SCV category growth re-accelerating (plays to Tata's ~48% share in SCV created with Ace); within pickups, growth skewing toward small pickups (Intra-type) where Tata is stronger; three-box pickup identified as 'Achilles heel.'
FY27 execution agenda: 4 SCV + 5 pickup launches; connected vehicle rollout to SCVPU starting with EVs; charging ecosystem tie-ups: 13 CPOs, 25,000+ charging points, plus captive solutions.

subsections.label: Digital business (Swami Nathan): scale, monetization, and agentic-AI platform thesis
points: Fleet Edge: >1 million vehicles connected; ~500k customers onboarded; engagement ~266 minutes/customer/month.
Mileage Sarthi: 150,000+ paying customers, 'median ~6% fuel efficiency improvement'; renewals >2.5x (now 'close to ~3x').
Freight Tiger: handles ~5% of recorded road trips in India (~9 million trips referenced); named World Economic Forum 'Technology Pioneer.'
Digital business: revenue +45%, ARPU +50%, overall digital ecosystem growth ~49% YoY.
Strategic positioning: claims a unique quadrant—OEM-grade data depth + OE-agnostic reach, plus truck + trip ecosystems; 'we're already here.'
Platform pivot: FY26 proved products scale independently; FY27 is 'about the platform' combining ecosystems into a flywheel where 'every kilometer makes our products better.'

AI thesis: moving from bolted-on AI to 'agent native from ground up' with agents for dispatch, exception handling, maintenance, and driver coaching; multi-layer monetization: subscription + transaction take + VAS (fastag/insurance/fuel cards) + data/intelligence.
5-year aspiration: 3 million vehicles connected; 'world's first OE-agnostic agentic native platform and a logistics operating system.'

subsections.label: Downstream/non-cyclical businesses: management's economic logic and monetization levers
points: Operations head stated downstream captures value 'full lifetime… 10 to 12 years'; downstream market potential ~1.5x truck sales, capex-light, improves customer satisfaction and buffers cyclicality.
Trucks head: service shift from transactional to contracted/annuity via AMC, FMS, on-site support, customer success centers—'uptime is equal to revenue.'

Parts & services (Vikram): multi-brand parts strategy (Tata Genuine / DuraFit / Pro-life refurb), dark store spare delivery pilots (6-hour promise in 6 cities), automotive fluids (TMGO since 2018; includes DEF) growing strongly, and aggregates (engines/gearboxes/axles) sold to adjacent industries leveraging engineering + service network.

subsections.label: Industry outlook & management framing of the inflection
points: CEO highlighted mega-trends shifting from classic ACES to: ADAS regulation, Connected, decarbonization, and software-defined vehicle (SDV).
In CVs, SDV is framed around 'value creation… and energy management… to help decarbonization… [and] TCO reduction.'

India CV demand fundamentals: long-term visibility from freight growth; even 20% park growth implies ~1m vehicles in 4 years, suggesting FY26 industry levels are supportable even before replacement; replacement positioned as necessary for efficiency gains.
Regulatory map called 'stable'; key upcoming items: ADAS, and fuel-efficiency norms (HDFE/LDFE/N1 CAFE).

subsections.label: Pricing discipline
points: Reiterated as 'non-negotiable' and embedded across functions (engineering/ops/purchase), not just sales.
CEO: realization improvement is now 'part of the DNA,' with 90-day full issue resolution targets and incentives.

subsections.label: ADAS regulation stance
points: Management less concerned about compliance (already has 'level 2+' ADAS truck) and more focused on customer value—improving safety and potentially reducing turnaround time to lift customer revenue.

subsections.label: CV pure-play post de-merger
points: Post de-merger, FY26 described as first full year as an independent listed CV company (effective 1 Oct 2025); relisted as Tata Motors on 12 Nov (BSE/NSE).
Management cited 'sharp strategic focus and agility' as a pure-play CV entity.

subsections.label: Iveco acquisition (spelled 'AVECO/IVECO' in transcript)
points: Status: 'secured most regulatory approvals'; on course for completion by Q2 FY27.
Strategic rationale: global footprint expansion, powertrain/platform synergies, and access to Latin America.
CEO positioned combined group as having access to 'three growth markets… Africa, Latin America, and Asia ex-China.'

subsections.label: Digital consolidation into 'IQ Mobility'
points: Plan: house 'entire gamut of digital business under a new single entity called IQ Mobility.'
Freight Tiger became a subsidiary effective Q1 with Tata stake ~63%.
Stated ambition: create an integrated, tech-led logistics ecosystem, OE-agnostic, spanning truck + trip ecosystem with end-to-end solutions.

subsections.label: Strategy: three pillars + two enablers (CEO)
points: Pillar 1 - Strengthen the core: defend/grow domestic leadership, emphasize customer success, increase share of value pool, robust returns; Trucks - maintain leadership, focus on profitable growth, pricing discipline, alt fuels/EV, ADAS, next-gen products; Buses/Vans - selective participation in tenders, profitable growth; SCV/Pickups - recovery underway, address weaknesses in large pickup segment.
Pillar 2 - Scale new growth engines: lead CV electrification, expand downstream (parts/services) and digital to reduce cyclicality.
Pillar 3 - Strategic pivot to global growth: scale current international markets + leverage Iveco.
Cross-cutting enablers: (i) Technology + Digitalization + AI, (ii) Sustainability (moving toward SBTi 1.5°C pathway).

subsections.label: Iveco synergy buckets
points: Revenue: product cross-sell (e.g., Daily platform into India; Tata ILCV/HCV/SCV into LatAm where Tata has limited presence in Brazil/Argentina); leverage FPT for Tata aggregates business.
Opex: sourcing mix shift (Iveco low non-Western Europe sourcing vs peers), 'design-to-value' and frugality methods.
Working capital: deploy Tata's digital/operational systems ('sampravaha') to release WC.
Capex/engineering: longer-term platform sharing; incremental engineering shift to India for cost.

subsections.label: Near-term watch-outs
points: Diesel price increases (diesel ~50% of fleet operating cost), Middle East/geopolitical disruptions, commodity inflation, potential interest rate hikes.
CEO called these 'cyclical and manageable,' while tailwinds are 'structural and durable.'

subsections.label: Commodity headwinds
points: CFO acknowledged strong inflation; response is calibrated pricing + internal cost optimization, while targeting double-digit EBITDA through cycle.

subsections.label: DFC risk
points: CEO reiterated earlier stance—Eastern DFC aids mining/tippers; Western DFC may shift some tractor freight to rail but increases distribution demand (ILMCV/SCV) due to hub-to-spoke nature; road remains dominant due to convenience and improved predictability.

subsections.label: Iveco near-term performance context
points: CEO noted Iveco Q1 had strong buses + FPT growth; trucks up in Europe, down in Latin America.
Margin underperformance attributed to quality investments (esp. bus plant in France), expected to normalize by Iveco Q3 (Tata's Q2).

subsections.label: Outlook & financial guardrails (CFO)

Margins: sustain double-digit EBITDA through the cycle, teens in upcycle.
Investment intensity: 2–4% of revenue.

subsections.label: FY27 industry volume outlook (Q&A)
points: CEO expects Q1 double-digit growth YoY; full-year still 'higher single-digit growth' due to tough H2 base after prior-year GST-driven pickup.

quarters.summary: Domestic businesses delivered broad-based double-digit growth across all major operating segments (Power Generation +18%, Industrial +19%, Distribution & Aftermarket +20%) despite significant geopolitical uncertainty and unusually weak export markets, particularly in the Middle East. Management remains committed to full-year EBITDA delivery and reiterated the $2 billion (~INR16,600 crore) revenue aspiration by FY30, expecting profitability/margin improvement as pricing actions progressively flow through and cost optimization continues.

subsections.label: EBITDA Drivers
points: EBITDA for the quarter reflected 3 primary factors: lower export volumes, elevated commodity costs and the timing difference between cost inflation and price realization.
Management stated this is not a reflection of any deterioration in the competitiveness of the businesses.
Across virtually all businesses, pricing actions have already been implemented, but given the nature of contracts and customer agreements, realization occurs over different time frames.
As pricing actions progressively flow through over coming quarters, supported by ongoing cost optimization and operational excellence initiatives, profitability is expected to improve.

subsections.label: Employee Cost Increase Explanation
points: Employee-related expense increased materially year-on-year — Q1 bridge indicates an increase of approximately INR31 crores (a 40% increase).
Components: annual increments; ESOP-related expense to reward high-performing employees; capability additions and investments supporting future growth programs.
Some of these costs are structural and some are timing related; management does not want to characterize all of them as one-off.

What matters is the return on that cost base as revenue scales, particularly in international, high horsepower and aftermarket business — better fixed cost absorption and productivity is an explicit management priority.
Management declined to disclose the specific ESOP expense amount for the quarter.

subsections.label: Margin Trajectory / Gross Margin Commentary
points: Margin contracted in the quarter predominantly due to a massive increase in global commodity prices.
To counter this, price increases have been taken, but there is a lag between price increase and price realization.
Company is also working on cost control and operational excellence to help improve margin going forward.
Over the last 3 years, margin has improved by more than 400 basis points; management intends to continue improving margin going forward but declined to give a specific range for FY30.
