subsections.label: Order book strength & visibility
points: Standalone order book of ~INR 1,645 crores at year end, up ~23% YoY, providing strong visibility for coming years.

BTS order book grew 2.3x over the last 3 years with a 32% CAGR; entity-level order book grew 1.7x over 3 years with a 20% CAGR, and this trajectory is expected to continue especially with increased focus on BTS.
BTS book-to-bill ratio remains healthy: ~INR 250 crores of BTS revenue booked against ~INR 400 crores of orders booked in the standalone business in FY26.

subsections.label: BTS order inflow growth commentary
points: BTS standalone order inflow for FY26 was ~INR 470 crores (analyst cited ~INR 466 crores), reflecting slower growth as some large program orders take time to conclude; a portion of these orders spilled over into the current fiscal year.
Previously reported BTS numbers included some subsidiary contribution; the numbers have been recast to focus only on the BTS business within the standalone entity, affecting comparability.
An additional INR 100-150 crores of orders that were expected last year have been pushed to the current fiscal, and management considers these fairly well secured and expects them to come in.

Outlook for BTS in the current fiscal year is described as fairly strong, with the company expecting to continue growing the BTS business at a healthy rate, though management declined to give specific quarterly/annual order booking guidance.

subsections.label: New order wins during FY26
points: Secured a marquee AESA radar program from HAL for the UHM platform — an important validation of Centum's capabilities in advanced radar systems and indigenous defense electronics; opportunity size exceeds INR 570 crores over the life cycle of the project.

UHM order divided into 2 phases: development phase (~INR 66-67 crores, without tax, expected to complete in ~2 years) and a remainder phase (500+ crores) to be executed through FY30/FY31, contingent on successful demonstration of the development phase.

Scope of work on UHM is a full turnkey radar system delivered to HAL, covering development, qualification, certification and airborne certification support, working closely with HAL on platform integration.

Secured a second complete radar system order for satellite and space debris tracking application (a long-range, high-power radar), valued at ~INR 30 crores for one system — complementary to the airborne UHM radar system in the product portfolio.
Virupaksha order: won 2 of the 4 critical subsystems (antenna array and exciter-receiver) that integrate into a full radar; a relatively small development contract valued at less than INR 10 crores.
Continued healthy traction across electronic warfare, aerospace, test systems and other high-reliability defense electronics opportunities.

subsections.label: BTS vs EMS order book mix / revenue read-through
points: More than 50% of the order book is now BTS, while BTS contributes ~28% of revenue currently; management explained that BTS execution cycle is ~2 to 2.5 years while EMS is an annuity business with a shorter firm order horizon (6-9 months) plus a longer, unreported forecast.
The order book split between EMS and BTS is not by itself indicative of the future revenue split because of differing execution cycles.

Directionally, over the medium term, both businesses are expected to grow well, with the mix moving moderately, but not significantly different from the current mix, and perhaps a little more towards BTS.

key_figures.label: Semiconductor equipment segment target annual revenue

subsections.label: BTS performance drivers
points: FY26 was a particularly strong year for BTS with revenue growth of ~37% YoY, primarily driven by strong execution across space-based payload programs, radar subsystems, subsystems for land and missile programs, and other strategic defense and aerospace platforms.

subsections.label: EMS performance drivers
points: EMS delivered revenue growth of ~21% YoY, supported by strong customer ramp-ups, healthy order inflows, and continued diversification across strategic end markets, including a successful ramp-up with a leading semiconductor equipment OEM and new business wins across industrial electronics, electrification, grid automation and defense export programs.

Particular encouragement noted in the Semiconductor Equipment segment where customer engagements continue to deepen alongside increasing global semiconductor investments and supply chain diversification towards India.

subsections.label: Margin profile by business model (not by end-market vertical)
points: BTS carries an EBITDA margin profile of around 20%.

EMS across industries is fairly pegged at 9-10% EBITDA margin, occasionally reaching ~11% before resetting due to price pressure, since it largely operates on a cost-plus contract manufacturing basis.

No major EBITDA margin differentiation exists within EMS across end-market segments (industrial, transport, healthcare, etc.) except on a momentary/temporary basis, e.g., tighter margins in early quarters of ramping up a new customer before scale, yield, process and supply chain efficiencies normalize margins.
At the combined (BTS + EMS) level, business mix is a key margin driver given the meaningfully different margin profiles of the two business models.

subsections.label: Defense & Aerospace revenue split across BTS and EMS
points: Defense and Aerospace is addressed in both business models: BTS standalone revenue is almost entirely defense/space-related, but there is also a substantial contribution of orders and revenue from the Defense segment within the EMS numbers.

subsections.label: Semiconductor equipment segment outlook
points: Growth from the semiconductor equipment customer segment is progressing broadly in line with expectations, largely driven by a key anchor customer.
Discussions have begun with a couple of other semiconductor customers, but these are still in preliminary stages; major growth currently comes from the anchor customer.

subsections.label: IP and design capability
points: Strong and deep domain knowledge in design and IP creation of technologies, many created for the first time in the country, cited as a key differentiator on the defense/BTS side.
Examples of IP creation include space-based electronic warfare payloads, hyperspectral imaging payloads, and the major program for an airborne radar platform (UHM).
Management characterizes this IP depth as fairly differentiated from what many other companies in the space can offer.

subsections.label: Product portfolio complementarity
points: The new space debris tracking long-range, high-power radar order is described as complementary to the airborne UHM radar system, broadening the company's radar solutions product portfolio.

Planned capex for next fiscal year

subsections.label: Capacity and capability investments
points: Continued investment towards manufacturing capability expansion, including additional manufacturing lines, process automation initiatives, and systems integration capabilities to support future growth.

Capability enhancement and customer diversification remain key focus areas; completed more than 80 new product introductions during the year, supporting faster customer ramp-ups and new business wins.

subsections.label: FY27 capex plan
points: Planned capex for next fiscal year expected to be in the order of INR 40-45 crores, with roughly 50% or slightly higher directed towards R&D capabilities in the BTS segment.

subsections.label: Global positioning and export orientation
points: Company has long been an export-oriented business with quality, reliability, performance, and internal systems/processes maintained at global standards.

Big global customers are increasingly looking to indigenize production of electronics previously imported or sourced from other parts of the world, choosing India as a key destination — giving Centum a strong edge in winning these opportunities.
Increased global defense budgets and demand tailwinds noted in Europe and the Middle East, linked to ongoing wars and Make in India push.

subsections.label: Sourcing geography for PCB/CCL supply
points: Bare boards/PCBs are procured from multiple suppliers across different geographies depending on the segment being served — China for certain industrial applications, Europe for military applications, and Indian suppliers for some defense and space applications.

subsections.label: Copper-clad laminate (CCL) and PCB supply constraints
points: Supply chain bottlenecks are an emerging theme in the EMS business, not limited to CCL — this affects PCB lead times specifically.
Increase in lead times observed over the last couple of months for CCL/PCB supply; orders need to be placed further in advance to secure supply, but deliveries continue to meet requirements so far.
Situation needs to be monitored closely as it evolves over the course of the year.

subsections.label: Component category constraints (memory)
points: Increased lead times observed in specific component categories like memories, driven by demand pull from AI data center build-out.
Proactive mitigation measures are being taken by the supply chain team; challenges are still being worked on and monitored closely.

subsections.label: Middle East / West Asia war impact on supply chain
points: Certain short-term impacts were seen at the end of Q4 due to logistics delays as a result of the Middle East war.

No major supply disruptions are currently being seen directly as a result of the war; some opportunities are also being seen as a result of the ongoing conflict via customers/programs engaged in the region, which will continue to be monitored.

subsections.label: Customer/competitor dynamics in system integration
points: As the company moves up the value chain into system integration, it may in certain programs compete with, and in other programs collaborate with, its own customers (largely HAL, DRDO, and in certain cases BEL); management views this as a natural evolutionary process of the ecosystem, not unique to India, and seen worldwide.

subsections.label: Growth drivers and differentiation
points: Defense and aerospace remain a key focus area, driven by both the Make in India push and increased global demand/budgets in Europe and the Middle East due to ongoing wars.

On the EMS side, being a long-standing export-oriented business with global-standard quality/reliability/systems is cited as a differentiator that helps win business from global customers indigenizing their electronics production in India.

subsections.label: Overseas subsidiary restructuring
points: Decisive restructuring actions initiated last quarter with respect to underperforming overseas operations, aimed at realigning management focus and capital allocation towards the core India business; the restructuring process is progressing broadly in line with expectations.
Canada: operations were discontinued during Q4 FY26 and the wind-up process is under progress.

Europe: the French subsidiary entered the 'redressement judiciaire' (legal restructuring) process during March 2026; currently progressing through a court-supervised asset sale process; multiple preliminary bids already received, with final bids expected shortly.

Subject to court approval, the divestment process is expected to be substantially concluded by July 2026; the court process is expected to conclude by around June, with some parts of the business/people potentially taken over and the remainder moving into liquidation.

No net realization is expected from the sale of the European businesses; the balance sheet carries a significant amount of liabilities held for disposal, with liabilities held for disposal exceeding assets by over INR 100 crores, so no write-down is expected to hit the consolidated books.
Company will evaluate the point in time of cessation of control to determine consolidation requirements — deconsolidation could occur as early as Q1 FY27, or worst case Q2 FY27.

Financials relating to overseas subsidiaries have been classified under discontinued operations beginning this quarter, providing clearer visibility into the performance of the continuing core business.

These restructuring actions represent a continuation of the strategy outlined last quarter, intended to allow the company to move forward with significantly greater focus, operational clarity, and financial discipline.

subsections.label: Strategic focus and rationale
points: Overseas subsidiaries have historically been masking the strong performance of the standalone core India business, dragging down both revenue and margins over recent years; the Board took the decisive step to restructure and exit these businesses to focus on India ESDM platform opportunities.
Going forward, consolidated numbers are expected to carry less relevance from a P&L standpoint; focus should be on standalone performance.

subsections.label: Supply chain risk - copper clad laminate / PCB
points: Specialized CCL capacity is tightening globally, raising PCB lead times; increased severity over the past few months requires placing orders further in advance.

subsections.label: Supply chain risk - components
points: Component categories like memory chips are seeing longer lead times due to demand pull from AI data center build-out.

subsections.label: Geopolitical risk - Middle East/West Asia war
points: Short-term logistics delays occurred at the end of Q4 due to the Middle East war; no major long-term supply disruption seen so far, but the situation is being monitored as it evolves; further extension of the crisis could pose procurement challenges if it worsens.

subsections.label: Overseas subsidiary restructuring uncertainty
points: Precise financial impact for Q1 FY27 from discontinued operations cannot be forecast due to uncertainty over court process outcomes and timing of loss of control/deconsolidation.
May month is typically a slow month in France, adding to revenue slowdown risk in the affected businesses ahead of full resolution.
Liabilities held for disposal at the European subsidiaries exceed assets held for disposal by over INR 100 crores.

subsections.label: Margin/mix risk
points: EBITDA margin came in below the guided range in FY26 due to EMS product mix, an outcome management attributes to timing of program mix shifting into the current fiscal year.

subsections.label: Competitive/ecosystem risk
points: As Centum moves up the value chain into systems integration, it may end up competing against some of its own current customers (HAL, DRDO, BEL) on certain programs.

subsections.label: Growth and margin targets
points: Medium-term standalone revenue growth target maintained at 25-30% CAGR, expected to continue at the combined BTS+EMS level with both businesses growing at fairly similar rates, though certain years may see one segment grow faster than the other.

Combined-level EBITDA margin target of 13-15% maintained; this is expected to be achieved with the current year seeing better EMS margins as the previously delayed product mix gets executed, aided also by operating leverage as growth kicks in.
Management declined to give specific year-on-year or quarterly guidance on order booking/revenue, citing multi-year industry tailwinds as the basis for the medium-term target instead.

BTS and EMS mix over the medium term is expected to remain moderately similar to the current mix, perhaps shifting a little more towards BTS, without materially changing margin trajectory outside the 13-15% target range.

subsections.label: European subsidiary divestment timeline
points: Divestment of the French subsidiary expected to be substantially concluded by July 2026, subject to court approval; court process itself expected to conclude around June 2026.
No net cash realization expected from the European business sale process.
Deconsolidation of the European subsidiary anticipated by Q1 FY27 in the optimized scenario, or worst case by Q2 FY27.

subsections.label: Semiconductor segment target
points: Targeting to reach approximately USD 30 million in annual revenue from the semiconductor equipment customer segment over the next 2-3 years, progressing broadly in line with expectations, largely driven by the anchor customer.

Lead times for memory and other component categories have increased due to demand pull from AI data center build-out; proactive mitigation measures underway.

risk_register.note: Short-term logistics delays seen at end of Q4; no major long-term supply disruptions currently seen, but being monitored; some opportunities also arising from the conflict.

risk_register.risk: Competing with own customers as company moves up value chain
risk_register.note: As Centum takes on more systems integration work, it may in certain programs compete against customers such as HAL, DRDO, BEL, described as a natural ecosystem evolution seen worldwide.

themes.label: Overseas restructuring / discontinued operations
themes.note: Canada wind-up and French subsidiary court-supervised sale progressing, expected substantially concluded by July 2026, with no net realization expected and consolidated numbers deemed less relevant going forward.

themes.label: Standalone core business momentum
themes.note: Standalone revenue grew ~25% YoY in FY26 with margin improvement, driven by strong execution across BTS and EMS.

themes.label: Order book growth and visibility
themes.note: Standalone order book grew ~23% YoY to ~INR 1,645 crores, with BTS order book up 2.3x over 3 years (32% CAGR), providing strong multi-year visibility.

themes.label: Defense & Aerospace tailwinds
themes.note: Marquee HAL AESA radar (UHM) win worth over INR 570 crores and a second radar system order (~INR 30 crores) for space debris tracking reflect strong traction in defense/space programs.

themes.label: Margin mix (BTS vs EMS)
themes.note: BTS carries ~20% EBITDA margin vs EMS at 9-11%; FY26 combined margin fell slightly short of the 13-15% guided range due to EMS product mix timing.

themes.label: Supply chain constraints (CCL, memory)
themes.note: Global tightness in copper-clad laminate capacity and memory component lead times (driven partly by AI data center demand) is increasing PCB/component lead times, requiring earlier order placement.

themes.label: Export-oriented / India ESDM positioning
themes.note: Global customers indigenizing electronics production are choosing India, leveraging Centum's export-oriented quality standards, as a key growth driver alongside Make in India defense tailwinds.

key_takeaways: For the full year, our standalone business delivered revenue growth of approximately 25% year-on-year, while profitability also improved meaningfully, reflecting a stronger execution, better program mix and operating discipline.
We closed the year with a standalone order book of approximately INR 1,645 crores, representing a growth of around 23% year-on-year and providing strong visibility for the coming years.
In our build-to-specification business, FY26 was a particularly strong year with revenue growth of approximately 37% year-on-year.
The EMS business delivered revenue growth of approximately 21% year-on-year supported by strong customer ramp-ups, healthy order inflows, and continued diversification across strategic end markets.

One of the key milestones during the year was securing a marquee AESA radar program from HAL for the UHM platform... The overall opportunity size for this program exceeds INR 570 crores over the life cycle of the project.

In Canada, operations were discontinued during Q4 FY26 and the wind-up process is under progress. In Europe, the French subsidiary entered the redressement judiciaire or the legal restructuring process during March 2026, and we are currently progressing through a court-supervised asset sale process.

For the whole year, standalone revenue stood at a record INR 973 crores, reaching a strong growth of 25% year-on-year... during the financial year, the profitability was impacted by onetime exceptional item amounting to INR 203 crores relating to provisions and impairments in overseas subsidiaries.

Our balance sheet also remained healthy with total debt to equity maintained at a comfortable 0.28x and adjusted net working capital days improving to 142 days in FY26 from the previous year's 159 days... and the adjusted ROCE also improved significantly to 21.16% from 12.40%.
pressing_questions: Sir, we basically had some losses on our book historically. So will that basically -- will we have tax benefit for a few years going forward?
Sir, my final question with respect to the disinvestment of your foreign subsidiary. How much are we expecting as a quarterly loss from Q1 FY27?

Sir, if I squeeze a small question with respect to the HAL order. Sir, this is INR 570 crores order. So I just want to understand what will be the total addressable market? I mean, once you are done with the development part and if you go on to do the execution work for the HAL. How much will it…?

CEIGALL.about: Founded in 2002, Ceigall India Limited is an infrastructure construction company with expertise in specialized structural projects, including elevated roads, flyovers, bridges, railway overpasses, tunnels, highways, expressways, and runways.[1]

quarters.summary: Management reiterated FY27 guidance of minimum 15% revenue growth, EBITDA margin sustained at 11%-12.5%, and order inflow of ~INR6,000 crores (of which ~INR600 crores achieved in Q1 with rest expected during the year). Execution visibility remains strong with a robust and diversified order book of INR18,568 crores, continued HAM monetization/capital recycling strategy validated by the Malout-Abohar-Sadhuwali divestment, and continued but conservative expansion into renewable energy (Solar+BESS, T&D) and international markets.

subsections.label: Margin improvement drivers
points: Margins improved to ~13.5% this quarter versus guidance of 11%-12.5% for the full year; management attributed this to the start of 3 new projects during the quarter (2 Maharashtra solar projects MH1 and MH2, and the Indore-Ujjain HAM road project), plus another 3 projects about to start after receiving appointed dates in Q1 of July, which will improve numbers going forward.
Management confirmed they are still maintaining full-year EBITDA margin guidance of 11%-12.5% despite the stronger Q1 print.

subsections.label: Depreciation trend
points: Depreciation fell from ~INR13 crores in the previous quarter to INR9.5 crores in Q1 FY27; block value is constant and charged at the same rate, but the fall is due to certain assets sold in the previous financial year and the WDV depreciation method being applied.
This is expected to be the recurring run rate going forward, though it will increase if more assets are purchased during the year, otherwise it will keep reducing every year at similar levels.

subsections.label: Other income trend
points: Other income fell from INR15 crores in Q1 FY26 to INR9.5 crores in Q1 FY27 primarily due to loss of royalty income (no longer being charged) and reduced FD interest income, as IPO proceeds (on which interest was earlier earned) have been 100% utilized as of the last quarter of FY26.
Remaining ~INR320 crores of FDs in the books will continue generating interest income at prevailing rates; management expects other income to remain in line with the Q1 FY27 level.

subsections.label: ROE vs ROCE
points: Consolidated ROE declined sharply to 14% in FY26 even as ROCE remained comparatively stable around 19%-20% over the same period; management attributed this purely to the rise in equity share capital (to INR2,098 crores at end of FY26) post-IPO/QIP capital raises, increasing the base and reducing ROE, not a genuine decline in return on incremental capital deployed.

subsections.label: Commercial paper rationale
points: The company approved issuance of commercial papers worth ~INR100 crores on a private placement basis, to be carved out of existing working capital limits.
Rationale: better ROI on commercial papers (6.8%-7%) versus WCDL (7.5%-7.8%), reducing finance cost, and providing greater market visibility for the company.

subsections.label: Capex plan
points: Q1 FY27 capex of INR14 crores was primarily for a launcher purchased in Danapur.

From IPO proceeds, more than INR100 crores worth of machinery has already been paid for; further specialized machinery will be purchased only as and when required, as the company otherwise has ample machinery for project execution.
Full-year capex guidance stands at INR30-35 crores.

key_figures.label: Prior-year order inflow concentration in Q4

subsections.label: Order book diversification
points: Order book today spans EPC, HAM, DBFOT, and tariff-based renewable/transmission projects, and is much more diversified than a few years ago, now including metro rail, renewable energy, T&D, industrial infrastructure and other specialized infrastructure projects in addition to highways and expressways.
This diversification allows participation in multiple growth opportunities while reducing dependence on a single infrastructure segment.

subsections.label: Order inflow seasonality/timing
points: Order inflow guidance for FY27 is INR6,000 crores; ~INR600 crores achieved in Q1, with the rest expected to be achieved during the year.
Q1 order inflow was relatively modest; management indicated this is a timing issue, as order inflow normally comes in Q3 and Q4 — last year, Q4 alone contributed ~45% of the order book.

subsections.label: Execution visibility
points: 39 ongoing projects across multiple infrastructure segments provide healthy execution visibility over coming years.

Signed concession agreement for Ambala-Chandigarh-Zirakpur HAM; subsequent to quarter-end received appointed dates for VRK 11, VRK 12, and Indore-Ujjain Greenfield HAM projects, enabling commencement of execution.
Emerged as L1 bidder in a joint venture for a highway project in Arunachal, providing additional execution visibility and further strengthening the project pipeline.

subsections.label: Northern Ayodhya bypass execution slowdown
points: Execution fell to ~INR42 crores in Q1; management clarified there is no fundamental issue — progress is steady and milestones have been achieved ahead of time historically, but the last 1.5 months saw rain (monsoon), and payment can only be made once a milestone is achieved, which caused the reported dip.

subsections.label: VRK 11/12 and Southern Ludhiana-Bhatinda execution targets
points: Targeting at least 20%-25% execution for both VRK 11 and VRK 12 projects in FY27.
Southern Ayodhya execution is on track.

Southern Ludhiana-Bhatinda faces a land availability challenge (only 62% of land available), so targeted execution is lower at ~15% this year, versus an analyst's higher estimate of 25-30%; otherwise the project is doable.

subsections.label: Rewa solar project status
points: Three requirements for the project: PPA, land, and transmission. PPA has been signed and land is available; transmission line tenders have reportedly already been floated by the authority and are expected to conclude soon.
Once transmission is in place, the company is ready to start; described as an easy project because everything is built in one location.
Under PM-KUSUM, projects have already started in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh and are progressing well.

subsections.label: International expansion
points: Company is being very conservative in going global; has quoted a few tenders, including one in Romania and a few in Dubai.
Due to the current war situation, the company is being more conservative now, especially as its order book is robust in India; wants to take baby steps internationally.
Bidding for a few more international projects that could not be disclosed on the call; details will be shared once bids are made.
No meaningful revenue contribution expected from Ceigall Global PTE Limited (the UAE entity) disclosed for FY27/FY28; company wants to grow internationally but very conservatively.

subsections.label: HAM asset monetization / capital recycling
points: Successful monetization of the first HAM asset through divestment of the Malout-Abohar-Sadhuwali project during the quarter, described as an important milestone validating the company's capital recycling strategy built over the last few years.

Strategy: execute quality assets, create value through efficient project delivery, monetize mature assets at the right stage, and re-deploy capital into new opportunities to support future growth while maintaining a strong balance sheet and improving capital efficiency.

Management noted the divestment delivered IRR much higher than what was originally guided to investors, and indicated intent to continue selling completed projects going forward as has been done in the past.

subsections.label: Platform diversification strategy
points: Since IPO, the company has steadily diversified into niche sectors addressing the country's evolving energy requirements, including Solar+BESS and transmission & distribution, while maintaining steady growth in the highway sector.
This reflects a strategy of leveraging strong execution capabilities to build a presence in high-growth sectors and create sustainable, long-term value.
Company operates across almost 11 verticals, targeting a 25% IRR at the project level.

subsections.label: Seasonal/monsoon impact
points: Q1 is generally a seasonally softer quarter for the construction industry due to the onset of monsoon in several parts of the country, impacting near-term execution optics despite steady underlying progress.

subsections.label: Land acquisition challenge
points: Southern Ludhiana-Bhatinda HAM project faces a land availability challenge, with only 62% of required land currently available, constraining execution to ~15% in FY27 versus higher potential.

subsections.label: Geopolitical conservatism
points: Company is adopting a more conservative approach to international bidding (Romania, Dubai) because of the current war situation.

subsections.label: FY27 revenue and margin guidance
points: Revenue growth guidance raised from the earlier 10%-15% range to a minimum of 15% for FY27.
EBITDA margin guidance maintained at 11%-12.5% for FY27 despite a stronger-than-guided Q1 print of ~13.4%.

subsections.label: Order inflow guidance
points: Guided investors to INR6,000 crores order inflow for FY27; ~INR600 crores achieved in Q1, with the rest expected to be achieved during the year, consistent with the historical pattern of inflow concentration in Q3/Q4.

subsections.label: Equity commitment schedule for HAM and Solar
points: At IPO, equity put in was INR253 crores; as of date this has grown to INR692 crores (INR439 crores additional put in since IPO).
Balance equity commitment for FY27 is INR859 crores, split as INR310 crores for solar and INR550 crores for highway/HAM projects.
Balance equity commitment for FY28 is INR744 crores (tentative), split as ~INR296-300 crores for solar and INR444 crores for HAM.

The INR550 crores HAM equity commitment for FY27 is spread across all 11 HAM projects, incrementally, including Ludhiana-Bhatinda (~INR53 crores), Ayodhya bypass projects (~INR61 crores and ~INR53 crores), VRK 11 (~INR97 crores) and VRK 12 (~INR139 crores), Southern Ludhiana bypass (~INR38 crores), Indore-Ujjain (~INR60 crores), Bihar Sahebganj (~INR50 crores), and Zirakpur (~INR16 crores).

Sanction terms require 50% upfront liquidity infusion for VRK 11 and VRK 12, which is factored into the total commitment; equity for other ongoing projects like Northern Ayodhya, Southern Ayodhya, and Ludhiana-Bhatinda will be infused as progress is achieved.
Q1 FY27 cumulative equity invested in HAM and solar combined was INR23 crores.

subsections.label: Appointed date (AD) timelines for new HAM projects
points: Financial closure (FC) date for the Bihar HAM project expected next month (~Q3), and for the Punjab project close to November.
Once FC is completed, execution should start within a maximum of two to three months, as banks have already been tied up.
Appointed dates for both Bihar and Punjab projects are expected by Q4 FY27, with Bihar potentially as early as Q3.

subsections.label: Working capital outlook
points: Working capital intensity is expected to definitely improve in FY27, aided by relaxation given by the government, with further improvement expected in FY28.

subsections.label: Renewable margin outlook
points: Management has guided investors that renewable energy margins will be similar to traditional/road EPC margins, while trying to achieve better returns.

key_takeaways: One of the most important developments during the quarter was a successful monetization of the first hybrid annuity model, or HAM, asset through a divestment of Malout-Abohar-Sadhuwali project.
This is an important milestone for the company as it validates the capital recycling strategy that we have been working towards over the last few years.
During the quarter, we have signed a PPA for a Solar BESS at Morena, emerged as L1 for one of the standalone battery storage projects.

We have signed the concession agreement of Ambala-Chandigarh-Zirakpur HAM. Subsequent to the quarter end, we received the appointed dates of VRK 11, VRK 12, Indore-Ujjain Greenfield HAM project, enabling commencement of the execution.
We also emerged as L1 bidder in a joint venture for a highway project in Arunachal.
As on 30th June 2026, our order book stood at INR18,568 crores, providing strong multiple year revenue visibility.

Standalone revenue from operations for Q1 FY27 stood at INR901 crores as against INR818 crores in Q1 FY26, registering a 10.2% year-on-year growth. Standalone EBITDA margin improved to 13.4% from 11.4% in Q1 FY26.
Consolidated revenue from operations for Q1 FY27 stood at INR970 crores as against INR838 crores in the corresponding quarter of the previous year, registering a 15.7% growth year-on-year.
pressing_questions: Over the next 3 years, what will be the biggest driver of shareholder value? Like will it be revenue growth, margin expansion, asset monetization, or higher ROCE?

Consolidated ROE has fallen sharply to 14% in FY '26, even though ROCE has been comparatively more stable somewhere around 19%, 20% over the same period. Is this decline in ROE purely a function of the equity base expanding post-IPO and post-QIP type capital raises, or is there a genuine decline in return on the incremental capital deployed that we should be concerned about?

Could you elaborate on the near-term pipeline, what it looks like in the two international markets? And whether we should expect meaningful revenue contribution from the Ceigall Global PTE Limited or the UAE entity within FY '27 and FY '28?

quarters.summary: FY26 was a strong growth year for Ceigall, driven by consistent EPC execution and robust order inflows across highways, urban mobility and renewables; management guided FY27 revenue growth of minimum 15%, EBITDA margin of 11%-12.5%, order inflow guidance of minimum INR5,500 crores, with renewables contributing 20%-25% of revenue, and expressed confidence in strong order book, improving execution environment and expanding sectoral presence.

subsections.label: Q4 Performance Drivers
points: Fourth quarter has been a strong execution quarter, capitalizing on the strong construction window, enabling the company to deliver its best quarterly performance of the year.
Standalone and consolidated revenue growth in Q4 reflects the company's ability to scale operations effectively during peak construction seasons.

subsections.label: Margin Drivers
points: Last year the company started four HAM projects which have majorly contributed to PAT margins; increase in turnover is also one of the reasons for increase in overall PAT.
EBITDA from pure operations is in the range of 11% to 12.5%, which has been constantly maintained over the last 3 years.
Other income (bonus, royalty, FDR interest) is dependent on execution and on subcontractor contracts, and is uncertain/variable in nature, separate from operations margin.

FY25 and FY24 EBITDA margins included bonus and royalty income (e.g., INR20 crores royalty and bonus in FY25, and a bonus for Karnal-Pehowa in FY24), which management says should not be conflated with the operations-only margin.

Increased raw material costs are compensated by the department via an escalation circular, now linked to monthly basis instead of every 3 months, meaning higher costs are ultimately paid by the authority to the EPC contractor.

subsections.label: Balance Sheet & Capital Allocation
points: Company continued to maintain a disciplined de-leveraging posture.
Committed to optimizing capital structure using standalone debt and deploying HAM monetization proceeds towards both growth and de-leveraging.
Unencumbered cash and FDR figures were corrected during the call from originally stated INR266 crores (cash) and INR146 crores (FDR) to the actual INR166 crores (cash) and INR75 crores (FDR).

subsections.label: Working Capital / Receivables
points: Trade payables days rose sharply from 79 to 138 days because payments billed in March are released by the department in April, and payments to creditors are linked to receivables, hence timing lag.

Unbilled revenue days rose from 94 to 133 days primarily due to withdrawal of the Atmanirbhar notification in April '24, which had allowed monthly billing from April 1; billing reverted to milestone-linked cycles with billing cycles of ~10%/>INR100 crores given project sizes mostly above INR1,000 crores; this is expected to improve now that monthly billing has resumed under a new notification.

subsections.label: Equity Investment Plan
points: Next three years pending equity investment of INR1,937 crores, of which ~INR800 crores is for renewables and the rest for HAM roads.
Equity funding to be supported by strong cash flow, cash accruals, and proceeds from HAM asset monetization (Neo transactions).

subsections.label: Order Inflow & Diversification
points: Order inflow for FY26 significantly surpassed the annual guidance of INR5,000 crores.
During the year, the company entered five new verticals and expanded footprint into three new states, providing strong multi-year revenue visibility.
Q4 FY26 witnessed healthy order inflow across renewable and road sectors.
Management remains confident about the inflow pipeline going into FY27; sees no shortage of bidding opportunities across verticals.
LOA of Sahebganj–Areraj–Bettiah corridor is the single biggest project Ceigall has received till date.

Q4 FY26 was a strong quarter for order awards with meaningful inflow across renewable and power transmission segments, including multiple solar and battery energy storage projects, strengthening presence in the energy transition space, viewed as a strategic milestone reflecting successful diversification.

subsections.label: International & Domestic Bid Pipeline
points: Company has opened offices in Singapore and Dubai and appointed a CEO-International; expansion was slowed due to war-related uncertainty and is now proceeding since entering the renewable vertical (company now has ~11 verticals).
Key criteria for bidding overseas: EBITDA margins and IRR at concessional level.

Romania project is a highway, tunnel, and bridges combination, single 17 km project; company qualified alone among 12 bidders (others bid in consortium); if won, would represent ~65%-70% of current order book; management calls it a conservative bid given difficulty of winning L1, and notes cost is high in EU vs India due to currency/cost structure, not scope; bid opening delayed, bid validity nearing expiry.
Company is bidding on projects mostly above INR2,000 crores, positioned above competitors due to higher net worth as a listed company; expects strong flow of NHAI bids ahead.

subsections.label: NHAI Order Awarding Context
points: NHAI awarding earlier in the year was slowed pending cabinet approvals for several good projects; this quarter good tender volume is expected.
Company is not dependent on NHAI orders alone, given diversification into renewables (35% of FY26 order book inflow) and other verticals.

subsections.label: Order Book Segment Mix
points: Execution engine comprises 37 ongoing projects across various stages: 19 EPC projects, 10 HAM projects, 1 DBFOT project, and 7 renewable-based projects.
Order book diversification spans tunnels, railways, metros, transmission & distribution, and renewables, reducing dependence on any single segment.
Among HAM projects, only one is from MPRDC; the rest of the HAM projects are from NHAI.

subsections.label: Revenue Visibility from Unstarted Projects
points: Certain projects (e.g., Morena, and HAM projects awaiting 80% land clearance) will not start execution until preconditions like transmission line completion or land handover are met; minimum guided revenue visibility already factors this in, and more projects starting would improve numbers further.

subsections.label: Renewable & Power Transmission Progress
points: Received LOA for solar park projects in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh; Morena Solar Park project in Madhya Pradesh is now part of the order book.
PPA signed for Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh solar projects and execution has commenced.
Velgaon 400 KV substation in Maharashtra is progressing.

Solar Maharashtra project: lease done for a 50+ megawatt project already, with an additional 75+ megawatt expected this month; land development, fencing, and piling already started; good results expected in the next 3 months.
Madhya Pradesh solar project: land leasing in progress, expected to close within 10 days, after which execution will start.

T&D (transmission & distribution) project: construction already in progress; land already acquired (as land must be purchased, unlike solar where land is leased); site development and fencing started; orders placed for transmission and GIS equipment.

BESS Morena project: acquisition has not started; project is contingent on government providing land, transmission connectivity, and PPA; only LOA received so far, PPA yet to be signed, and transmission line tender not yet received — project will start only once transmission line work is completed.

subsections.label: HAM Monetization / Capital Recycling
points: FY26 has been a defining year for the company's capital recycling strategy.
Entered into a binding document for the Malout Abohar Sadhuwali asset with NEO Asset Management — the first transaction of its kind for Ceigall, validating the execute-monetize-recycle framework.
Non-binding offers signed for Bathinda-Dabwali and Jalbehra Shahbad assets, currently under due diligence.
Company has a clear pipeline of HAM asset monetization ahead.

Expected proceeds timing: Malout-Abohar-Sadhuwali proceeds expected in Q1 (this month/this quarter), Bathinda-Dabwali expected in Q2, and Jalbehra Shahbad expected in Q3 — providing a quarterly inflow cadence; proceeds will flow directly into standalone books.

subsections.label: Strategic Diversification
points: Meaningful progress made in renewable energy, power transmission, wind turbine generation, and industrial infrastructure during FY26.
Various awards secured in solar, BESS, and transmission projects, positioning the company to benefit from India's energy transition.
Delhi-Amritsar-Katra Expressway project successfully achieved COD during the year, an important project-lifecycle milestone.

subsections.label: International Expansion Strategy
points: Company opened offices in Singapore and Dubai and appointed a CEO-International as part of international foray strategy.
Expansion pace previously slowed due to geopolitical/war-related uncertainty; now proceeding given renewable-vertical entry providing ample opportunity.

subsections.label: Macro & Geopolitical Risks
points: Global macroeconomic environment continues to be challenging with geopolitical ambiguity, inflationary pressure, and supply chain uncertainties persisting.
War-related uncertainty had slowed the pace of international expansion (offices in Singapore/Dubai, international bidding).

subsections.label: Cost Inflation / Escalation
points: Increased raw material costs (e.g., iron ore cost inflation) are compensated by the government department via an escalation circular now linked to monthly basis (previously linked to 3 months), so cost increases are ultimately borne by the authority and paid to the EPC contractor.

subsections.label: Working Capital Risk
points: Trade payables days increased sharply (79 to 138 days) and unbilled revenue days increased sharply (94 to 133 days) during FY26, linked to billing/payment cycle timing and withdrawal of the Atmanirbhar monthly-billing notification in April '24; expected to improve following resumption of monthly billing under a new notification.

subsections.label: Project Execution Preconditions
points: Certain projects (Morena BESS, other HAM projects) cannot start execution until government provides land, transmission connectivity, and PPA, or until 80% land clearance is achieved for HAM projects — creating execution timing risk.

subsections.label: Bidding Norms Tightening
points: Tightening of technical and financial eligibility norms in the bidding process — higher net worth requirement, additional performance securities, and greater emphasis on PPP projects — continues to favour established players with proven execution capabilities, which management views as positive for Ceigall but reflects a broader industry shift in risk/entry barriers.

subsections.label: FY27 Outlook
points: Company guiding for minimum 15% revenue growth in FY27 with renewable sector contributing close to 20%-25% of total revenue, further building diversification.
EBITDA margins expected to sustain between 11% and 12.5%.
Order inflow guidance of minimum INR5,500 crores for FY27.
Management remains focused on strengthening execution, expanding order book, building a diversified asset-based portfolio with long-term revenue visibility, while maintaining financial discipline.
Confident about momentum into FY27 based on strong order book, improving execution environment, and expanding sectoral presence.

Management describes its guidance approach as conservative — historically guiding between 10%-15% revenue growth and consistently achieving/surpassing it; this time guidance is set at a minimum of 15%.

ADANIENSOL.about: AESL, part of the Adani portfolio, is a multidimensional organization with presence in various facets of the energy domain, namely power transmission, distribution, smart metering, and cooling solutions. AESL is India's largest private transmission company.[1]

quarters.summary: Q1 FY27 marks AESL's transition into a full-scale utility platform with all four businesses (transmission, distribution, smart metering, energy solutions) firing simultaneously; management expects consistent quarter-on-quarter growth going forward, continued execution/capital discipline, HVDC project pipeline (KPS-1 ~Dec'29, Rajasthan/Bhadla-Fatehpur early FY29), annual STU+central transmission bidding opportunity of ~INR1 lakh crore, and Energy Solutions platform (5 GW supply tie-up, 350 MW C&I, targeting 7.5 GW RTC market opportunity by 2031) to be scaled further with more long-term sales contracts expected soon.

The Q-o-Q decline visible in the presentation is due to reduced capex this year, as only 21 lakh meters were installed this quarter, affecting the accounting treatment where capex/construction is booked as both expense and revenue.
Management directed analysts to the press release, which provides operating EBITDA for smart meters based on the conventional method, versus the presentation's accounting-treatment-based numbers.

subsections.label: Business mix and diversification
points: AESL described as most diversified utility platform with transmission (28,000 ckm), leading urban distribution utilities serving Mundra and Mumbai, India's largest smart metering platform, and a rapidly scaling Energy Solutions platform.
Transmission and Energy Solutions saw significant growth in Q1; Distribution and Smart Metering growing at a stable pace.

subsections.label: IntelliSmart acquisition
points: Company is acquiring IntelliSmart; approval pending before CCI, after which formal takeover will occur.
Return profile of IntelliSmart expected to be similar to AESL's own smart meter profitability, benefiting from capex/opex reductions achieved via scale over the last two years.
Contract has provisions for natural volume growth beyond the combined 4.7 crore meter portfolio.
Cumulative smart meter installations of 1.34 crore (13.4 million) meters against an order book of 2.46 crore (24.6 million) meters; 21 lakh meters installed this quarter.

Remaining smart meter tender opportunity of 10-11 crore (100-120 million) meters over next 3-4 years, across balance states including Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, part of Andhra Pradesh, plus partial quantum in other states.

subsections.label: Energy Solutions business structure (C&I)
points: Two distinct parts of C&I business: (1) taking long-term positions on supply-side capacity and selling in the market (higher margin), and (2) providing energy solution services to consumers (e.g., cement, coal) managing their developed capacity (service-fee based, lower margin, but higher volume).
Objective is to tie up most capacity on both purchase and sales sides to minimize P&L variability, retaining only a small liquid/open position for optimization depending on market conditions.
Currently 350 MW of C&I customers tied up on sales side; remainder sold via exchange and bilateral contracts with distribution utilities.

Bilateral contract tenures range from 1 month to 13 months; pricing varies widely (bundled vs individual power) from INR3 to INR13-15/unit; 3,500 MWh of battery storage being leveraged to create differentiated products.
Battery storage contracted on long-term fixed-hire basis, similar to wind and solar contracting from Adani Green.

Timing mismatch exists between purchase-side tie-ups (advance) and consumption-side tie-ups, providing short-term trading opportunities and margin capture, but this is expected to narrow as long-term sale contracts are finalized.
Renewable/green supply capacity of 5,000 MW tied up, with ~4,000 MW sourced from sister company AVL and the balance from third parties.
Of the ~3,300 MU total volume, 400-500 million units currently sold under long-term contract basis.

subsections.label: Revenue-to-EBITDA mechanics of Energy Solutions
points: Business has two revenue streams: (1) simple services/trading business — high volume, lower margin (~INR0.03/unit initially cited); (2) supply stack and consumption stack — larger EBITDA generator based on ~5 GW of take-or-pay supply (internal + external generators) plus 3,500 MWh storage, sold to data centers, utilities, complex contracts, C&I, and group companies.

Margin is the spread between long-term sale price to utilities/consumers and long-term purchase cost from generators; last-mile transmission infra provided to consumers is booked as capex with associated margins.

Buy-side rates are fixed for longer tenure; sell-side has some open/short-term exposure (exchanges, bilateral) creating additional trading margin, though this is expected to be minimal on a long-term basis.

Quarter's results were aided by delayed monsoon driving higher demand and market prices versus last year; company acknowledges seasonal/quarter-to-quarter variability (summer vs monsoon/winter, irrigation demand spikes) will persist until purchase and sale positions are matched back-to-back.

subsections.label: Data center demand
points: Data center volume currently negligible (only one ~20-25 MW servicing contract), but significant long-term contracts from big customers/utilities expected going forward.
For every GW of IT load, ~1.5x consumption load is required; for 1.5 GW consumption load, 3.5x-4x renewable capacity needed if supplied from renewables, plus significant storage.

Customer green-mix preferences vary widely — from indifferent to very high green-percentage mandates; market is described as mature, with consumers understanding they must pay for storage costs if seeking high green share.
Data center demand in India is expected to be grid-connected (not off-grid), mostly on national grid.

subsections.label: Adani Green relationship
points: AGEL does not sell directly to data centers; it creates capacity and ties up long-term with utilities (SECI), third parties, and now with AESL as a customer.
AESL considered the primary solutioning entity for group-level energy solutions; virtually all C&I exposure expected to run through Energy Solutions entity, not directly through AGEL.

Regarding Maharashtra's ~2.5 GW round-the-clock power contract (won by Adani Power involving Adani Green sourcing), AESL confirmed it will be a party to that contract even though the PPA/LOI is with Adani Power; AESL expected to be a major participant.

subsections.label: Market opportunity sizing (Energy Solutions)
points: Company disclosed market opportunity of 7.5 GW+ by 2031 that it believes it can encash, driven by data center pipeline (disclosed separately by AEL), distribution companies seeking complex RTC solutions instead of separate solar/wind/storage procurement, and a burgeoning C&I space estimated at ~50 GW+ market by 2030-31.

7.5 GW figure represents RTC (round-the-clock) market opportunity, not GWh; management clarified this should not be interpreted as a simple multiplication (7.5 GW x 24 x 365) since it will be a mix of different consumer stacks.

subsections.label: State transmission utility (STU) activity
points: Maharashtra is very active on STU projects currently; Rajasthan and UP have also started STU activity.

Over the last 4-5 years significant interstate transmission lines were built to deliver power to states; now states must augment intra-state transmission capacity to deliver power to end consumers, driving STU opportunity.

subsections.label: Urban/city center transmission demand
points: Cities are witnessing massive demand growth and will need to augment transmission capacity around city centers where overhead lines cannot be used, creating opportunity for HVDC-type solutions similar to the Mumbai HVDC project commissioned last year, which helped the region during this summer.

subsections.label: IntelliSmart acquisition
points: Acquisition of IntelliSmart is pending CCI approval; formal takeover to follow once approvals are in place.
Combined AESL + IntelliSmart smart meter portfolio expected to reach 4.7 crore (47 million) meters, with contract provisions for further natural volume growth.

subsections.label: Group inter-company solutioning
points: AESL positioned as the group's neutral solutioning entity for energy solutions across group companies (e.g., Adani Green, Adani Power) and third parties.

subsections.label: Right-of-way (ROW) challenges
points: ROW challenges remain present on the ground and are an industry-wide issue.
Company manages this by taking ROW decisions at ground level rather than fully depending on state machinery/administration support, working in parallel to clear ROW.
Most projects are concentrated in regions where AESL already has strong presence, allowing better anticipation of ground-level challenges and advance preparation.

subsections.label: Parallel distribution license regulatory delay
points: Parallel licenses applied for remain pending with the commission; no movement currently.
Maharashtra government has reportedly advised the commission to wait until the central government's tariff policy amendment is finalized before proceeding.

subsections.label: Revenue/margin variability in Energy Solutions
points: Quarter-to-quarter and year-to-year variability expected in Energy Solutions revenue/margins due to open positions being exposed to seasonal market price swings (summer vs monsoon/winter, irrigation demand spikes), and this quarter benefited from a delayed monsoon driving higher demand and prices versus last year.
Company's strategy is to minimize this variability by closing long-term positions on both purchase and sales sides without much time lag.

subsections.label: Transmission and HVDC pipeline outlook
points: Every year an opportunity of about INR1 lakh crore of bidding (combining central and state projects) is expected.
Lot of opportunity expected to arise from various STU projects going forward given Maharashtra, Rajasthan, UP activity.
Company has maintained ~25% market share historically and will continue at that level, translating to roughly INR20,000-25,000 crores of capex addition every year.

Two HVDC projects currently — one under bidding, one going to bidding shortly; HVDC volumes expected to continue given renewables need to be delivered over long distances, and now also due to load-center (city) demand for HVDC given overhead line constraints in dense urban areas.
KPS-1 HVDC project expected to commission by December 2029; Rajasthan (Bhadla-Fatehpur) HVDC project expected to commission at the beginning of 2029.

subsections.label: Energy Solutions platform outlook
points: Company aims to convert most Energy Solutions revenue into annuity-type long-term revenue with a small open position retained for optimization based on market conditions.
Most of the current 3,300-odd MU volume is expected to get absorbed into long-term sale contracts soon, following the long-term purchase-side tie-up already done.
Long-term contracts covering most of the capacity signed on the purchase side are at a very advanced stage, reducing the current timing gap between purchase tie-ups and sales.
Significant volume growth expected from the data center segment over time, though currently negligible.
Company plans a detailed C&I business presentation after completing next financial year, at the call around May next year (per context carried from prior quarter).

guidance_ledger.statement: We expect that every year, we would have an opportunity of about INR1 lakh crores bidding combining minimum central as well as various state projects.
We have been doing a market share of about 25%, and we will at least continue that part from our side.
Roughly about INR20,000 crores, INR25,000 crores of capex addition every year.
STU, I think annually, the volume would be about to start with about INR20,000 crores, INR25,000 crores projects. That is the least that I expect from STU side.
This KPS HVDC would be somewhere in FY29, around December '29.
Rajasthan would be at the beginning of '29.
We believe that HVDC volumes will continue... we see demand of HVDC project coming from load center side as well.
The market opportunity we believe we'll be able to encash is 7.5 gigawatt plus by 2031.
The C&I space... is a burgeoning space with close to 50 gigawatt plus market by 2030, '31.

Balanced portfolio is about 10 crores to 11 crores or 100 million to 120 million. The remaining states are Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, a part of Andhra, and there are a few states where part quantum is also left out.

Most of the tied-up capacity on a purchase side has also tied up on our sales side... we will endeavour to do that, then most of the capacity is back to back locked-up and we don't create much of the volatility in our numbers.
As far as return profile of IntelliSmart is concerned, more or less, it will be on a similar line that we have... profitability of those numbers would be very similar to what we have for AESL.
We will have a detailed presentation on C&I once we complete next financial year and have this call again somewhere in May next year.
We will have about INR22,000 crores of capex next year (transmission ~15,500, distribution ~2,350, smart metering ~3,900), so between 21,000 to 22,000.
FY28 capex will be around 23,000, of which transmission ~20,000, distribution ~2,000, smart metering ~1,500 (order book only, excludes additional orders); overall between 22,000 to 25,000.
Capitalization number in FY27 would be about 21,000-22,000 crores.
In FY28, capitalization could be about 13,000 crores; thereafter capitalization will improve in transmission as HVDC projects start getting commissioned from FY29.
We plan to do transmission capex of about INR15,000-16,000 crores with INR8,000 crores of WIP, and plan to capitalize about INR14,500-15,000 crores out of this block.
We will continue to maintain that leverage in the ratio of around 4.5x to 4.7x.
Next year probably we'll be doing about minimum about 1 crore meters.

guidance_ledger.metric: New transmission opportunity value from market share
guidance_ledger.statement: Maintaining 25-30% market share converts to INR40,000-50,000-odd crores of new opportunity in transmission itself.
12-month pipeline would be about INR80,000 crores to INR1 lakh crores, depending on how bidding process proceeds; we expect bids of that magnitude will get finalized.

guidance_ledger.metric: EBITDA (revenue run-rate add from FY26 commissioning)
guidance_ledger.statement: This year's capitalization for transmission will add another INR1,600 crores of EBITDA (revenue) on a fully run-rate basis from projects commissioned this financial year.
Given the capitalization plan, we expect consolidated EBITDA (operating profit) could be around INR11,500 crores next year.
Once all existing under-construction transmission projects get completed with locked-in tariffs, transmission EBITDA will be 3x from existing transmission EBITDA trajectory.
Distribution business currently has INR2,500 crores EBITDA, which will translate to close to INR3,000-3,200 crores.
Smart meter business will start generating INR2,400 crores to INR3,000-odd crores of EBITDA trajectory once the entire smart meter portfolio is realized.
Currently the number is INR1,300-odd crores which is the full year tariff from the Mumbai HVDC project, which we will start accruing from next financial year.
Evaluation at MERC and STU level is ongoing; management cannot commit currently whether it will start working from this fiscal.

Management stated it will separately walk through the entire borrowing program for next 4-5 years; two things certain: leverage will not reach 4.5x-4.6x ceiling, and INR77,000 crores of capex is locked in over 4 years.

risk_register.note: Industry-specific issue that remains on the ground; managed via ground-level decisions and parallel working rather than full dependence on state machinery, plus concentration of projects in regions of existing presence aids preparedness.
Matter pending with the commission with no movement; Maharashtra government reportedly advised commission to wait for central government's tariff policy amendment before proceeding.

risk_register.risk: Seasonal/quarterly variability in Energy Solutions margins
risk_register.note: Open positions expose P&L to seasonal price/demand swings (summer vs monsoon/winter, irrigation spikes); this quarter's strong result partly aided by delayed monsoon raising demand and market prices versus last year; company aims to reduce this via back-to-back long-term contracting.
Not discussed this quarter (was raised in prior quarter regarding MERC/STU evaluation).

risk_register.risk: ROW (Right of Way) challenges from landowners/general public despite compensation orders
risk_register.note: Despite collector compensation orders as per government policy, some individuals/groups still create obstruction; police protection increasingly used; governments are systematically working to resolve this.

risk_register.risk: Regulatory/policy debate on transmission cost vs. battery storage (BESS)
risk_register.note: Ongoing policy-level debate on whether to push co-located BESS to optimize transmission cost; could affect quantum of future transmission capacity needed, though not expected to eliminate the need.

risk_register.risk: Compensation policy revision (change in law) risk
risk_register.note: Any government revision to compensation could be treated as change in law pass-through; company neutral to it but doesn't expect significant near-term revision.

risk_register.risk: China equipment sourcing restriction under TBCB
risk_register.note: Per TBCB bid conditions cannot use Chinese-manufactured equipment; no import from China envisaged, so not seen as a constraint.

risk_register.risk: Sector-wide equipment supply constraints (GIS, transformers, reactors, HVDC components)
risk_register.note: New domestic capacity being added by OEMs (e.g., GE, Hitachi) investing in India; supply-related issues easing out; no AESL project delayed due to equipment delivery delay owing to strategic procurement.
Evaluation still ongoing at MERC and STU level; management cannot commit on commissioning timing.

risk_register.risk: Land possession delay for Khavda-Olpad HVDC (Olpad)
risk_register.note: Olpad land possession from Power Grid expected in about a month; construction cannot start at Olpad until possession secured.

themes.label: C&I business emergence
themes.note: Energy Solutions platform transitioned from incubation to full-scale business with 5 GW supply tie-up, 350 MW C&I customers, and INR590 crores EBIT in Q1.

themes.label: Smart metering scale-up
themes.note: 1.34 crore meters installed cumulatively against 2.46 crore order book; IntelliSmart acquisition to expand combined portfolio to 4.7 crore meters.

themes.label: HVDC project execution
themes.note: KPS-1 HVDC targeted for December 2029 and Rajasthan (Bhadla-Fatehpur) HVDC for early 2029; HVDC volumes expected to continue driven by renewable delivery and city-center load demand.

themes.label: Capex ramp-up
themes.note: Quarterly capex of ~INR3,500 crores delivered; annual capex addition of INR20,000-25,000 crores expected from market share-linked transmission opportunity plus similar STU volume.

themes.label: ROW & land acquisition challenges
themes.note: ROW challenges remain an industry-wide issue but are managed via ground-level parallel execution and project concentration in familiar regions.

themes.label: Leverage & capital discipline
themes.note: Management reiterated focus on execution and capital discipline even during high-growth period to reduce cost of capital and improve credit quality.

themes.label: Market opportunity sizing
themes.note: Energy Solutions targeting 7.5 GW+ RTC market opportunity by 2031, within a broader ~50 GW+ C&I market by 2030-31.

key_takeaways: AESL has transitioned into a full-scale utility platform in Q1 FY27, with all 4 business verticals (transmission, distribution, smart metering, energy solutions) now operating at full scale.
Delivered quarterly capex of close to INR3,500 crores.

Completed smart meter installation of 1.34 crore (13.4 million) meters cumulatively against an order book of 2.46 crore (24.6 million); combined with IntelliSmart acquisition, portfolio will reach ~4.7 crore (47 million) meters.
Energy Solutions platform has tied up about 5,000 MW of green energy supply capacity and about 350 MW of C&I customers, with long-term contracts expected shortly.
Energy Solutions EBIT of INR590 crores in Q1, with ~INR570 crores from long-term contracted positions and the balance from power trading/services.
Significant growth seen in transmission and energy solutions in Q1; distribution and smart metering growing at a stable pace.
Market opportunity for the Energy Solutions RTC business targeted at 7.5 GW+ by 2031, with the C&I space seen as a ~50 GW+ market by 2030-31.
Right-of-way challenges remain an industry issue but are being managed through ground-level, parallel execution approaches.
pressing_questions: Nikhil Nigania (Bernstein) asked whether AESL is competing with Adani Green to sell to the same customers (e.g., data centers), and sought clarification on AESL's role versus Adani Power in the Maharashtra ~2.5 GW round-the-clock power contract with MSEDCL — management said the PPA/LOI was issued to Adani Power but AESL will be a major participant; Nigania indicated he would take further color offline.

Mahesh Patil (ICICI Securities) sought status update on the parallel distribution licenses applied for; management indicated the matter remains pending with the commission with no movement, awaiting central government tariff policy amendment.

quarters.summary: Management guided to a sharp capex and EBITDA ramp-up over FY27-FY28, driven by transmission (HVDC projects, RAB growth), continued smart metering scale-up, and an emerging C&I business, while maintaining leverage discipline (4.5x-4.7x net leverage) and improving credit ratings. Consolidated transmission EBITDA is expected to roughly 3x over the next 36-40 months as the INR72,000 crore under-construction pipeline gets commissioned, with distribution EBITDA rising to ~INR3,000-3,200 crores and smart meter EBITDA to ~INR2,400-3,000 crores.

subsections.label: Credit rating & interest cost
points: Most assets are now rated AAA+ or AAA, a significant improvement even while capex is being scaled up significantly.
Interest cost is going down as a consequence of improved credit ratings, translating into incremental returns for shareholders.
Refinanced a $500 million bond via Apollo, a U.S. insurance investor, demonstrating financial and operational strength even amid challenging geopolitical conditions.

subsections.label: Cash flow and leverage
points: Assets are generally financed in a 70:30 debt:equity ratio; only the equity portion is funded via internal accruals, balance through debt.
Management stated full comfort in meeting all existing capex requirements across transmission, smart meter and distribution despite negative free cash flow.

Net leverage guidance maintained at 4.5x to 4.7x; management stated that leverage is not expected to reach that ceiling despite capex ramp-up, and locked-in capex of INR77,000 crores over 4 years is already committed.
CFO to walk through the entire borrowing program for next 4-5 years separately with an analyst offline.

subsections.label: Growth trajectory in operating profit
points: Operating profit was range-bound between INR4,000-4,500 crores annually for FY19-20 through FY22-23.
A step-up occurred in subsequent years: ~INR6,000 crores, then INR7,000 crores in FY25, and about INR8,000 crores in FY26.
Growth attributed to capex-based businesses (transmission, distribution, smart metering) where profitability is added upon capitalization; C&I is the exception as a non-capex-based growth driver.
Management indicated at least 3x the current transmission EBITDA trajectory once all locked-in transmission projects (with locked-in tariffs) are commissioned over the next 36-40 months.
No FY26 revenue was yet added from Mumbai HVDC in the current financial year’s numbers; full-year impact will begin flowing through in FY27.

subsections.label: CWIP/SCA accounting clarification
points: Accounting treatment has changed: SCA (service concession assets) and CWIP are tracked separately from normal conventional assets.
Once an asset is commissioned it becomes part of contracted assets; while under construction it remains part of SCA assets; both fall under non-financial assets.

Reconciliation between FY26 CWIP (~INR8,000 crores) and next year's capitalization guidance (~INR15,000 crores in transmission) explained by heavy equipment (transformers, substations) typically procured toward the fag end of a project and capitalized immediately without passing through CWIP — as occurred with the HVDC project.

subsections.label: Transmission
points: Improved market share to almost 29% of projects that went into bidding this year, up from historical 20-25%.
Will maintain market share discipline between 25% and 30%, translating to INR40,000-50,000-odd crores of new opportunity in transmission itself.
Fatehpur-Bhadla HVDC: construction has begun at both substation and line level; no significant ROW challenges faced; significant capex expected to start from the current year (FY27/28).

Khavda-Olpad HVDC: all contracts finalized; construction not yet started; Khavda land already under possession with preparative work started, environment/forest clearance proposals submitted, and ROW permission applications begun; Olpad land possession expected from Power Grid in about a month; construction to start at both sites once possession is secured.

HVDC Pole 2 (Mumbai): evaluation ongoing at MERC and STU level; management believes Mumbai will require additional transmission capacity but cannot commit on timing given the project is still under evaluation.
Mumbai HVDC commissioned fully (100%) in FY26, on a single commissioning date of 15th March; project cost was INR7,000 crores, with no additional cost or tariff being claimed.

subsections.label: Distribution (AEML)
points: AEML continues to harden assets, adding INR1,500-2,000 crores of capex every year while keeping tariffs largely constant.
Efficiency gains are transferred to investors for incremental returns while customer tariffs remain the same and service levels improve — described as a win-win.
AEML rated the number one distribution company in the country for the last 4 years.
Distribution EBIT was down about 14% in FY26 even though volumes were up and losses improved (context provided by analyst, unconfirmed by management with a specific driver).

subsections.label: Smart Metering
points: Deployment surpassed the FY26 target of 70 lakh meters, installing about 83 lakh meters on the ground — described as potentially the highest by any operator, not only in India but globally.
Smart metering is viewed as a perpetual opportunity beyond the current contractual concession period, given industry structure, with future extension or new bidding opportunities expected.
Two ways to gain additional concessions: existing contract swelling (already grown from 2.3 crore to 2.46 crore) and the balance market opportunity of 9-10 crore meters.

Pending state opportunities include Karnataka, Tamil Nadu (already approved), Telangana (whole state), Andhra Pradesh (part), Gujarat (part), and MP (part), awaiting RDSS approval from the central government; states likely to bid once respective elections are over.

subsections.label: C&I (Commercial & Industrial)
points: C&I identified as a major growth driver for the next year alongside transmission and smart metering.

About 5,000 MW of renewable capacity contracted, with dozens of third-party consumers aggregating about 1,400 MW (1.54 GW) already tied to customers; remaining capacity to be matched to customers going forward.

Even if hyperscalers/data centers become deemed distribution licensees, they will still need to source power with peculiar requirements — positioning AESL (with solar, wind and BESS capacity) to offer power infra and supply-side solutions; the end customer relationship remains unchanged.

Margins on the 1.5 GW tied-up capacity are in excess of INR0.50 per unit; remaining capacity currently operates on the merchant market, subject to day-to-day market conditions; margin certainty will increase once contracts (medium/long term) are finalized.
Detailed C&I presentation planned for the next earnings call in May next year, once FY27 is complete.

subsections.label: District cooling (emerging business)
points: District cooling business being incubated, expected to start picking up in 4-5 years' time.
A concession secured for a cluster development project in Chennai.

Management is actively engaging with various state governments to tie up opportunities at an early stage as large new development clusters emerge across the country; currently not sizable but expected to be significant going forward.

subsections.label: Capex scale-up and RAB growth
points: AEML consolidated capex across transmission, distribution and smart metering has increased significantly, nearing INR15,000 crores.

Management guided to continue improving capex and reach about INR20 (thousand) crores of capex this year (as stated verbatim), while also improving credit ratings — usually a challenging combination during rapid capex scale-up.

RAB continues to grow: AEML RAB has roughly doubled from INR5,400 crores to over INR10,500 crores; transmission RAB-based assets have grown by INR7,000 crores from the HVDC addition to a prior base of INR10,000 crores.
Management will continue to ensure the proportion of regulatory asset base (RAB) versus competitive asset base remains healthy, driving growth and cash generation.

subsections.label: HVDC project commissioning cadence and timeline
points: HVDC projects (part of the transmission capex pipeline) are expected to start getting commissioned from FY29, after which capitalization in transmission will improve further.
Mumbai HVDC was commissioned completely (100%) in the last month of FY26, on a single date, 15th March, at a project cost of INR7,000 crores.

subsections.label: Equipment sourcing / China exposure
points: Per TBCB bid conditions, the company cannot use any equipment manufactured in China; no import from China is envisaged for TBCB projects, including via EPC suppliers/equipment contractors.

Sector-wide supply-side challenges (GIS, transformers, reactors) are easing out, with new domestic capacity being added; OEMs (e.g., GE, Hitachi) have invested in India in manufacturing capacities, including for HVDC components.

Company avoided equipment delivery delays even in the difficult period due to strategic procurement practices and ordering equipment well in advance; no AESL project has been delayed due to equipment delivery delay.
